There is no basis for restricting the increase to an increase in obedience; rather, the apparent meaning of the verse is generality, as the making of the increase a recompense for gratitude indicates. So whoever thanks Allah for what He has provided for him, Allah will expand his provision; whoever thanks Allah for the obedience He has enabled him to perform, He will increase him in obedience; and whoever thanks Him for the health He has bestowed on him, Allah will increase him in health, and similar.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Mas'ud that he used to recite ﴿And those after them, none knows them except Allah﴾ and would say: "The genealogists have lied."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Amr ibn Maymun a similar report.

Ibn al-Dara'is related from Abu Mijlaz, who said: A man said to Ali ibn Abi Talib: "I am the most knowledgeable of people in genealogy." He said: "You are not [knowledgeable] of people's genealogies." He said: "Yes, I am." Ali said to him: "Tell me about His saying: ﴿And 'Ad and Thamud and the companions of the Rass, and many generations between them﴾ [al-Furqan: 38]." He said: "I trace the genealogy of that multitude." He said: "Tell me about His saying: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, none knows them except Allah﴾." So he fell silent.

Abu Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "We have not found anyone who knows what lies beyond Ma'add ibn Adnan."

Abu Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Between Adnan and Isma'il there are thirty fathers who are not known."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying: ﴿But they put their hands to their mouths﴾, that he said: "When they heard the Book of Allah they marvelled and returned their hands to their mouths, ﴿and said: Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent, and indeed we are in grave doubt about that to which you invite us﴾" — meaning: "We do not believe you in what you have brought, for we have strong doubt concerning it."

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Abu Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from Ibn Mas'ud: "﴿But they put their hands to their mouths﴾" — he said: "They bit down on them."

And in another wording: "On their fingertips, out of rage at their messengers."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verses 6–12 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "And when Moses said" — the adverbial clause (al-zarf) is connected to an implied verb, which is "remember": i.e., remember the time when Moses said. And "when He delivered you" (idh anjakum) is connected to "remember" (udhkuru): i.e., remember His favour upon you at the time of His delivering you from the people of Pharaoh; or it is connected to "favour" (al-ni'mah), or to the complement of "upon you" (alaykum), meaning: settled upon you at the time of His delivering you. It is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "favour," where by "favour" is meant bounty or gift. "They afflict you with the evil of torment" — i.e., they desire you; it is said: sama-hu zulman, meaning he inflicted injustice upon him. The root of al-sawm is going forth in pursuit of a thing. "The evil of torment" is a verbal noun of sa'a, ya'su'u, and what is intended is the evil torment: their enslaving them and employing them in arduous labour. "They slaughter your sons" is conjoined to "they afflict you with the evil of torment," even though slaughter is of the same kind as evil torment, in order to take it out of the category of ordinary torment, so that it appears as though it were a different kind, because of its severity. With the conjunction omitted, as in the other verse, the slaughter is an explanation of "the evil of torment." "And they spare your women" — i.e., they leave them alive, to humiliate and degrade them. "And in that," referring to what was mentioned of their deeds, "is a great trial from your Lord" — i.e., a test for you. The explanation of this verse has already been given fully in Surat al-Baqarah.

"And when your Lord proclaimed" — "proclaimed" (ta'adhdhana) is in the sense of "announced" (adhina), as al-Farra' said.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "There must be in tafa'ala an added meaning not present in af'ala, as if it were said: 'And when your Lord announced, a clear announcement from which doubts are removed and suspicions dispelled.'"

The meaning: "And when your Lord proclaimed, and said, 'If you give thanks...'" Or "proclaimed" is treated as "said," since it is a kind of speech. This is from the words of Moses to his people, and it is conjoined to "the favour of God." That is: remember the favour of God upon you, and remember when your Lord proclaimed. It is said that it is conjoined to his saying "when He delivered you," i.e., remember the favour of God, Exalted, in these two times, for this proclamation is also a favour. It is also said that it is from the words of God, Glorified is He, i.e., "And remember, O Muhammad, when your Lord proclaimed."

Ibn Mas'ud recited "And when your Lord said," and the meaning is the same, as has already been mentioned. The lam in "If you give thanks" is the lam that prepares for the oath. His saying "I will surely increase you" fills the place of the answers of both the condition and the oath. Likewise the lam in "And if you are ungrateful" and his saying "Indeed My punishment is severe" fills the place of both answers as well. The meaning: If you give thanks for My favour upon you with what has been mentioned, I will surely increase you in favour upon favour, as a bounty from Me. It is also said: I will surely increase you in obedience to Me; it is also said: I will surely increase you in reward. The first is more apparent, so thanks is the cause of increase. "And if you are ungrateful, denying that and rejecting it, indeed My punishment is severe," so some of it must befall you, as it befalls. It is also said that the answer is omitted, i.e., "And if you are ungrateful, I will surely punish you," and what is mentioned is the reason for the omitted answer.

"And Moses said: If you disbelieve, you and all who are on the earth together" — i.e., if you disbelieve His favour, Exalted is He, you and all creation, and do not give thanks for it, then indeed God, Glorified is He, is Free of need of your gratitude; He does not need it, and no deficiency reaches Him by that. "Praiseworthy" — i.e., deserving of praise in Himself, because of the abundance of His favour, even if you do not thank Him, or others among the angels praise Him.

"Has there not come to you the report of those before you?" It is possible that this is an address from Moses to his people, and then it falls under reminding them of the Days of God. It is also possible that it is from the speech of God, Glorified is He, initially addressing the people of Moses and reminding them of the earlier generations, their reports, and the coming of God's messengers to them. It is also possible that it is an initial address from God, Glorified is He, to the people of Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, warning them against opposing him. Al-naba' is the report, and its plural is al-anba', and from it is the poet's saying:

"Did there not come to you, while the reports spread, what the she-camel of the sons of Ziyad suffered?"

"And the people of Noah" is a substitute for the relative pronoun, or an explanatory apposition. "And 'Ad and Thamud and those after them" — i.e., after these mentioned, "no one knows them but God," i.e., no one counts their number or encompasses them in knowledge except God, Glorified is He. The relative pronoun is the subject and its predicate is "no one knows them but God," and the clause is parenthetical. Or the relative pronoun is conjoined to what precedes it, and "no one knows them but God" is a parenthetical insertion. The absence of knowledge from other than God is either referring to their attributes, conditions, characters, and the spans of their lives, meaning these matters are known to God alone and to no other; or it refers to their essences, meaning no one knows the essences of those who came after them except God, Glorified is He.

The clause "their messengers came to them with clear proofs" is resumptive, explaining the report mentioned in "Has there not come to you the report of those before you?" That is, the messengers came to them with manifest miracles and clear laws. "But they put their hands to their mouths" — i.e., they placed the hands of their own selves to their mouths, biting them in rage at what the messengers brought, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "They bite their fingertips out of rage" (Al 'Imran 119), because the messengers came to them with the folly of their minds and the reviling of their idols. It is also said that the meaning is that they pointed with their fingers to their mouths when the messengers came to them with clear proofs, i.e., "Be silent, and leave what you have brought," rejecting them and refuting their words. It is also said that the meaning is that they pointed to themselves and to what issues from them of speech, which is their saying, "Indeed we deny what you have been sent with," i.e., you have no answer to us other than what we have said to you with these tongues of ours. It is also said that they placed their hands on their mouths in mockery and wonder, as one does when laughter overcomes him and he places his hand on his mouth. It is also said that the meaning is: they answered the messengers' words and disbelieved them with their mouths, so the first pronoun refers to the messengers and the second to the disbelievers. It is also said that they put their hands into the mouths of the messengers in rejection of their words, so on this view the first pronoun refers to the disbelievers and the second to the messengers. It is also said the meaning is: they gestured to the messengers to be silent. It is also said they took the hands of the messengers and placed them over the messengers' mouths to silence them and cut off their speech. It is also said that "hands" here means blessings, i.e., they rejected the messengers' blessings with their mouths, meaning by speech and denial; and by blessings here is meant what was brought to them of laws.

Abu 'Ubaydah said, and he spoke well: it is a figure of speech, meaning they did not believe and did not respond. The Arabs say of a man who refrains from answering and falls silent: "He has put his hand in his mouth." Al-Akhfash said likewise. Al-Qutaybi objected to this, saying: "No one has been heard among the Arabs saying 'He returned his hand into his mouth' when he abandons what he was commanded; rather the meaning is 'they bit the hands out of rage and anger,'" as in the poet's saying:

"They would bite in their mouths the anger of the envious, until they bite my palms."

This is the view we put forward above all these sayings, and from it is the poet's saying:

"Had Salma seen my emaciation, she would have bitten the tips of her hand from grief."

And this is the closest of the interpretations to the verse, if what Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash mentioned is not authentically reported from the Arabs.

If what they mentioned is sound, then interpreting the verse accordingly is closer. "And they said: Indeed we deny what you have been sent with" — i.e., the disbelievers said to the messengers: "Indeed we deny what you have been sent with of clear proofs, according to your claim." "And indeed we are in grave doubt about what you call us to" — i.e., in great doubt concerning what you call us to, of belief in God alone and abandoning all else, "disquieting" — i.e., causing unease. It is said: arabtuhu, when you do an act that causes suspicion and doubt. Al-rayb is the restlessness of the soul and its lack of tranquillity.

It has been said: how did they openly declare disbelief and then their affair was based on doubt? It is answered that they meant: "We are disbelievers in your messengership; and if we descend from this position, then at least we doubt the soundness of your prophethood." With the utmost doubt there is no hope of their acknowledging your prophethood.

The clause "Their messengers said: Is there doubt about God?" is resumptive, answering an implied question, as though it were said: "What did the messengers say to them?" The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, i.e., is there doubt concerning His oneness, Glorified is He, and it is in the utmost clarity and manifestness? Then the messengers, after denying it to the disbelievers, mentioned the evidences that confirm this denial, showing that there is no doubt about His existence, Glorified is He, and His oneness.

They said: "Originator of the heavens and the earth" — i.e., their Creator, their Inventor, their Originator, their Bringer into existence after non-existence, who calls you to belief in Him and to His oneness. "That He may forgive you some of your sins." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "min" is extra, and the basis for this is His saying elsewhere: "Indeed God forgives all sins" (al-Zumar 53). Sibawayh said: it is partitive, and it is permissible to mention a part while intending the whole. It is also said: the partitive is literal, and it does not follow from the forgiveness of all sins for the community of Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, that all of them are forgiven for others. This verse is cited by those who permit the addition of "min" in affirmative speech. It is also said: "min" indicates substitution, not extra and not partitive, i.e., that the forgiveness be in place of the sins. "And that He may defer you to a specified term" — i.e., to a time specified with Him, Glorified is He, which is death; so He will not punish you in this world.

"They said: You are only humans like us" — i.e., you are nothing but humans like us in form and appearance, eating and drinking as we eat and drink, and you are not angels. "You wish to turn us away" — they described them first as human, then by their desire to turn them away from what their fathers used to worship, secondly; i.e., you want to turn us away from the deities of our fathers, the idols and the like. "So bring us a clear authority, if you are truthful, that you are sent from God" — i.e., a manifest proof showing the soundness of what you claim. The messengers had indeed brought them a manifest authority and clear proof, but this kind of their obstinacy and one of their shifting ploys was of that sort.

"Their messengers said to them: We are only humans like you" — i.e., we are not, in form and appearance, anything but humans like you, as you say. "But God bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants" — i.e., He bestows grace upon whom He wills among them with prophethood; it is said: with success and guidance. "And it was not for us to bring you an authority" — i.e., it was not right or proper for us to bring you a proof of the proofs except by God's permission, i.e., except by His will; and that is not within our power.

It is said: the authority here means what the disbelievers demanded of the signs out of obstinacy. It is also said it is more general than that, for whatever God wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. "And upon God let the faithful put their trust" — i.e., upon Him alone; this is a command from them to the believers to rely upon God rather than anyone else.

It seems the messengers intended by this command to the believers a primary command to themselves; therefore they said: "And why should we not put our trust in God?" — i.e., what excuse do we have for not relying upon Him, Glorified is He? "When He has already guided us to our ways" — i.e., while He has already done for us what requires our reliance upon Him, by guiding us to the path that leads to His mercy, which is what He prescribed for His servants and made obligatory for them to follow. "And we will surely bear patiently what you have harmed us with" — by what comes from you of denial of us and baseless demands. "And upon God let the trusting put their trust." It is said: the first reliance means its initiation, and by this, striving for its continuance and firmness. It is also said: the meaning of the first is that those who ask for miracles must rely upon God, Glorified is He, for their attainment, not upon us; so if He wills He manifests them, and if He wills He does not.

The meaning of the second is: displaying reliance upon God in repelling the evil of the disbelievers and their folly.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' concerning His saying: "And when your Lord proclaimed, 'If you give thanks, I will surely increase you'": He said: Moses informed them from their Lord that if they gave thanks for the favour, He would increase them from His bounty, widen their provision, and make them prevail over the world.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan concerning "I will surely increase you": he said: in obedience to Me.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verse 6–12 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Ali ibn Salih a similar report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sufyan al-Thawri concerning the verse, that he said: "Let not your souls go after this world, for it is less than that in the sight of Allah. Rather, He says: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favour]﴾ — [increase you] from My obedience."

Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi related from Anas, who said: "A beggar came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he ordered that he be given a date, but he did not take it. Another came to him and he ordered that he be given a date, and he accepted it and said: 'A date from the Messenger of Allah!' So he said to the slave girl: 'Go to Umm Salamah and give him the forty dirhams that she has.'" In the chain of Ahmad is Umarah ibn Zadhan. Ahmad, Ya'qub ibn Sufyan and Ibn Hibban declared him trustworthy (thiqah). Ibn Ma'in said: "Salih." Abu Zur'ah said: "There is no harm in him." Abu Hatim said: "His hadith is written down but not used as evidence; he is not firm (laysa bil-matin)." al-Bukhari said: "He sometimes becomes confused (yadtarib) in his hadith." Ahmad said: "Strange (munkar) hadiths have been related from him." Abu Dawud said: "He is not of that standing." al-Daraqutni weakened him, and Ibn Adi said: "There is no harm in him."

al-Bukhari in his History and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi in al-Mukhtarah related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is granted five [things] will not be deprived of five [things]," and among them: "Whoever is granted gratitude will not be deprived of increase."

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir Abi Hurayrah related that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Four [things]: whoever is given them will not be deprived of four [things] from Allah," and among them: "Whoever is given gratitude will not be deprived of increase?"

There is no basis for restricting the increase to an increase in obedience; rather, the apparent meaning of the verse is generality, as the making of the increase a recompense for gratitude indicates. So whoever thanks Allah for what He has provided for him, Allah will expand his provision; whoever thanks Allah for the obedience He has enabled him to perform, He will increase him in obedience; and whoever thanks Him for the health He has bestowed on him, Allah will increase him in health, and similar.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Mas'ud that he used to recite ﴿And those after them, none knows them except Allah﴾ and would say: "The genealogists have lied."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Amr ibn Maymun a similar report.

Ibn al-Dara'is related from Abu Mijlaz, who said: A man said to Ali ibn Abi Talib: "I am the most knowledgeable of people in genealogy." He said: "You are not [knowledgeable] of people's genealogies." He said: "Yes, I am." Ali said to him: "Tell me about His saying: ﴿And 'Ad and Thamud and the companions of the Rass, and many generations between them﴾ [al-Furqan: 38]." He said: "I trace the genealogy of that multitude." He said: "Tell me about His saying: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, none knows them except Allah﴾." So he fell silent.

Abu Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "We have not found anyone who knows what lies beyond Ma'add ibn Adnan."

Abu Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Between Adnan and Isma'il there are thirty fathers who are not known."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying: ﴿But they put their hands to their mouths﴾, that he said: "When they heard the Book of Allah they marvelled and returned their hands to their mouths, ﴿and said: Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent, and indeed we are in grave doubt about that to which you invite us﴾" — meaning: "We do not believe you in what you have brought, for we have strong doubt concerning it."

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Abu Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from Ibn Mas'ud: "﴿But they put their hands to their mouths﴾" — he said: "They bit down on them."

And in another wording: "On their fingertips, out of rage at their messengers."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verses 6–12 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "And when Moses said" — the adverbial clause (al-zarf) is connected to an implied verb, which is "remember": i.e., remember the time when Moses said. And "when He delivered you" (idh anjakum) is connected to "remember" (udhkuru): i.e., remember His favour upon you at the time of His delivering you from the people of Pharaoh; or it is connected to "favour" (al-ni'mah), or to the complement of "upon you" (alaykum), meaning: settled upon you at the time of His delivering you. It is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "favour," where by "favour" is meant bounty or gift. "They afflict you with the evil of torment" — i.e., they desire you; it is said: sama-hu zulman, meaning he inflicted injustice upon him. The root of al-sawm is going forth in pursuit of a thing. "The evil of torment" is a verbal noun of sa'a, ya'su'u, and what is intended is the evil torment: their enslaving them and employing them in arduous labour. "They slaughter your sons" is conjoined to "they afflict you with the evil of torment," even though slaughter is of the same kind as evil torment, in order to take it out of the category of ordinary torment, so that it appears as though it were a different kind, because of its severity. With the conjunction omitted, as in the other verse, the slaughter is an explanation of "the evil of torment." "And they spare your women" — i.e., they leave them alive, to humiliate and degrade them. "And in that," referring to what was mentioned of their deeds, "is a great trial from your Lord" — i.e., a test for you. The explanation of this verse has already been given fully in Surat al-Baqarah.

"And when your Lord proclaimed" — "proclaimed" (ta'adhdhana) is in the sense of "announced" (adhina), as al-Farra' said.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "There must be in tafa'ala an added meaning not present in af'ala, as if it were said: 'And when your Lord announced, a clear announcement from which doubts are removed and suspicions dispelled.'"

The meaning: "And when your Lord proclaimed, and said, 'If you give thanks...'" Or "proclaimed" is treated as "said," since it is a kind of speech. This is from the words of Moses to his people, and it is conjoined to "the favour of God." That is: remember the favour of God upon you, and remember when your Lord proclaimed. It is said that it is conjoined to his saying "when He delivered you," i.e., remember the favour of God, Exalted, in these two times, for this proclamation is also a favour. It is also said that it is from the words of God, Glorified is He, i.e., "And remember, O Muhammad, when your Lord proclaimed."

Ibn Mas'ud recited "And when your Lord said," and the meaning is the same, as has already been mentioned. The lam in "If you give thanks" is the lam that prepares for the oath. His saying "I will surely increase you" fills the place of the answers of both the condition and the oath. Likewise the lam in "And if you are ungrateful" and his saying "Indeed My punishment is severe" fills the place of both answers as well. The meaning: If you give thanks for My favour upon you with what has been mentioned, I will surely increase you in favour upon favour, as a bounty from Me. It is also said: I will surely increase you in obedience to Me; it is also said: I will surely increase you in reward. The first is more apparent, so thanks is the cause of increase. "And if you are ungrateful, denying that and rejecting it, indeed My punishment is severe," so some of it must befall you, as it befalls. It is also said that the answer is omitted, i.e., "And if you are ungrateful, I will surely punish you," and what is mentioned is the reason for the omitted answer.

"And Moses said: If you disbelieve, you and all who are on the earth together" — i.e., if you disbelieve His favour, Exalted is He, you and all creation, and do not give thanks for it, then indeed God, Glorified is He, is Free of need of your gratitude; He does not need it, and no deficiency reaches Him by that. "Praiseworthy" — i.e., deserving of praise in Himself, because of the abundance of His favour, even if you do not thank Him, or others among the angels praise Him.

"Has there not come to you the report of those before you?" It is possible that this is an address from Moses to his people, and then it falls under reminding them of the Days of God. It is also possible that it is from the speech of God, Glorified is He, initially addressing the people of Moses and reminding them of the earlier generations, their reports, and the coming of God's messengers to them. It is also possible that it is an initial address from God, Glorified is He, to the people of Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, warning them against opposing him. Al-naba' is the report, and its plural is al-anba', and from it is the poet's saying:

"Did there not come to you, while the reports spread, what the she-camel of the sons of Ziyad suffered?"

"And the people of Noah" is a substitute for the relative pronoun, or an explanatory apposition. "And 'Ad and Thamud and those after them" — i.e., after these mentioned, "no one knows them but God," i.e., no one counts their number or encompasses them in knowledge except God, Glorified is He. The relative pronoun is the subject and its predicate is "no one knows them but God," and the clause is parenthetical. Or the relative pronoun is conjoined to what precedes it, and "no one knows them but God" is a parenthetical insertion. The absence of knowledge from other than God is either referring to their attributes, conditions, characters, and the spans of their lives, meaning these matters are known to God alone and to no other; or it refers to their essences, meaning no one knows the essences of those who came after them except God, Glorified is He.

The clause "their messengers came to them with clear proofs" is resumptive, explaining the report mentioned in "Has there not come to you the report of those before you?" That is, the messengers came to them with manifest miracles and clear laws. "But they put their hands to their mouths" — i.e., they placed the hands of their own selves to their mouths, biting them in rage at what the messengers brought, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "They bite their fingertips out of rage" (Al 'Imran 119), because the messengers came to them with the folly of their minds and the reviling of their idols. It is also said that the meaning is that they pointed with their fingers to their mouths when the messengers came to them with clear proofs, i.e., "Be silent, and leave what you have brought," rejecting them and refuting their words. It is also said that the meaning is that they pointed to themselves and to what issues from them of speech, which is their saying, "Indeed we deny what you have been sent with," i.e., you have no answer to us other than what we have said to you with these tongues of ours. It is also said that they placed their hands on their mouths in mockery and wonder, as one does when laughter overcomes him and he places his hand on his mouth. It is also said that the meaning is: they answered the messengers' words and disbelieved them with their mouths, so the first pronoun refers to the messengers and the second to the disbelievers. It is also said that they put their hands into the mouths of the messengers in rejection of their words, so on this view the first pronoun refers to the disbelievers and the second to the messengers. It is also said the meaning is: they gestured to the messengers to be silent. It is also said they took the hands of the messengers and placed them over the messengers' mouths to silence them and cut off their speech. It is also said that "hands" here means blessings, i.e., they rejected the messengers' blessings with their mouths, meaning by speech and denial; and by blessings here is meant what was brought to them of laws.

Abu 'Ubaydah said, and he spoke well: it is a figure of speech, meaning they did not believe and did not respond. The Arabs say of a man who refrains from answering and falls silent: "He has put his hand in his mouth." Al-Akhfash said likewise. Al-Qutaybi objected to this, saying: "No one has been heard among the Arabs saying 'He returned his hand into his mouth' when he abandons what he was commanded; rather the meaning is 'they bit the hands out of rage and anger,'" as in the poet's saying:

"They would bite in their mouths the anger of the envious, until they bite my palms."

This is the view we put forward above all these sayings, and from it is the poet's saying:

"Had Salma seen my emaciation, she would have bitten the tips of her hand from grief."

And this is the closest of the interpretations to the verse, if what Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash mentioned is not authentically reported from the Arabs.

If what they mentioned is sound, then interpreting the verse accordingly is closer. "And they said: Indeed we deny what you have been sent with" — i.e., the disbelievers said to the messengers: "Indeed we deny what you have been sent with of clear proofs, according to your claim." "And indeed we are in grave doubt about what you call us to" — i.e., in great doubt concerning what you call us to, of belief in God alone and abandoning all else, "disquieting" — i.e., causing unease. It is said: arabtuhu, when you do an act that causes suspicion and doubt. Al-rayb is the restlessness of the soul and its lack of tranquillity.

It has been said: how did they openly declare disbelief and then their affair was based on doubt? It is answered that they meant: "We are disbelievers in your messengership; and if we descend from this position, then at least we doubt the soundness of your prophethood." With the utmost doubt there is no hope of their acknowledging your prophethood.

The clause "Their messengers said: Is there doubt about God?" is resumptive, answering an implied question, as though it were said: "What did the messengers say to them?" The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, i.e., is there doubt concerning His oneness, Glorified is He, and it is in the utmost clarity and manifestness? Then the messengers, after denying it to the disbelievers, mentioned the evidences that confirm this denial, showing that there is no doubt about His existence, Glorified is He, and His oneness.

They said: "Originator of the heavens and the earth" — i.e., their Creator, their Inventor, their Originator, their Bringer into existence after non-existence, who calls you to belief in Him and to His oneness. "That He may forgive you some of your sins." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "min" is extra, and the basis for this is His saying elsewhere: "Indeed God forgives all sins" (al-Zumar 53). Sibawayh said: it is partitive, and it is permissible to mention a part while intending the whole. It is also said: the partitive is literal, and it does not follow from the forgiveness of all sins for the community of Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, that all of them are forgiven for others. This verse is cited by those who permit the addition of "min" in affirmative speech. It is also said: "min" indicates substitution, not extra and not partitive, i.e., that the forgiveness be in place of the sins. "And that He may defer you to a specified term" — i.e., to a time specified with Him, Glorified is He, which is death; so He will not punish you in this world.

"They said: You are only humans like us" — i.e., you are nothing but humans like us in form and appearance, eating and drinking as we eat and drink, and you are not angels. "You wish to turn us away" — they described them first as human, then by their desire to turn them away from what their fathers used to worship, secondly; i.e., you want to turn us away from the deities of our fathers, the idols and the like. "So bring us a clear authority, if you are truthful, that you are sent from God" — i.e., a manifest proof showing the soundness of what you claim. The messengers had indeed brought them a manifest authority and clear proof, but this kind of their obstinacy and one of their shifting ploys was of that sort.

"Their messengers said to them: We are only humans like you" — i.e., we are not, in form and appearance, anything but humans like you, as you say. "But God bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants" — i.e., He bestows grace upon whom He wills among them with prophethood; it is said: with success and guidance. "And it was not for us to bring you an authority" — i.e., it was not right or proper for us to bring you a proof of the proofs except by God's permission, i.e., except by His will; and that is not within our power.

It is said: the authority here means what the disbelievers demanded of the signs out of obstinacy. It is also said it is more general than that, for whatever God wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. "And upon God let the faithful put their trust" — i.e., upon Him alone; this is a command from them to the believers to rely upon God rather than anyone else.

It seems the messengers intended by this command to the believers a primary command to themselves; therefore they said: "And why should we not put our trust in God?" — i.e., what excuse do we have for not relying upon Him, Glorified is He? "When He has already guided us to our ways" — i.e., while He has already done for us what requires our reliance upon Him, by guiding us to the path that leads to His mercy, which is what He prescribed for His servants and made obligatory for them to follow. "And we will surely bear patiently what you have harmed us with" — by what comes from you of denial of us and baseless demands. "And upon God let the trusting put their trust." It is said: the first reliance means its initiation, and by this, striving for its continuance and firmness. It is also said: the meaning of the first is that those who ask for miracles must rely upon God, Glorified is He, for their attainment, not upon us; so if He wills He manifests them, and if He wills He does not.

The meaning of the second is: displaying reliance upon God in repelling the evil of the disbelievers and their folly.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' concerning His saying: "And when your Lord proclaimed, 'If you give thanks, I will surely increase you'": He said: Moses informed them from their Lord that if they gave thanks for the favour, He would increase them from His bounty, widen their provision, and make them prevail over the world.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan concerning "I will surely increase you": he said: in obedience to Me.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verse 6–12 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Ali ibn Salih a similar report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sufyan al-Thawri concerning the verse, that he said: "Let not your souls go after this world, for it is less than that in the sight of Allah. Rather, He says: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favour]﴾ — [increase you] from My obedience."

Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi related from Anas, who said: "A beggar came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he ordered that he be given a date, but he did not take it. Another came to him and he ordered that he be given a date, and he accepted it and said: 'A date from the Messenger of Allah!' So he said to the slave girl: 'Go to Umm Salamah and give him the forty dirhams that she has.'" In the chain of Ahmad is Umarah ibn Zadhan. Ahmad, Ya'qub ibn Sufyan and Ibn Hibban declared him trustworthy (thiqah). Ibn Ma'in said: "Salih." Abu Zur'ah said: "There is no harm in him." Abu Hatim said: "His hadith is written down but not used as evidence; he is not firm (laysa bil-matin)." al-Bukhari said: "He sometimes becomes confused (yadtarib) in his hadith." Ahmad said: "Strange (munkar) hadiths have been related from him." Abu Dawud said: "He is not of that standing." al-Daraqutni weakened him, and Ibn Adi said: "There is no harm in him."

al-Bukhari in his History and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi in al-Mukhtarah related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is granted five [things] will not be deprived of five [things]," and among them: "Whoever is granted gratitude will not be deprived of increase."

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir Abi Hurayrah related that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Four [things]: whoever is given them will not be deprived of four [things] from Allah," and among them: "Whoever is given gratitude will not be deprived of increase?"

There is no basis for restricting the increase to an increase in obedience; rather, the apparent meaning of the verse is generality, as the making of the increase a recompense for gratitude indicates. So whoever thanks Allah for what He has provided for him, Allah will expand his provision; whoever thanks Allah for the obedience He has enabled him to perform, He will increase him in obedience; and whoever thanks Him for the health He has bestowed on him, Allah will increase him in health, and similar.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Mas'ud that he used to recite ﴿And those after them, none knows them except Allah﴾ and would say: "The genealogists have lied."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Amr ibn Maymun a similar report.

Ibn al-Dara'is related from Abu Mijlaz, who said: A man said to Ali ibn Abi Talib: "I am the most knowledgeable of people in genealogy." He said: "You are not [knowledgeable] of people's genealogies." He said: "Yes, I am." Ali said to him: "Tell me about His saying: ﴿And 'Ad and Thamud and the companions of the Rass, and many generations between them﴾ [al-Furqan: 38]." He said: "I trace the genealogy of that multitude." He said: "Tell me about His saying: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, none knows them except Allah﴾." So he fell silent.

Abu Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "We have not found anyone who knows what lies beyond Ma'add ibn Adnan."

Abu Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Between Adnan and Isma'il there are thirty fathers who are not known."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying: ﴿But they put their hands to their mouths﴾, that he said: "When they heard the Book of Allah they marvelled and returned their hands to their mouths, ﴿and said: Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent, and indeed we are in grave doubt about that to which you invite us﴾" — meaning: "We do not believe you in what you have brought, for we have strong doubt concerning it."

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Abu Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from Ibn Mas'ud: "﴿But they put their hands to their mouths﴾" — he said: "They bit down on them."

And in another wording: "On their fingertips, out of rage at their messengers."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verses 6–12 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "And when Moses said" — the adverbial clause (al-zarf) is connected to an implied verb, which is "remember": i.e., remember the time when Moses said. And "when He delivered you" (idh anjakum) is connected to "remember" (udhkuru): i.e., remember His favour upon you at the time of His delivering you from the people of Pharaoh; or it is connected to "favour" (al-ni'mah), or to the complement of "upon you" (alaykum), meaning: settled upon you at the time of His delivering you. It is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "favour," where by "favour" is meant bounty or gift. "They afflict you with the evil of torment" — i.e., they desire you; it is said: sama-hu zulman, meaning he inflicted injustice upon him. The root of al-sawm is going forth in pursuit of a thing. "The evil of torment" is a verbal noun of sa'a, ya'su'u, and what is intended is the evil torment: their enslaving them and employing them in arduous labour. "They slaughter your sons" is conjoined to "they afflict you with the evil of torment," even though slaughter is of the same kind as evil torment, in order to take it out of the category of ordinary torment, so that it appears as though it were a different kind, because of its severity. With the conjunction omitted, as in the other verse, the slaughter is an explanation of "the evil of torment." "And they spare your women" — i.e., they leave them alive, to humiliate and degrade them. "And in that," referring to what was mentioned of their deeds, "is a great trial from your Lord" — i.e., a test for you. The explanation of this verse has already been given fully in Surat al-Baqarah.

"And when your Lord proclaimed" — "proclaimed" (ta'adhdhana) is in the sense of "announced" (adhina), as al-Farra' said.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "There must be in tafa'ala an added meaning not present in af'ala, as if it were said: 'And when your Lord announced, a clear announcement from which doubts are removed and suspicions dispelled.'"

The meaning: "And when your Lord proclaimed, and said, 'If you give thanks...'" Or "proclaimed" is treated as "said," since it is a kind of speech. This is from the words of Moses to his people, and it is conjoined to "the favour of God." That is: remember the favour of God upon you, and remember when your Lord proclaimed. It is said that it is conjoined to his saying "when He delivered you," i.e., remember the favour of God, Exalted, in these two times, for this proclamation is also a favour. It is also said that it is from the words of God, Glorified is He, i.e., "And remember, O Muhammad, when your Lord proclaimed."

Ibn Mas'ud recited "And when your Lord said," and the meaning is the same, as has already been mentioned. The lam in "If you give thanks" is the lam that prepares for the oath. His saying "I will surely increase you" fills the place of the answers of both the condition and the oath. Likewise the lam in "And if you are ungrateful" and his saying "Indeed My punishment is severe" fills the place of both answers as well. The meaning: If you give thanks for My favour upon you with what has been mentioned, I will surely increase you in favour upon favour, as a bounty from Me. It is also said: I will surely increase you in obedience to Me; it is also said: I will surely increase you in reward. The first is more apparent, so thanks is the cause of increase. "And if you are ungrateful, denying that and rejecting it, indeed My punishment is severe," so some of it must befall you, as it befalls. It is also said that the answer is omitted, i.e., "And if you are ungrateful, I will surely punish you," and what is mentioned is the reason for the omitted answer.

"And Moses said: If you disbelieve, you and all who are on the earth together" — i.e., if you disbelieve His favour, Exalted is He, you and all creation, and do not give thanks for it, then indeed God, Glorified is He, is Free of need of your gratitude; He does not need it, and no deficiency reaches Him by that. "Praiseworthy" — i.e., deserving of praise in Himself, because of the abundance of His favour, even if you do not thank Him, or others among the angels praise Him.

"Has there not come to you the report of those before you?" It is possible that this is an address from Moses to his people, and then it falls under reminding them of the Days of God. It is also possible that it is from the speech of God, Glorified is He, initially addressing the people of Moses and reminding them of the earlier generations, their reports, and the coming of God's messengers to them. It is also possible that it is an initial address from God, Glorified is He, to the people of Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, warning them against opposing him. Al-naba' is the report, and its plural is al-anba', and from it is the poet's saying:

"Did there not come to you, while the reports spread, what the she-camel of the sons of Ziyad suffered?"

"And the people of Noah" is a substitute for the relative pronoun, or an explanatory apposition. "And 'Ad and Thamud and those after them" — i.e., after these mentioned, "no one knows them but God," i.e., no one counts their number or encompasses them in knowledge except God, Glorified is He. The relative pronoun is the subject and its predicate is "no one knows them but God," and the clause is parenthetical. Or the relative pronoun is conjoined to what precedes it, and "no one knows them but God" is a parenthetical insertion. The absence of knowledge from other than God is either referring to their attributes, conditions, characters, and the spans of their lives, meaning these matters are known to God alone and to no other; or it refers to their essences, meaning no one knows the essences of those who came after them except God, Glorified is He.

The clause "their messengers came to them with clear proofs" is resumptive, explaining the report mentioned in "Has there not come to you the report of those before you?" That is, the messengers came to them with manifest miracles and clear laws. "But they put their hands to their mouths" — i.e., they placed the hands of their own selves to their mouths, biting them in rage at what the messengers brought, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "They bite their fingertips out of rage" (Al 'Imran 119), because the messengers came to them with the folly of their minds and the reviling of their idols. It is also said that the meaning is that they pointed with their fingers to their mouths when the messengers came to them with clear proofs, i.e., "Be silent, and leave what you have brought," rejecting them and refuting their words. It is also said that the meaning is that they pointed to themselves and to what issues from them of speech, which is their saying, "Indeed we deny what you have been sent with," i.e., you have no answer to us other than what we have said to you with these tongues of ours. It is also said that they placed their hands on their mouths in mockery and wonder, as one does when laughter overcomes him and he places his hand on his mouth. It is also said that the meaning is: they answered the messengers' words and disbelieved them with their mouths, so the first pronoun refers to the messengers and the second to the disbelievers. It is also said that they put their hands into the mouths of the messengers in rejection of their words, so on this view the first pronoun refers to the disbelievers and the second to the messengers. It is also said the meaning is: they gestured to the messengers to be silent. It is also said they took the hands of the messengers and placed them over the messengers' mouths to silence them and cut off their speech. It is also said that "hands" here means blessings, i.e., they rejected the messengers' blessings with their mouths, meaning by speech and denial; and by blessings here is meant what was brought to them of laws.

Abu 'Ubaydah said, and he spoke well: it is a figure of speech, meaning they did not believe and did not respond. The Arabs say of a man who refrains from answering and falls silent: "He has put his hand in his mouth." Al-Akhfash said likewise. Al-Qutaybi objected to this, saying: "No one has been heard among the Arabs saying 'He returned his hand into his mouth' when he abandons what he was commanded; rather the meaning is 'they bit the hands out of rage and anger,'" as in the poet's saying:

"They would bite in their mouths the anger of the envious, until they bite my palms."

This is the view we put forward above all these sayings, and from it is the poet's saying:

"Had Salma seen my emaciation, she would have bitten the tips of her hand from grief."

And this is the closest of the interpretations to the verse, if what Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash mentioned is not authentically reported from the Arabs.

If what they mentioned is sound, then interpreting the verse accordingly is closer. "And they said: Indeed we deny what you have been sent with" — i.e., the disbelievers said to the messengers: "Indeed we deny what you have been sent with of clear proofs, according to your claim." "And indeed we are in grave doubt about what you call us to" — i.e., in great doubt concerning what you call us to, of belief in God alone and abandoning all else, "disquieting" — i.e., causing unease. It is said: arabtuhu, when you do an act that causes suspicion and doubt. Al-rayb is the restlessness of the soul and its lack of tranquillity.

It has been said: how did they openly declare disbelief and then their affair was based on doubt? It is answered that they meant: "We are disbelievers in your messengership; and if we descend from this position, then at least we doubt the soundness of your prophethood." With the utmost doubt there is no hope of their acknowledging your prophethood.

The clause "Their messengers said: Is there doubt about God?" is resumptive, answering an implied question, as though it were said: "What did the messengers say to them?" The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, i.e., is there doubt concerning His oneness, Glorified is He, and it is in the utmost clarity and manifestness? Then the messengers, after denying it to the disbelievers, mentioned the evidences that confirm this denial, showing that there is no doubt about His existence, Glorified is He, and His oneness.

They said: "Originator of the heavens and the earth" — i.e., their Creator, their Inventor, their Originator, their Bringer into existence after non-existence, who calls you to belief in Him and to His oneness. "That He may forgive you some of your sins." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "min" is extra, and the basis for this is His saying elsewhere: "Indeed God forgives all sins" (al-Zumar 53). Sibawayh said: it is partitive, and it is permissible to mention a part while intending the whole. It is also said: the partitive is literal, and it does not follow from the forgiveness of all sins for the community of Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, that all of them are forgiven for others. This verse is cited by those who permit the addition of "min" in affirmative speech. It is also said: "min" indicates substitution, not extra and not partitive, i.e., that the forgiveness be in place of the sins. "And that He may defer you to a specified term" — i.e., to a time specified with Him, Glorified is He, which is death; so He will not punish you in this world.

"They said: You are only humans like us" — i.e., you are nothing but humans like us in form and appearance, eating and drinking as we eat and drink, and you are not angels. "You wish to turn us away" — they described them first as human, then by their desire to turn them away from what their fathers used to worship, secondly; i.e., you want to turn us away from the deities of our fathers, the idols and the like. "So bring us a clear authority, if you are truthful, that you are sent from God" — i.e., a manifest proof showing the soundness of what you claim. The messengers had indeed brought them a manifest authority and clear proof, but this kind of their obstinacy and one of their shifting ploys was of that sort.

"Their messengers said to them: We are only humans like you" — i.e., we are not, in form and appearance, anything but humans like you, as you say. "But God bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants" — i.e., He bestows grace upon whom He wills among them with prophethood; it is said: with success and guidance. "And it was not for us to bring you an authority" — i.e., it was not right or proper for us to bring you a proof of the proofs except by God's permission, i.e., except by His will; and that is not within our power.

It is said: the authority here means what the disbelievers demanded of the signs out of obstinacy. It is also said it is more general than that, for whatever God wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. "And upon God let the faithful put their trust" — i.e., upon Him alone; this is a command from them to the believers to rely upon God rather than anyone else.

It seems the messengers intended by this command to the believers a primary command to themselves; therefore they said: "And why should we not put our trust in God?" — i.e., what excuse do we have for not relying upon Him, Glorified is He? "When He has already guided us to our ways" — i.e., while He has already done for us what requires our reliance upon Him, by guiding us to the path that leads to His mercy, which is what He prescribed for His servants and made obligatory for them to follow. "And we will surely bear patiently what you have harmed us with" — by what comes from you of denial of us and baseless demands. "And upon God let the trusting put their trust." It is said: the first reliance means its initiation, and by this, striving for its continuance and firmness. It is also said: the meaning of the first is that those who ask for miracles must rely upon God, Glorified is He, for their attainment, not upon us; so if He wills He manifests them, and if He wills He does not.

The meaning of the second is: displaying reliance upon God in repelling the evil of the disbelievers and their folly.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' concerning His saying: "And when your Lord proclaimed, 'If you give thanks, I will surely increase you'": He said: Moses informed them from their Lord that if they gave thanks for the favour, He would increase them from His bounty, widen their provision, and make them prevail over the world.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan concerning "I will surely increase you": he said: in obedience to Me.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verse 6–12 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Ali ibn Salih a similar report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sufyan al-Thawri concerning the verse, that he said: "Let not your souls go after this world, for it is less than that in the sight of Allah. Rather, He says: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favour]﴾ — [increase you] from My obedience."

Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi related from Anas, who said: "A beggar came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he ordered that he be given a date, but he did not take it. Another came to him and he ordered that he be given a date, and he accepted it and said: 'A date from the Messenger of Allah!' So he said to the slave girl: 'Go to Umm Salamah and give him the forty dirhams that she has.'" In the chain of Ahmad is Umarah ibn Zadhan. Ahmad, Ya'qub ibn Sufyan and Ibn Hibban declared him trustworthy (thiqah). Ibn Ma'in said: "Salih." Abu Zur'ah said: "There is no harm in him." Abu Hatim said: "His hadith is written down but not used as evidence; he is not firm (laysa bil-matin)." al-Bukhari said: "He sometimes becomes confused (yadtarib) in his hadith." Ahmad said: "Strange (munkar) hadiths have been related from him." Abu Dawud said: "He is not of that standing." al-Daraqutni weakened him, and Ibn Adi said: "There is no harm in him."

al-Bukhari in his History and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi in al-Mukhtarah related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is granted five [things] will not be deprived of five [things]," and among them: "Whoever is granted gratitude will not be deprived of increase."

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir Abi Hurayrah related that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Four [things]: whoever is given them will not be deprived of four [things] from Allah," and among them: "Whoever is given gratitude will not be deprived of increase?"

There is no basis for restricting the increase to an increase in obedience; rather, the apparent meaning of the verse is generality, as the making of the increase a recompense for gratitude indicates. So whoever thanks Allah for what He has provided for him, Allah will expand his provision; whoever thanks Allah for the obedience He has enabled him to perform, He will increase him in obedience; and whoever thanks Him for the health He has bestowed on him, Allah will increase him in health, and similar.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Mas'ud that he used to recite ﴿And those after them, none knows them except Allah﴾ and would say: "The genealogists have lied."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Amr ibn Maymun a similar report.

Ibn al-Dara'is related from Abu Mijlaz, who said: A man said to Ali ibn Abi Talib: "I am the most knowledgeable of people in genealogy." He said: "You are not [knowledgeable] of people's genealogies." He said: "Yes, I am." Ali said to him: "Tell me about His saying: ﴿And 'Ad and Thamud and the companions of the Rass, and many generations between them﴾ [al-Furqan: 38]." He said: "I trace the genealogy of that multitude." He said: "Tell me about His saying: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, none knows them except Allah﴾." So he fell silent.

Abu Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "We have not found anyone who knows what lies beyond Ma'add ibn Adnan."

Abu Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Between Adnan and Isma'il there are thirty fathers who are not known."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying: ﴿But they put their hands to their mouths﴾, that he said: "When they heard the Book of Allah they marvelled and returned their hands to their mouths, ﴿and said: Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent, and indeed we are in grave doubt about that to which you invite us﴾" — meaning: "We do not believe you in what you have brought, for we have strong doubt concerning it."

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Abu Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from Ibn Mas'ud: "﴿But they put their hands to their mouths﴾" — he said: "They bit down on them."

And in another wording: "On their fingertips, out of rage at their messengers."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verses 6–12 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "And when Moses said" — the adverbial clause (al-zarf) is connected to an implied verb, which is "remember": i.e., remember the time when Moses said. And "when He delivered you" (idh anjakum) is connected to "remember" (udhkuru): i.e., remember His favour upon you at the time of His delivering you from the people of Pharaoh; or it is connected to "favour" (al-ni'mah), or to the complement of "upon you" (alaykum), meaning: settled upon you at the time of His delivering you. It is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "favour," where by "favour" is meant bounty or gift. "They afflict you with the evil of torment" — i.e., they desire you; it is said: sama-hu zulman, meaning he inflicted injustice upon him. The root of al-sawm is going forth in pursuit of a thing. "The evil of torment" is a verbal noun of sa'a, ya'su'u, and what is intended is the evil torment: their enslaving them and employing them in arduous labour. "They slaughter your sons" is conjoined to "they afflict you with the evil of torment," even though slaughter is of the same kind as evil torment, in order to take it out of the category of ordinary torment, so that it appears as though it were a different kind, because of its severity. With the conjunction omitted, as in the other verse, the slaughter is an explanation of "the evil of torment." "And they spare your women" — i.e., they leave them alive, to humiliate and degrade them. "And in that," referring to what was mentioned of their deeds, "is a great trial from your Lord" — i.e., a test for you. The explanation of this verse has already been given fully in Surat al-Baqarah.

"And when your Lord proclaimed" — "proclaimed" (ta'adhdhana) is in the sense of "announced" (adhina), as al-Farra' said.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "There must be in tafa'ala an added meaning not present in af'ala, as if it were said: 'And when your Lord announced, a clear announcement from which doubts are removed and suspicions dispelled.'"

The meaning: "And when your Lord proclaimed, and said, 'If you give thanks...'" Or "proclaimed" is treated as "said," since it is a kind of speech. This is from the words of Moses to his people, and it is conjoined to "the favour of God." That is: remember the favour of God upon you, and remember when your Lord proclaimed. It is said that it is conjoined to his saying "when He delivered you," i.e., remember the favour of God, Exalted, in these two times, for this proclamation is also a favour. It is also said that it is from the words of God, Glorified is He, i.e., "And remember, O Muhammad, when your Lord proclaimed."

Ibn Mas'ud recited "And when your Lord said," and the meaning is the same, as has already been mentioned. The lam in "If you give thanks" is the lam that prepares for the oath. His saying "I will surely increase you" fills the place of the answers of both the condition and the oath. Likewise the lam in "And if you are ungrateful" and his saying "Indeed My punishment is severe" fills the place of both answers as well. The meaning: If you give thanks for My favour upon you with what has been mentioned, I will surely increase you in favour upon favour, as a bounty from Me. It is also said: I will surely increase you in obedience to Me; it is also said: I will surely increase you in reward. The first is more apparent, so thanks is the cause of increase. "And if you are ungrateful, denying that and rejecting it, indeed My punishment is severe," so some of it must befall you, as it befalls. It is also said that the answer is omitted, i.e., "And if you are ungrateful, I will surely punish you," and what is mentioned is the reason for the omitted answer.

"And Moses said: If you disbelieve, you and all who are on the earth together" — i.e., if you disbelieve His favour, Exalted is He, you and all creation, and do not give thanks for it, then indeed God, Glorified is He, is Free of need of your gratitude; He does not need it, and no deficiency reaches Him by that. "Praiseworthy" — i.e., deserving of praise in Himself, because of the abundance of His favour, even if you do not thank Him, or others among the angels praise Him.

"Has there not come to you the report of those before you?" It is possible that this is an address from Moses to his people, and then it falls under reminding them of the Days of God. It is also possible that it is from the speech of God, Glorified is He, initially addressing the people of Moses and reminding them of the earlier generations, their reports, and the coming of God's messengers to them. It is also possible that it is an initial address from God, Glorified is He, to the people of Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, warning them against opposing him. Al-naba' is the report, and its plural is al-anba', and from it is the poet's saying:

"Did there not come to you, while the reports spread, what the she-camel of the sons of Ziyad suffered?"

"And the people of Noah" is a substitute for the relative pronoun, or an explanatory apposition. "And 'Ad and Thamud and those after them" — i.e., after these mentioned, "no one knows them but God," i.e., no one counts their number or encompasses them in knowledge except God, Glorified is He. The relative pronoun is the subject and its predicate is "no one knows them but God," and the clause is parenthetical. Or the relative pronoun is conjoined to what precedes it, and "no one knows them but God" is a parenthetical insertion. The absence of knowledge from other than God is either referring to their attributes, conditions, characters, and the spans of their lives, meaning these matters are known to God alone and to no other; or it refers to their essences, meaning no one knows the essences of those who came after them except God, Glorified is He.

The clause "their messengers came to them with clear proofs" is resumptive, explaining the report mentioned in "Has there not come to you the report of those before you?" That is, the messengers came to them with manifest miracles and clear laws. "But they put their hands to their mouths" — i.e., they placed the hands of their own selves to their mouths, biting them in rage at what the messengers brought, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "They bite their fingertips out of rage" (Al 'Imran 119), because the messengers came to them with the folly of their minds and the reviling of their idols. It is also said that the meaning is that they pointed with their fingers to their mouths when the messengers came to them with clear proofs, i.e., "Be silent, and leave what you have brought," rejecting them and refuting their words. It is also said that the meaning is that they pointed to themselves and to what issues from them of speech, which is their saying, "Indeed we deny what you have been sent with," i.e., you have no answer to us other than what we have said to you with these tongues of ours. It is also said that they placed their hands on their mouths in mockery and wonder, as one does when laughter overcomes him and he places his hand on his mouth. It is also said that the meaning is: they answered the messengers' words and disbelieved them with their mouths, so the first pronoun refers to the messengers and the second to the disbelievers. It is also said that they put their hands into the mouths of the messengers in rejection of their words, so on this view the first pronoun refers to the disbelievers and the second to the messengers. It is also said the meaning is: they gestured to the messengers to be silent. It is also said they took the hands of the messengers and placed them over the messengers' mouths to silence them and cut off their speech. It is also said that "hands" here means blessings, i.e., they rejected the messengers' blessings with their mouths, meaning by speech and denial; and by blessings here is meant what was brought to them of laws.

Abu 'Ubaydah said, and he spoke well: it is a figure of speech, meaning they did not believe and did not respond. The Arabs say of a man who refrains from answering and falls silent: "He has put his hand in his mouth." Al-Akhfash said likewise. Al-Qutaybi objected to this, saying: "No one has been heard among the Arabs saying 'He returned his hand into his mouth' when he abandons what he was commanded; rather the meaning is 'they bit the hands out of rage and anger,'" as in the poet's saying:

"They would bite in their mouths the anger of the envious, until they bite my palms."

This is the view we put forward above all these sayings, and from it is the poet's saying:

"Had Salma seen my emaciation, she would have bitten the tips of her hand from grief."

And this is the closest of the interpretations to the verse, if what Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash mentioned is not authentically reported from the Arabs.

If what they mentioned is sound, then interpreting the verse accordingly is closer. "And they said: Indeed we deny what you have been sent with" — i.e., the disbelievers said to the messengers: "Indeed we deny what you have been sent with of clear proofs, according to your claim." "And indeed we are in grave doubt about what you call us to" — i.e., in great doubt concerning what you call us to, of belief in God alone and abandoning all else, "disquieting" — i.e., causing unease. It is said: arabtuhu, when you do an act that causes suspicion and doubt. Al-rayb is the restlessness of the soul and its lack of tranquillity.

It has been said: how did they openly declare disbelief and then their affair was based on doubt? It is answered that they meant: "We are disbelievers in your messengership; and if we descend from this position, then at least we doubt the soundness of your prophethood." With the utmost doubt there is no hope of their acknowledging your prophethood.

The clause "Their messengers said: Is there doubt about God?" is resumptive, answering an implied question, as though it were said: "What did the messengers say to them?" The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, i.e., is there doubt concerning His oneness, Glorified is He, and it is in the utmost clarity and manifestness? Then the messengers, after denying it to the disbelievers, mentioned the evidences that confirm this denial, showing that there is no doubt about His existence, Glorified is He, and His oneness.

They said: "Originator of the heavens and the earth" — i.e., their Creator, their Inventor, their Originator, their Bringer into existence after non-existence, who calls you to belief in Him and to His oneness. "That He may forgive you some of your sins." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "min" is extra, and the basis for this is His saying elsewhere: "Indeed God forgives all sins" (al-Zumar 53). Sibawayh said: it is partitive, and it is permissible to mention a part while intending the whole. It is also said: the partitive is literal, and it does not follow from the forgiveness of all sins for the community of Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, that all of them are forgiven for others. This verse is cited by those who permit the addition of "min" in affirmative speech. It is also said: "min" indicates substitution, not extra and not partitive, i.e., that the forgiveness be in place of the sins. "And that He may defer you to a specified term" — i.e., to a time specified with Him, Glorified is He, which is death; so He will not punish you in this world.

"They said: You are only humans like us" — i.e., you are nothing but humans like us in form and appearance, eating and drinking as we eat and drink, and you are not angels. "You wish to turn us away" — they described them first as human, then by their desire to turn them away from what their fathers used to worship, secondly; i.e., you want to turn us away from the deities of our fathers, the idols and the like. "So bring us a clear authority, if you are truthful, that you are sent from God" — i.e., a manifest proof showing the soundness of what you claim. The messengers had indeed brought them a manifest authority and clear proof, but this kind of their obstinacy and one of their shifting ploys was of that sort.

"Their messengers said to them: We are only humans like you" — i.e., we are not, in form and appearance, anything but humans like you, as you say. "But God bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants" — i.e., He bestows grace upon whom He wills among them with prophethood; it is said: with success and guidance. "And it was not for us to bring you an authority" — i.e., it was not right or proper for us to bring you a proof of the proofs except by God's permission, i.e., except by His will; and that is not within our power.

It is said: the authority here means what the disbelievers demanded of the signs out of obstinacy. It is also said it is more general than that, for whatever God wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. "And upon God let the faithful put their trust" — i.e., upon Him alone; this is a command from them to the believers to rely upon God rather than anyone else.

It seems the messengers intended by this command to the believers a primary command to themselves; therefore they said: "And why should we not put our trust in God?" — i.e., what excuse do we have for not relying upon Him, Glorified is He? "When He has already guided us to our ways" — i.e., while He has already done for us what requires our reliance upon Him, by guiding us to the path that leads to His mercy, which is what He prescribed for His servants and made obligatory for them to follow. "And we will surely bear patiently what you have harmed us with" — by what comes from you of denial of us and baseless demands. "And upon God let the trusting put their trust." It is said: the first reliance means its initiation, and by this, striving for its continuance and firmness. It is also said: the meaning of the first is that those who ask for miracles must rely upon God, Glorified is He, for their attainment, not upon us; so if He wills He manifests them, and if He wills He does not.

The meaning of the second is: displaying reliance upon God in repelling the evil of the disbelievers and their folly.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' concerning His saying: "And when your Lord proclaimed, 'If you give thanks, I will surely increase you'": He said: Moses informed them from their Lord that if they gave thanks for the favour, He would increase them from His bounty, widen their provision, and make them prevail over the world.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan concerning "I will surely increase you": he said: in obedience to Me.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verse 6–12 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Ali ibn Salih a similar report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sufyan al-Thawri concerning the verse, that he said: "Let not your souls go after this world, for it is less than that in the sight of Allah. Rather, He says: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favour]﴾ — [increase you] from My obedience."

Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi related from Anas, who said: "A beggar came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he ordered that he be given a date, but he did not take it. Another came to him and he ordered that he be given a date, and he accepted it and said: 'A date from the Messenger of Allah!' So he said to the slave girl: 'Go to Umm Salamah and give him the forty dirhams that she has.'" In the chain of Ahmad is Umarah ibn Zadhan. Ahmad, Ya'qub ibn Sufyan and Ibn Hibban declared him trustworthy (thiqah). Ibn Ma'in said: "Salih." Abu Zur'ah said: "There is no harm in him." Abu Hatim said: "His hadith is written down but not used as evidence; he is not firm (laysa bil-matin)." al-Bukhari said: "He sometimes becomes confused (yadtarib) in his hadith." Ahmad said: "Strange (munkar) hadiths have been related from him." Abu Dawud said: "He is not of that standing." al-Daraqutni weakened him, and Ibn Adi said: "There is no harm in him."

al-Bukhari in his History and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi in al-Mukhtarah related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is granted five [things] will not be deprived of five [things]," and among them: "Whoever is granted gratitude will not be deprived of increase."

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir Abi Hurayrah related that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Four [things]: whoever is given them will not be deprived of four [things] from Allah," and among them: "Whoever is given gratitude will not be deprived of increase?"

There is no basis for restricting the increase to an increase in obedience; rather, the apparent meaning of the verse is generality, as the making of the increase a recompense for gratitude indicates. So whoever thanks Allah for what He has provided for him, Allah will expand his provision; whoever thanks Allah for the obedience He has enabled him to perform, He will increase him in obedience; and whoever thanks Him for the health He has bestowed on him, Allah will increase him in health, and similar.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Mas'ud that he used to recite ﴿And those after them, none knows them except Allah﴾ and would say: "The genealogists have lied."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Amr ibn Maymun a similar report.

Ibn al-Dara'is related from Abu Mijlaz, who said: A man said to Ali ibn Abi Talib: "I am the most knowledgeable of people in genealogy." He said: "You are not [knowledgeable] of people's genealogies." He said: "Yes, I am." Ali said to him: "Tell me about His saying: ﴿And 'Ad and Thamud and the companions of the Rass, and many generations between them﴾ [al-Furqan: 38]." He said: "I trace the genealogy of that multitude." He said: "Tell me about His saying: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, none knows them except Allah﴾." So he fell silent.

Abu Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "We have not found anyone who knows what lies beyond Ma'add ibn Adnan."

Abu Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Between Adnan and Isma'il there are thirty fathers who are not known."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying: ﴿But they put their hands to their mouths﴾, that he said: "When they heard the Book of Allah they marvelled and returned their hands to their mouths, ﴿and said: Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent, and indeed we are in grave doubt about that to which you invite us﴾" — meaning: "We do not believe you in what you have brought, for we have strong doubt concerning it."

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Abu Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from Ibn Mas'ud: "﴿But they put their hands to their mouths﴾" — he said: "They bit down on them."

And in another wording: "On their fingertips, out of rage at their messengers."

(p-742).

His statement: "And those who disbelieved said to their messengers, 'We will surely expel you from our land or you must return to our religion.'" The "those who disbelieved" are these speakers, a group of the rebellious who refused to answer the messengers. The *lam* in ﴿لَنُخْرِجَنَّكم﴾ (*lam*, the one that introduces the oath, *al-lam al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam*) means: "By God, we will surely expel you from our land, or you will return to our religion." They were not content with rejecting what the messengers brought and with not complying with what they called them to, so they became bold against them with this threat, and offered them a choice between leaving their land or returning to their disbelieving religion.
