Ibn al-Mubarak in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir narrated from Uqbah ibn Amir, traced back (to the Prophet), and within it he mentioned the hadith of the intercession (*shafa'ah*), then said: "The disbeliever will say at that time: 'The believers have found someone who intercedes for them, so who will intercede for us? None but Iblis, for it is he who led us astray.' So they will come to Iblis and say: 'The believers have found someone who intercedes for them. Stand up and intercede for us, for it was you who led us astray.' Iblis will stand up and rise from his gathering with the foulest smell anyone has ever smelled. Then he will admonish them with Hell, and at that time he will say: ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I broke my promise to you﴾," and the verse is cited in full. Al-Suyuti declared its isnad (chain of narration) weak, and perhaps the reason for that is that its isnad includes Rishdin ibn Sa'd, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad ibn An'um, from Dujayn al-Hajri, from Uqbah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan, who said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Iblis will stand up as a preacher upon a pulpit of fire and say: 'Indeed, Allah promised you...' up to his saying: ﴿nor can you help me﴾," he said: "(that means) nor can you support me. ﴿I disbelieve in your associating me with Allah before﴾," he said: "(that means) by your obedience to me in the world."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Sha'bi regarding this verse, who said: "There are two preachers who will stand on the Day of Resurrection: Iblis and Isa. As for Iblis, he will stand among his party and say this statement mentioned in the verse. As for Isa, he will say: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: 'Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.' And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them; but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117]."

(p-746) Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿I cannot help you, nor can you help me﴾, who said: "I cannot benefit you, nor can you benefit me. ﴿I disbelieve in your associating me with Allah before﴾," he said: "His association (of him) is his worship (of him)."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah regarding ﴿I cannot help you﴾, who said: "I cannot relieve you (of your distress)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding His saying: ﴿Their greeting therein will be, "Peace"﴾, who said: "The angels will greet them with peace in Paradise."

[p. 744]

**His saying: "Have you not seen that Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth"** (﴿ألم تر أن الله خلق السماوات والأرض بالحق﴾). The "seeing" here is of the heart (*ru'yah qalbiyyah*), and the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as an indirect address to his community. Or the address is to everyone who is fit to receive it.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *khaliq al-samawat* (the Creator of the heavens). The meaning of "in truth" is: in the proper manner that befits creating them, so that they serve as evidence of His perfect power.

Then He explained His perfect power, glory be to Him, and His independence from each of His creatures, saying: **"If He wills, He can take you away and bring a new creation"** (﴿إن يشأ يذهبكم ويأت بخلق جديد﴾). He annihilates those who exist, brings into existence those who do not, destroys the disobedient, and brings those who obey Him from among His creatures. The context allows that this new creation may be of the human kind, and it allows that it may be of a different kind.

**"And that is not difficult for Allah"** (﴿وما ذلك على الله بعزيز﴾), i.e., not impossible, because He, glory be to Him, is capable of everything. This implies that Allah, exalted is He, is the one who deserves that His reward be hoped for and His punishment be feared.

Therefore He followed this with the mention of the conditions of the Hereafter, saying: **"And they will all come forth before Allah"** (﴿وبرزوا لله جميعا﴾), i.e., they will come forth from their graves on the Day of Resurrection. *Al-buruz* is manifestation, and *al-baraz* is a wide open space because of its openness. From this comes the phrase *imra'ah barzah*, meaning a woman who shows herself to men. So the meaning of *baraza* is that they appeared from their graves.

The past tense is used for the future to emphasise that its occurrence is certain, as is established in *'ilm al-ma'ani* (the science of meanings in Arabic rhetoric). He said "they came forth before Allah" even though He, glory be to Him, knows them, and nothing about their conditions is hidden from Him, whether they come forth or not. This is because they used to hide from people's eyes when committing sins, and they thought that this was hidden from Allah, exalted is He. So the statement is framed according to what they believed.

**"Then the weak will say to those who were arrogant"** (﴿فقال الضعفاء للذين استكبروا﴾), i.e., the weak followers will say to the powerful leaders who were arrogant because of their leadership: **"Indeed, we were followers of you"** (﴿إنا كنا لكم تبعا﴾), i.e., in the world, so we denied the messengers and disbelieved in Allah by following you. *Al-tabaʿ* is the plural of *tabi'* (follower), or it is a verbal noun described with it for emphasis, or it is understood as "those who are followers." Al-Zajjaj said: He gathered them at their gathering, so the follower and the one followed came together.

**"Then the weak will say to those who were arrogant among their great ones, who turned away from worshipping Allah"** (﴿فقال الضعفاء للذين استكبروا﴾). "Indeed, we were followers of you" (﴿إنا كنا لكم تبعا﴾). *Tabaʿ* is the plural of *tabi'*, like *khadim* and *khadam*, *haris* and *haras*, *rasid* and *rasad*. **"Can you then avail us anything"** (﴿فهل أنتم مغنون عنا﴾), i.e., can you ward off from us any of the punishment of Allah? It is said *aghna 'anhu* when one wards off harm from him, and *aghnahu* when one brings benefit to him.

**"They will say: If Allah had guided us, we would have guided you"** (﴿قالوا لو هدانا الله لهديناكم﴾). i.e., the arrogant ones replied to the words of the oppressed. The sentence is a new sentence, as if a question had been asked: "How did they reply?" The meaning is: if Allah had guided us to faith, we would have guided you to it. It is also said: if Allah had guided us to the path of Paradise, we would have guided you to it. It is also said: if Allah had saved us from the punishment, we would have saved you from it.

**"It is all the same for us whether we bear it with impatience or with patience; we have no place of escape"** (﴿سواء علينا أجزعنا أم صبرنا ما لنا من محيص﴾). i.e., bearing it with impatience and bearing it with patience are equal for us. The interrogative particle *hamzah* and *am* are used to emphasise the equality, as in His saying: "It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them" (Baqarah 2:6). **"We have no place of escape"** (﴿ما لنا من محيص﴾), i.e., no refuge and no way of flight from the punishment. It is said: *haasa fulan 'an kadha*, meaning he fled and turned aside, *yahis haisan*, *huyusan*, and *hayasanan*. The meaning is: we have no way by which we can keep far from the Fire. It is possible that this is part of the speech of both groups, although the apparent meaning is that it is part of the speech of the arrogant ones.

**"And Satan will say when the matter has been decided"** (﴿وقال الشيطان لما قضي الأمر﴾). i.e., he said this statement to both groups. The meaning of **"when the matter has been decided"** (﴿لما قضي الأمر﴾) is: when the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire have entered the Fire, as will be explained in Surah Maryam. **"Indeed, Allah promised you a true promise"** (﴿إن الله وعدكم وعد الحق﴾), which is His promise, glory be to Him, of resurrection and reckoning, and of rewarding the good-doer for his good deeds and the evil-doer for his evil deeds. **"And I promised you, but I failed you"** (﴿ووعدتكم فأخلفتكم﴾), i.e., I promised you a false promise, that there is no resurrection, no reckoning, no Paradise and no Fire, and so I failed you in what I promised you of that.

Al-Farra' said: "a true promise" (*wa'd al-haqq*) is from the annexation of a thing to itself, like their saying *masjid al-jami'* (the congregational mosque). The Basrans said: the meaning is "He promised you the promise of the true day."

**"I had no authority over you"** (﴿وما كان لي عليكم من سلطان﴾), i.e., no domination over you by producing a proof for what I promised you and made attractive to you. **"Except that I called you, and you responded to me"** (﴿إلا أن دعوتكم فاستجبتم لي﴾), i.e., except the mere calling of you to error and misguidance without any proof or evidence. His calling them is not of the same kind as authority, so that it could be excepted from it. Rather, the exception is disjunctive, meaning: "but I called you and you responded to me," i.e., you hastened to answer me. It is also said: the meaning of authority here is compulsion, i.e., I had no compulsion over you that would force you to answer me. It is also said: this exception belongs to the type of the line of poetry:

*"Their greeting among themselves is a painful blow"*

as an exaggeration in negating authority from himself. It is as if he said: authority over you would exist only if the calling itself were accompanied by authority, and it is definitely not so. So do not blame me for what you have fallen into because of my promise to you of falsehood and my failure of that promise. **"But blame yourselves"** (﴿ولوموا أنفسكم﴾), for responding to me merely by a call that has no authority or proof behind it. Whoever accepts false promises and claims that deviate from the path of truth has brought harm upon himself and has cut off his own nose. Especially since this false call of mine and my corrupt promise came in opposition to Allah's promise to you, a true promise, and His call to you to the Abode of Peace, along with the presence of a proof that is not hidden from any sensible person and is obscure only to one who has been forsaken.

Close to this is the case of one who follows the opinions of men that oppose what is in the Book of Allah, glory be to Him, and what is in the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), and prefers them over what is in those two. He has responded to falsehood for which no proof has been established and which no evidence indicates, and he has put the proof and the evidence behind his back, as many of those who follow men do, who turn away from the path of truth through their poor choice. O Allah, forgive us.

**"I cannot help you, nor can you help me"** (﴿ما أنا بمصرخكم وما أنتم بمصرخي﴾). It is said *sarakha fulan* when he calls for help, *yasrukhu surakhan* and *sarkhan*. *Istasrakha* has the same meaning as *sarakha*. *Al-musrikh* is the one who helps, and *al-mustasrikh* is the one who asks for help. It is said: *istasrakhani fa-asrakhtuhu*, and *al-sarikh* is the voice of one who asks for help. *Al-sarikh* also means the one who cries out, and it means both the one who helps and the one who asks for help. It is one of the words with opposite meanings, as is found in *al-Sihah*.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: *al-sarikh* is the one who asks for help, and *al-musrikh* is the one who helps.

The meaning of the verse is: I cannot help you from the punishment you are in, and you cannot help me from what I am in. This contains guidance for them to the fact that Satan, in that state, is afflicted with the same punishment they are afflicted with, and needs someone to help him and rescue him from what he is in. So how can they hope to get help from one who needs someone to help him?

From what came in the same manner as these statements in Arab speech is the saying of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

*"So do not despair; I am not one who will call for your help, and with me there is no help or support for you."*

The word **"my helpers"** (*musrikhiyya*, مُصْرِخِيَّ) is read with a fatha on the *ya'* in the recitation of the majority. Al-A'mash and Hamzah read it with a kasra on the *ya'*, according to the original rule for two consecutive sukun letters (the *ya'* of the pronoun and the *ya'* of the stem).

Al-Farra' said: Hamzah's recitation is a mistake on his part, and few are free from error.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is a poor recitation, and there is no justification for it except a weak one, meaning what we mentioned, that he kasra'd it according to the original rule for two consecutive sukun letters.

Qutrub said: this is the dialect of the Banu Yarbu', who add a *ya'* to the *ya'* of the possessive. Al-Farra' cited, regarding what came in this recitation, the poet's verse:

*"I said to her: O Ta', is there any desire in you for me? She said to him: You are not the one who is pleased."*

**"Indeed I disbelieve in your having associated me with Allah before this"** (﴿إني كفرت بما أشركتمونى من قبل﴾). When he removed the veil from them, showing that he cannot avail them anything against the punishment of Allah and cannot help them with any kind of help, he declared to them that he disbelieves in their associating him with Allah in lordship before this time at which Satan said this statement to them. This refers to what they did in the world by making him a partner. Satan stood before them on that Day in a position that breaks their backs and cuts their hearts. He first made clear to them that the promises he used to make to them in the world were false and opposed the true promise from Allah, glory be to Him, and that he had failed them in what he promised them of those promises and had not kept any of them for them. Then he made clear to them, second, that they had accepted his words without anything that would call for acceptance, nor anything that would be acceptable to the intellect of any sensible person, because of the absence of the proof that a sensible person must have in accepting the words of another. Then he made clear, third, that there was from him nothing but the mere empty call, devoid of proof and empty of even the slightest thing that sensible people hold on to. Then he rebuked them, fourth, for what they had fallen into, rejected their blame of him, and commanded them to blame themselves, because it was they who accepted pure falsehood, whose falseness is not hidden from anyone with even the least intellect. Then he made clear to them, fifth, that he has no victory, no help, and cannot bring them any benefit or repel any harm from them, but is like them in having fallen into the trial and being unable to escape this ordeal. Then he declared to them, sixth, that he has disbelieved in what they had believed about him and had ascribed to him, so their regrets multiplied upon them and their calamities followed one after another. If the sentence **"Indeed, the wrongdoers will have a painful punishment"** (﴿إن الظالمين لهم عذاب أليم﴾) is part of his speech, as some have held, then it is a seventh kind of his speech with which he addressed them. He affirmed wrongdoing for them and then mentioned what their recompense for it would be, a painful punishment. This is not the case according to the one who said it is the beginning of a statement from Allah, glory be to Him.

The majority of the exegetes held that *ma* in **"what you associated me with"** (﴿ما أشركتمون﴾) is a verbal (masdariyyah) particle. It was also said that it may be a relative pronoun, meaning: "I disbelieve in the one you associated me with," which is Allah, mighty and majestic. This would be a report of his disbelief in Allah when He commanded him to prostrate to Adam.

**"And those who believed and did righteous deeds will be admitted into gardens beneath which rivers flow"** (﴿وأدخل الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات جنات تجري من تحتها الأنهار﴾). When He, glory be to Him, informed about the condition of the people of the Fire, He then informed about the condition of the people of Paradise.

The majority read *udkhila* in the passive voice. Al-Hasan read *wa-adkhala* in the active voice, in the future tense, meaning: "And I will admit those who believed." Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned their eternal abiding in the gardens and the non-cessation of their bliss. Then He mentioned that this was **"by the permission of their Lord"** (﴿بإذن ربهم﴾), i.e., by His granting success, His kindness and His guidance. This is according to the recitation of the majority. As for the recitation of al-Hasan, "by the permission of their Lord" is connected to His saying: **"Their greeting therein will be peace"** (﴿تحيتهم فيها سلام﴾), i.e., the greeting of the angels in Paradise is peace, by the permission of their Lord.

The explanation of this has already been given in Surah Yunus.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah, concerning His saying: **"And bring a new creation"** (﴿ويأت بخلق جديد﴾), that he said: "a different creation."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj, concerning His saying: "Then the weak will say", that he said: "the followers, to those who were arrogant," and he said: "to the leaders."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, concerning His saying: **"It is all the same for us whether we bear it with impatience or with patience"** (﴿سواء علينا أجزعنا أم صبرنا﴾), that Zayd ibn Aslam said: "They bore impatience for a hundred years, and they bore patience for a hundred years."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ka'b ibn Malik, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying "It is all the same for us..." (the verse), that he said: "The people of the Fire will say: Come, let us be patient. So they will be patient for five hundred years. When they see that this does not benefit them, they will say: Come, let us bear it with impatience. So they will weep for five hundred years. When they see that this does not benefit them, they will say: **'It is all the same for us whether we bear it with impatience or with patience; we have no place of escape.'"**

The apparent meaning is that this exchange between them took place after they had entered the Fire, as in His saying, exalted is He: **"And when they dispute in the Fire, the weak will say to those who were arrogant: Indeed, we were followers of you, so can you relieve us of a portion of the Fire? Those who were arrogant will say: Indeed, we are all in it. Indeed, Allah has judged between the servants"** (Ghafir 40:47–48).

Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 14, verses 19–23 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mubarak in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir narrated from Uqbah ibn Amir, traced back (to the Prophet), and within it he mentioned the hadith of the intercession (*shafa'ah*), then said: "The disbeliever will say at that time: 'The believers have found someone who intercedes for them, so who will intercede for us? None but Iblis, for it is he who led us astray.' So they will come to Iblis and say: 'The believers have found someone who intercedes for them. Stand up and intercede for us, for it was you who led us astray.' Iblis will stand up and rise from his gathering with the foulest smell anyone has ever smelled. Then he will admonish them with Hell, and at that time he will say: ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I broke my promise to you﴾," and the verse is cited in full. Al-Suyuti declared its isnad (chain of narration) weak, and perhaps the reason for that is that its isnad includes Rishdin ibn Sa'd, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad ibn An'um, from Dujayn al-Hajri, from Uqbah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan, who said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Iblis will stand up as a preacher upon a pulpit of fire and say: 'Indeed, Allah promised you...' up to his saying: ﴿nor can you help me﴾," he said: "(that means) nor can you support me. ﴿I disbelieve in your associating me with Allah before﴾," he said: "(that means) by your obedience to me in the world."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Sha'bi regarding this verse, who said: "There are two preachers who will stand on the Day of Resurrection: Iblis and Isa. As for Iblis, he will stand among his party and say this statement mentioned in the verse. As for Isa, he will say: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: 'Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.' And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them; but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117]."

(p-746) Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿I cannot help you, nor can you help me﴾, who said: "I cannot benefit you, nor can you benefit me. ﴿I disbelieve in your associating me with Allah before﴾," he said: "His association (of him) is his worship (of him)."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah regarding ﴿I cannot help you﴾, who said: "I cannot relieve you (of your distress)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding His saying: ﴿Their greeting therein will be, "Peace"﴾, who said: "The angels will greet them with peace in Paradise."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verse 24–27:

When Glorified is He mentioned the parable of the deeds of the disbelievers, that they are like ashes which the wind blows violently, then He mentioned the bliss of the believers and what Allah recompensed them with, namely their entry into the Garden, abiding therein forever, and the greeting of the angels to them, the Exalted here mentioned a parable for the good word, which is the word of Islam, that is: "There is no god but Allah," or what is more general than that of the words of goodness. He also mentioned a parable for the evil word, which is the word of shirk, or what is more general than that of the words of evil. So He said, addressing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or addressing whoever is fit for address: ﴿Have you not considered how Allah has set forth a parable?﴾ That is, He chose a parable and placed it in its fitting position. The accusative of "a parable" is because it is the object of "set forth," and "a word" is a substitute for it. It is permissible for "the word" to be in the accusative as an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to "a parable." It is also permissible for "the word" to be in the accusative by a verb understood, that is: He made a good word like a good tree, and judged that it is like it. The place of "like a tree" is accusative, being an adjective of "a word," or nominative by presupposing a subject, that is: it is like a tree. It is also permissible for "a word" to be the first of the two objects of "set forth," and it is delayed after the second object, which is "a parable," lest it be far from its adjective. The first is preferable. "A word" and what follows it is an explanation of the parable. Then He described the tree with His saying: ﴿Its root is firm﴾ that is, established, secure from being uprooted, by reason of its being firmly fixed in the earth by its roots, ﴿and its branches are in the sky﴾ that is, its top rises toward the direction of the sky, high in the air.

Then Glorified is He described it as ﴿yielding its fruit every season﴾, every time, ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾, by His will and His decree. It is said: it is the date palm. It is said: it is other than it.

It is said that what is meant by its yielding its fruit every season is every hour of the hours, of night or day, at all times, without distinction between winter and summer. It is said: what is meant is at different times without specification. It is said: every morning and evening. It is said: every month. It is said: every six months.

Al-Naḥḥas said: These statements are close in meaning and not contradictory, because "ḥīn" according to all the people of the language, except those who deviate among them, means a time, which occurs for a short or a long duration. Al-Aṣmaʿī recited the verse of al-Nābigha:

"He divorces her for a time, and for a time he takes her back."

Al-Naḥḥas said: This shows you that ḥīn means time.

"Ḥīn" has also occurred in some places where more is meant, such as His saying: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time from eternity?﴾ [al-Insān: 1].

The statements of the scholars on "ḥīn" have already been explained in Surat al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place and enjoyment for a time﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36].

Al-Zajjāj said: ḥīn is a time, whether long or short. ﴿And Allah sets forth parables for the people that they may remember﴾, that they may reflect upon the states of the origin and the return, and the wondrous works of His creation, which indicate His existence and His oneness. In setting forth parables there is an increase in reminder, understanding, and depiction of meanings.

﴿And the parable of an evil word﴾ its explanation has already passed. It is said: it is the disbeliever himself, and the good word is the believer himself. ﴿Like an evil tree﴾ that is, like the likeness of an evil tree. It is said: it is the colocynth tree. It is said: it is the garlic plant. It is said: the truffle. It is said: the moss. It is said: it is the dodder, with a damma on the first letter and a final letter with three dots, and it is a plant with no leaves and no roots in the earth.

The poet said:

"And it is dodder, with no root and no fruit."

It was also read as "and a parable, a word" in the accusative, coordinated with "a good word." ﴿Uprooted from above the earth﴾ that is, it was rooted out and pulled up from its base. From it is the saying of the poet:

"It is the exile which uproots your root."

The historian said: its body (juththa) was taken, and it is itself; al-juththa is the person's body. It is said: jatthahu means he pulled it out, and ijtatthahu means he uprooted it. The meaning of ﴿from above the earth﴾ is that it has no firm root and no roots firmly established in the earth. ﴿It has no stability﴾ that is, no settling upon the earth.

It is said: no steadfastness upon the earth, just as the disbeliever and his word have no proof, no steadfastness, and no good comes from him at all, and no good word or good deed rises up from him.

﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word﴾ that is, with the clear proof, which is the good word mentioned earlier.

It is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ that it is the word of testimony, the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and that is when the believer sits up in his grave. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "That is His saying: ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word﴾." It is said: the meaning of Allah's keeping them firm is that they persist upon the firm word. From it is the saying of ʿAbdullāh ibn Rawāḥa:

"May Allah keep firm for you what He has given you of goodness, the keeping firm of Moses, and victory like that with which they were victorious."

The meaning of "in the life of this world" is that they continue upon the firm word in the life of this world. A group said: what is meant by "the life of this world" in this verse is the grave, because the dead are in the world until they are resurrected, and the meaning of "and in the Hereafter" is at the time of reckoning.

It is said: what is meant by "the life of this world" is the time of questioning in the grave, and "in the Hereafter" is the time of questioning on the Day of Resurrection. al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, al-Bazzār, Abū Yaʿlā, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Ḥibbān, and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas, who said: "A tray of unripe dates was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: ﴿a parable, a good word like a good tree﴾ until he reached ﴿yielding its fruit every season by the permission of its Lord﴾, and he said: it is the date palm. ﴿And the parable of an evil word﴾ until he reached ﴿having no stability﴾, and he said: it is the bitter gourd."

It was also related as a statement of Anas (mawqūf), and al-Tirmidhī said: the mawqūf is more authentic.

Aḥmad and Ibn Mardawayh related, and al-Suyūṭī said with a good chain, from ʿUmar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying: "like a good tree," that he said: "It is the one whose leaves do not fall." He said: It is the date palm.

al-Bukhārī and others related from the ḥadīth of Ibn ʿUmar who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said one day to his Companions: "Indeed, among trees there is a tree whose leaf does not fall, and it is like the believer." He said: The people fell to thinking of the trees of the desert, and it came to my heart that it is the date palm, but I felt shy until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is the date palm." In another wording of al-Bukhārī he said: "Tell me of a tree like the Muslim man, whose leaves do not fall and which does not yield its fruit every season," and he mentioned something similar.

In a wording of Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Mardawayh from the ḥadīth of Ibn ʿUmar, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you know what the good tree is?" Then he said: "It is the date palm." Something similar has been related from a group of the Companions and the Successors.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His saying: ﴿yielding its fruit every season by the permission of its Lord﴾, that he said: every hour by night and day, winter and summer, and that is the parable of the believer who obeys his Lord by night and day, winter and summer.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from him concerning the verse that he said: it is green, then it becomes yellow.

He also related from him, concerning His saying "every season," that he said: the cutting of the dates.

al-Firyābī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from him also, concerning ﴿yielding its fruit every season﴾, that he said: it bears food every six months.

Abū ʿUbayd, Ibn Abī Shayba, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also, that he said: "ḥīn" here is a year.

al-Bayhaqī related from him also, that he said: "ḥīn" may be morning and evening.

Many statements from a number of the early scholars have been related on this matter.

al-Bukhārī, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan, and others related from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Muslim, when he is questioned in the grave, testifies that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. That is His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾."

Ibn Abī Shayba and al-Bayhaqī related from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib concerning His saying: ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe﴾, the verse, that he said: the keeping firm in the life of this world is when the two angels come to the man in the grave and say: "Who is your Lord?" He says: "My Lord is Allah." They say: "What is your religion?" He says: "My religion is Islam." They say: "Who is your prophet?" He says: "My prophet is Muhammad (ﷺ)." That is the keeping firm in the life of this world.

al-Bayhaqī related something similar from Ibn ʿAbbās.

al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abū Saʿīd concerning the verse, that he said: "in the Hereafter" is the grave.

Ibn Mardawayh related from ʿĀʾisha, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe﴾, the verse: 'This is in the grave.'"

al-Bayhaqī related something similar from her ḥadīth.

al-Bazzār also related from her, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, will this nation be tested in their graves? So how will it be with me, being a weak woman?" He said: ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe﴾, the verse.

Many ḥadīths have been transmitted about the angels questioning the deceased in his grave, about his answer to them, and about the punishment and trial of the grave, but this is not the place to expand upon them, and they are well known.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verse 24–27:

When Glorified is He mentioned the parable of the deeds of the disbelievers, that they are like ashes which the wind blows violently, then He mentioned the bliss of the believers and what Allah recompensed them with, namely their entry into the Garden, abiding therein forever, and the greeting of the angels to them, the Exalted here mentioned a parable for the good word, which is the word of Islam, that is: "There is no god but Allah," or what is more general than that of the words of goodness. He also mentioned a parable for the evil word, which is the word of shirk, or what is more general than that of the words of evil. So He said, addressing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or addressing whoever is fit for address: ﴿Have you not considered how Allah has set forth a parable?﴾ That is, He chose a parable and placed it in its fitting position. The accusative of "a parable" is because it is the object of "set forth," and "a word" is a substitute for it. It is permissible for "the word" to be in the accusative as an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to "a parable." It is also permissible for "the word" to be in the accusative by a verb understood, that is: He made a good word like a good tree, and judged that it is like it. The place of "like a tree" is accusative, being an adjective of "a word," or nominative by presupposing a subject, that is: it is like a tree. It is also permissible for "a word" to be the first of the two objects of "set forth," and it is delayed after the second object, which is "a parable," lest it be far from its adjective. The first is preferable. "A word" and what follows it is an explanation of the parable. Then He described the tree with His saying: ﴿Its root is firm﴾ that is, established, secure from being uprooted, by reason of its being firmly fixed in the earth by its roots, ﴿and its branches are in the sky﴾ that is, its top rises toward the direction of the sky, high in the air.

Then Glorified is He described it as ﴿yielding its fruit every season﴾, every time, ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾, by His will and His decree. It is said: it is the date palm. It is said: it is other than it.

It is said that what is meant by its yielding its fruit every season is every hour of the hours, of night or day, at all times, without distinction between winter and summer. It is said: what is meant is at different times without specification. It is said: every morning and evening. It is said: every month. It is said: every six months.

Al-Naḥḥas said: These statements are close in meaning and not contradictory, because "ḥīn" according to all the people of the language, except those who deviate among them, means a time, which occurs for a short or a long duration. Al-Aṣmaʿī recited the verse of al-Nābigha:

"He divorces her for a time, and for a time he takes her back."

Al-Naḥḥas said: This shows you that ḥīn means time.

"Ḥīn" has also occurred in some places where more is meant, such as His saying: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time from eternity?﴾ [al-Insān: 1].

The statements of the scholars on "ḥīn" have already been explained in Surat al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place and enjoyment for a time﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36].

Al-Zajjāj said: ḥīn is a time, whether long or short. ﴿And Allah sets forth parables for the people that they may remember﴾, that they may reflect upon the states of the origin and the return, and the wondrous works of His creation, which indicate His existence and His oneness. In setting forth parables there is an increase in reminder, understanding, and depiction of meanings.

﴿And the parable of an evil word﴾ its explanation has already passed. It is said: it is the disbeliever himself, and the good word is the believer himself. ﴿Like an evil tree﴾ that is, like the likeness of an evil tree. It is said: it is the colocynth tree. It is said: it is the garlic plant. It is said: the truffle. It is said: the moss. It is said: it is the dodder, with a damma on the first letter and a final letter with three dots, and it is a plant with no leaves and no roots in the earth.

The poet said:

"And it is dodder, with no root and no fruit."

It was also read as "and a parable, a word" in the accusative, coordinated with "a good word." ﴿Uprooted from above the earth﴾ that is, it was rooted out and pulled up from its base. From it is the saying of the poet:

"It is the exile which uproots your root."

The historian said: its body (juththa) was taken, and it is itself; al-juththa is the person's body. It is said: jatthahu means he pulled it out, and ijtatthahu means he uprooted it. The meaning of ﴿from above the earth﴾ is that it has no firm root and no roots firmly established in the earth. ﴿It has no stability﴾ that is, no settling upon the earth.

It is said: no steadfastness upon the earth, just as the disbeliever and his word have no proof, no steadfastness, and no good comes from him at all, and no good word or good deed rises up from him.

﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word﴾ that is, with the clear proof, which is the good word mentioned earlier.

It is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ that it is the word of testimony, the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and that is when the believer sits up in his grave. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "That is His saying: ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word﴾." It is said: the meaning of Allah's keeping them firm is that they persist upon the firm word. From it is the saying of ʿAbdullāh ibn Rawāḥa:

"May Allah keep firm for you what He has given you of goodness, the keeping firm of Moses, and victory like that with which they were victorious."

The meaning of "in the life of this world" is that they continue upon the firm word in the life of this world. A group said: what is meant by "the life of this world" in this verse is the grave, because the dead are in the world until they are resurrected, and the meaning of "and in the Hereafter" is at the time of reckoning.

It is said: what is meant by "the life of this world" is the time of questioning in the grave, and "in the Hereafter" is the time of questioning on the Day of Resurrection. What is meant is that when they are asked about their creed and religion, they make it clear with the firm word without stammering, hesitation, or ignorance, unlike one who has not been granted success who says: "I do not know," so it is said to him: "You did not know, nor did you learn." ﴿And Allah leaves the wrongdoers astray﴾ that is, He leaves them astray from their proof, which is the firm word, so they are unable to speak it in their graves or at the reckoning, just as He left them astray from following the truth in the world.

It is said: what is meant by "the wrongdoers" here is the disbelievers. It is said: every one who wrongs himself, even by merely turning away from the clear signs, does not stand firm in the times of trials and is not guided to the truth. Then Glorified is He mentioned that He does what He wills of keeping firm and forsaking, and none can repel His judgment, and He is not questioned about what He does.

Al-Farrāʾ said: that is, no power is denied to Him, and He is not questioned about what He does. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun in both places is to emphasize awe, as it has been said, and Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 14, verses 28–34 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿Have you not seen?﴾ This is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone suited to it. It expresses wonder at the state of the disbelievers, who replaced the blessing of Allah upon them with disbelief. That is, instead of thanking Him for it, they disbelieved in it. This was by their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) when Allah raised him up from among them and bestowed His blessing upon them through him.

The majority of the exegetes held that they are the disbelievers of Makkah and that the verse was revealed concerning them. It was also said that it was revealed concerning those who fought the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Badr. It was said that it was revealed concerning two clans of the tribes of Quraysh, Banu Makhzum and Banu Umayyah. It was said that it was revealed concerning the Arabs who had become Christians, namely Jabalah ibn al-Ayham and his companions. But this is open to question, for Jabalah and his companions did not embrace Islam until the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). It was also said that it is general, covering all the polytheists. And it was said that the meaning of ﴿replaced the blessing of Allah with disbelief﴾ is that when they disbelieved in it, Allah took it away from them, so they became those who had exchanged it for disbelief. ﴿And caused their people to alight in the abode of ruin﴾: that is, they brought their people down into the abode of ruin, because of what they had made attractive to them of disbelief. ﴿The abode of ruin﴾ is Hell. Al-bawar means destruction. It was also said that they are the leaders of Quraysh who caused their people to alight, on the day of Badr, in the abode of ruin, that is, destruction, which is the killing by which they were struck. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"I have not seen their like, champions of war, on the morning of battle when ruin was feared."*

The first interpretation is preferable because of His saying ﴿Hell﴾, which is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to ﴿the abode of ruin﴾. The phrase ﴿they will burn in it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥal), or it is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnaf) explaining how they come to dwell in it. ﴿And wretched is the settling place﴾: that is, wretched is their settling place therein, or wretched is Hell as a dwelling place. The object of the blame is omitted.

﴿And they set up rivals to Allah﴾ is conjoined to ﴿and caused [them] to alight﴾. That is, they made partners for Allah in lordship, or in naming, and these are the idols.

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿liyaḍillū﴾ with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, meaning "that they might lead themselves astray from the way of Allah." The lām here is the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿaqibah), meaning that their setting up rivals to Allah was followed by their going astray, since a rational person does not intend the misguidance of himself. The use of the lam of consequence here is apt, because it resembles the purpose and end in that it occurs at the final stage, and resemblance is one of the features that justify a figurative usage (majaz).

The rest read it with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, ﴿liyuḍillū﴾, meaning "that they might cause their people to go astray from the way of Allah." This is the purpose of their setting up rivals to Allah.

Then He threatened them, the Glorified, and said to His Prophet (ﷺ): **Say: "Enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire."** That is, enjoy what you are in of desires, and what your own souls have made attractive to you of ingratitude for blessings and misguidance of people. ﴿For your destination is to the Fire﴾: that is, your return and your place of return is to it, and nothing else. Since this was their state, and because of their extreme avidity for it and their immersion in it, they would not desist from it nor accept the advice of those who counsel them, the command to engage in it was placed in the position of a prohibition of approaching it, to make clear what their outcome would be and that they would inevitably proceed to the Fire, so they must take up the means that bring that about. Thus the clause ﴿for your destination is to the Fire﴾ is a justification for the command to enjoy. There is in it a threat beyond measure. It is also permissible that this clause be an answer to an omitted condition indicated by the context of the speech, as if it were said: "If you persist in that, then your destination is to the Fire." The first is preferable, and the Qur'anic structure points to it. This is like what is said to one who strives to oppose the ruler: "Do whatever opposition you wish, for your destination is the sword."

﴿Say to My servants who have believed: let them establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾. Since He had commanded him to say to those who changed the blessing of Allah into disbelief and set up rivals to Allah what he had said to them, He commanded him to say this to the group opposed to them, namely the group of believers. The thing said is omitted, indicated by what is mentioned: that is, "Say to My servants: establish [the prayer] and spend." So ﴿let them establish﴾ is in the jussive because it is the answer to the omitted imperative, and likewise ﴿let them spend﴾. Al-Farraʾ mentioned this meaning.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿let them establish﴾ is jussive in the sense of the lam (of command), meaning "so that they may establish," and the lam was dropped. Then he mentioned another reason for the jussive, similar to what al-Farraʾ mentioned. As for ﴿secretly and openly﴾, it is in the accusative either as a circumstantial state (ḥal), meaning "those who spend secretly and openly," or as an infinitive (maṣdar), meaning "spending in secret and spending openly," or as an adverb of time (ẓarf), meaning "at a time of secrecy and at a time of openness."

The majority said: the secret is what is hidden, and the open is what is manifest. It was also said: the secret is voluntary charity, and the open is obligatory charity. The explanation of this has already been given at the commentary on His saying: ﴿If you disclose your charities, it is good﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:271).

﴿Before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship﴾. Abu ʿUbaydah said: "trade" here means ransom, and "khilal" means friendship, and it is a verbal noun. Al-Wahidi said: this is the saying of all the people of the language.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: it is permissible that it be the plural of *khullah*, like *burmah* and *biram*, and *ʿulbah* and *ʿilab*. The meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection there is no trade, so that one who fell short in deeds may ransom himself from the punishment of Allah by giving some compensation for it; and there is no friendship, so that a close friend may intercede for his friend and rescue him from the punishment. So the Glorified commanded them to spend, in the ways of goodness, from what Allah has provided them while they are still in this worldly life and able to spend their wealth, before the Day of Resurrection comes, for they will not be able to do that then, indeed they will have no wealth at that time. So the clause, I mean ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship﴾, is for emphasizing the content of the command to spend from what Allah has provided.

It is possible that there is also in it an emphasis on the content of the command to establish the prayer, because neglecting it often comes from being occupied with trade and with caring for the rights of friends. The explanation of trade and friendship has already been given in al-Baqarah.

﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, He originated and invented them without a precedent, and created what is in them of celestial and terrestrial bodies. The noble name is the subject, and what follows is its predicate.

﴿And sent down from the sky water﴾: here "sky" means the direction of height. It includes the sphere according to the one who said that the beginning of rain is from it, and it includes the clouds according to the one who said that the beginning of rain is from them, and it includes the causes that stir up the clouds, such as the winds. The indefiniteness of *māʾ* (water) here is for the sense of kind, that is, a kind of water, and it is rainwater.

﴿And brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾: that is, He brought forth by that water from various fruits a provision for the children of Adam by which they live. The *min* in ﴿min al-thamarāt﴾ is for specification, like your saying "I spent of the dirhams." It was also said that it is for partitive meaning, because among the fruits some are provision for the children of Adam and some are not provision for them, namely those they do not eat and do not benefit from.

﴿And He subjected to you the ships to run through the sea by His command﴾: they run according to your will, and you use them for your interests. Therefore He said ﴿to run through the sea as you wish﴾ and according to what you seek, by His command, that is, by the command and will of Allah. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Baqarah.

﴿And He subjected to you the rivers﴾: that is, He made them submissive to you, so that you ride upon them and direct them where you wish.

﴿And He subjected to you the sun and the moon, constant [in their courses]﴾, for you to benefit by them and to be illuminated by their light. The accusative of *dāʾibayn* is a circumstantial state (ḥal). *Al-duʾūb* is the passing of a thing in its work in a customary manner, that is, constant in setting right what they set right of plants and other things. It was also said: constant in motion in obedience to the command of Allah. The meaning is that they run until the Day of Resurrection without slackening, and their course does not cease.

﴿And He subjected to you the night and the day﴾, alternating. The day is for your striving in matters of your livelihood and what you need of the affairs of your worldly life, and the night is for you to rest, as He the Glorified said: (p-749) ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty﴾ (al-Qasas 28:73).

﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾. Al-Akhfash said: that is, He gave you of every thing you asked of Him something, so *shayʾan* (something) was omitted. It was also said: the meaning is "He gave you of all that you asked of Him and of all that you did not ask of Him," so the other clause was omitted. This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

It was also said: the *min* is extra, meaning "He gave you all that you asked of Him." It was said: it is for partitive meaning, meaning "He gave you some of all that you asked of Him."

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and Qatadah read ﴿min kullin﴾ with tanwin on *kull*. On this reading it is permissible that *ma* be negative, meaning "He gave you of all of that while you were not asking for it." It is also permissible that *ma* be relative, meaning "He gave you of every thing which you asked of Him."

﴿And if you count the blessing of Allah, you cannot number it﴾: that is, if you undertake to count the blessings of Allah which He has bestowed upon you, even in summary, let alone in detail, you will not be able to enumerate them in any way, nor will you be able to confine them in any state. The origin of *iḥṣāʾ* (enumeration) is that the reckoner, when he reaches a particular unit of numbers, places a pebble to keep count with it. It is well known that if any single one of the servants tried to enumerate what Allah has bestowed upon him in the creation of one of his limbs, or one of his senses, he would never be able to do so, nor would it be possible for him at all. How then with what is beyond that of blessings in all that Allah created in his body? How then with what is beyond that of blessings reaching him at every moment, in their variety and the diversity of their kinds?

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-insān* is a generic noun by which the disbeliever specifically is intended, as He said: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ (al-ʿAṣr 103:2). ﴿Ungrateful﴾: that is, extremely ungrateful for the blessings of Allah upon him, denying them, not thankful to Allah, the Glorified, for them, as is fitting and obligatory for him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid the like of it.

Someone said: "O Commander of the Faithful, this is wrongdoing, so what about disbelief?" He said: "Indeed, man is surely a wrongdoer, a great disbeliever" (﴿Indeed, the human being is [often] wrongdoing and ungrateful﴾).

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 14, verses 28–34 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿Have you not seen?﴾ This is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone suited to it. It expresses wonder at the state of the disbelievers, who replaced the blessing of Allah upon them with disbelief. That is, instead of thanking Him for it, they disbelieved in it. This was by their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) when Allah raised him up from among them and bestowed His blessing upon them through him.

The majority of the exegetes held that they are the disbelievers of Makkah and that the verse was revealed concerning them. It was also said that it was revealed concerning those who fought the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Badr. It was said that it was revealed concerning two clans of the tribes of Quraysh, Banu Makhzum and Banu Umayyah. It was said that it was revealed concerning the Arabs who had become Christians, namely Jabalah ibn al-Ayham and his companions. But this is open to question, for Jabalah and his companions did not embrace Islam until the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). It was also said that it is general, covering all the polytheists. And it was said that the meaning of ﴿replaced the blessing of Allah with disbelief﴾ is that when they disbelieved in it, Allah took it away from them, so they became those who had exchanged it for disbelief. ﴿And caused their people to alight in the abode of ruin﴾: that is, they brought their people down into the abode of ruin, because of what they had made attractive to them of disbelief. ﴿The abode of ruin﴾ is Hell. Al-bawar means destruction. It was also said that they are the leaders of Quraysh who caused their people to alight, on the day of Badr, in the abode of ruin, that is, destruction, which is the killing by which they were struck. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"I have not seen their like, champions of war, on the morning of battle when ruin was feared."*

The first interpretation is preferable because of His saying ﴿Hell﴾, which is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to ﴿the abode of ruin﴾. The phrase ﴿they will burn in it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥal), or it is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnaf) explaining how they come to dwell in it. ﴿And wretched is the settling place﴾: that is, wretched is their settling place therein, or wretched is Hell as a dwelling place. The object of the blame is omitted.

﴿And they set up rivals to Allah﴾ is conjoined to ﴿and caused [them] to alight﴾. That is, they made partners for Allah in lordship, or in naming, and these are the idols.

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿liyaḍillū﴾ with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, meaning "that they might lead themselves astray from the way of Allah." The lām here is the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿaqibah), meaning that their setting up rivals to Allah was followed by their going astray, since a rational person does not intend the misguidance of himself. The use of the lam of consequence here is apt, because it resembles the purpose and end in that it occurs at the final stage, and resemblance is one of the features that justify a figurative usage (majaz).

The rest read it with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, ﴿liyuḍillū﴾, meaning "that they might cause their people to go astray from the way of Allah." This is the purpose of their setting up rivals to Allah.

Then He threatened them, the Glorified, and said to His Prophet (ﷺ): **Say: "Enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire."** That is, enjoy what you are in of desires, and what your own souls have made attractive to you of ingratitude for blessings and misguidance of people. ﴿For your destination is to the Fire﴾: that is, your return and your place of return is to it, and nothing else. Since this was their state, and because of their extreme avidity for it and their immersion in it, they would not desist from it nor accept the advice of those who counsel them, the command to engage in it was placed in the position of a prohibition of approaching it, to make clear what their outcome would be and that they would inevitably proceed to the Fire, so they must take up the means that bring that about. Thus the clause ﴿for your destination is to the Fire﴾ is a justification for the command to enjoy. There is in it a threat beyond measure. It is also permissible that this clause be an answer to an omitted condition indicated by the context of the speech, as if it were said: "If you persist in that, then your destination is to the Fire." The first is preferable, and the Qur'anic structure points to it. This is like what is said to one who strives to oppose the ruler: "Do whatever opposition you wish, for your destination is the sword."

﴿Say to My servants who have believed: let them establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾. Since He had commanded him to say to those who changed the blessing of Allah into disbelief and set up rivals to Allah what he had said to them, He commanded him to say this to the group opposed to them, namely the group of believers. The thing said is omitted, indicated by what is mentioned: that is, "Say to My servants: establish [the prayer] and spend." So ﴿let them establish﴾ is in the jussive because it is the answer to the omitted imperative, and likewise ﴿let them spend﴾. Al-Farraʾ mentioned this meaning.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿let them establish﴾ is jussive in the sense of the lam (of command), meaning "so that they may establish," and the lam was dropped. Then he mentioned another reason for the jussive, similar to what al-Farraʾ mentioned. As for ﴿secretly and openly﴾, it is in the accusative either as a circumstantial state (ḥal), meaning "those who spend secretly and openly," or as an infinitive (maṣdar), meaning "spending in secret and spending openly," or as an adverb of time (ẓarf), meaning "at a time of secrecy and at a time of openness."

The majority said: the secret is what is hidden, and the open is what is manifest. It was also said: the secret is voluntary charity, and the open is obligatory charity. The explanation of this has already been given at the commentary on His saying: ﴿If you disclose your charities, it is good﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:271).

﴿Before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship﴾. Abu ʿUbaydah said: "trade" here means ransom, and "khilal" means friendship, and it is a verbal noun. Al-Wahidi said: this is the saying of all the people of the language.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: it is permissible that it be the plural of *khullah*, like *burmah* and *biram*, and *ʿulbah* and *ʿilab*. The meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection there is no trade, so that one who fell short in deeds may ransom himself from the punishment of Allah by giving some compensation for it; and there is no friendship, so that a close friend may intercede for his friend and rescue him from the punishment. So the Glorified commanded them to spend, in the ways of goodness, from what Allah has provided them while they are still in this worldly life and able to spend their wealth, before the Day of Resurrection comes, for they will not be able to do that then, indeed they will have no wealth at that time. So the clause, I mean ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship﴾, is for emphasizing the content of the command to spend from what Allah has provided.

It is possible that there is also in it an emphasis on the content of the command to establish the prayer, because neglecting it often comes from being occupied with trade and with caring for the rights of friends. The explanation of trade and friendship has already been given in al-Baqarah.

The indefiniteness of *māʾ* (water) here is for the sense of kind, that is, a kind of water, and it is rainwater.

It was also said that it is for partitive meaning, because among the fruits some are provision for the children of Adam and some are not provision for them, namely those they do not eat and do not benefit from.

﴿And He subjected to you the ships to run through the sea by His command﴾: they run according to your will, and you use them for your interests. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Baqarah.

﴿And He subjected to you the rivers﴾: that is, He made them submissive to you, so that you ride upon them and direct them where you wish.

The accusative of *dāʾibayn* is a circumstantial state (ḥal). *Al-duʾūb* is the passing of a thing in its work in a customary manner, that is, constant in setting right what they set right of plants and other things. It is also permissible that this clause be an answer to an omitted condition indicated by the context of the speech, as if it were said: "If you persist in that, then your destination is to the Fire." The first is preferable, and the Qur'anic structure points to it. This is like what is said to one who strives to oppose the ruler: "Do whatever opposition you wish, for your destination is the sword."

﴿Say to My servants who have believed: let them establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾. Since He had commanded him to say to those who changed the blessing of Allah into disbelief and set up rivals to Allah what he had said to them, He commanded him to say this to the group opposed to them, namely the group of believers. The thing said is omitted, indicated by what is mentioned: that is, "Say to My servants: establish [the prayer] and spend." So ﴿let them establish﴾ is in the jussive because it is the answer to the omitted imperative, and likewise ﴿let them spend﴾. Al-Farraʾ mentioned this meaning.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿let them establish﴾ is jussive in the sense of the lam (of command), meaning "so that they may establish," and the lam was dropped. Then he mentioned another reason for the jussive, similar to what al-Farraʾ mentioned. As for ﴿secretly and openly﴾, it is in the accusative either as a circumstantial state (ḥal), meaning "those who spend secretly and openly," or as an infinitive (maṣdar), meaning "spending in secret and spending openly," or as an adverb of time (ẓarf), meaning "at a time of secrecy and at a time of openness."

The majority said: the secret is what is hidden, and the open is what is manifest. It was also said: the secret is voluntary charity, and the open is obligatory charity. The explanation of this has already been given at the commentary on His saying: ﴿If you disclose your charities, it is good﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:271).

﴿Before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship﴾. Abu ʿUbaydah said: "trade" here means ransom, and "khilal" means friendship, and it is a verbal noun. Al-Wahidi said: this is the saying of all the people of the language.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: it is permissible that it be the plural of *khullah*, like *burmah* and *biram*, and *ʿulbah* and *ʿilab*. The meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection there is no trade, so that one who fell short in deeds may ransom himself from the punishment of Allah by giving some compensation for it; and there is no friendship, so that a close friend may intercede for his friend and rescue him from the punishment. So the Glorified commanded them to spend, in the ways of goodness, from what Allah has provided them while they are still in this worldly life and able to spend their wealth, before the Day of Resurrection comes, for they will not be able to do that then, indeed they will have no wealth at that time. So the clause, I mean ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship﴾, is for emphasizing the content of the command to spend from what Allah has provided.

It is possible that there is also in it an emphasis on the content of the command to establish the prayer, because neglecting it often comes from being occupied with trade and with caring for the rights of friends. The explanation of trade and friendship has already been given in al-Baqarah.

﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, He originated and invented them without a precedent, and created what is in them of celestial and terrestrial bodies. The noble name is the subject, and what follows is its predicate.

﴿And sent down from the sky water﴾: here "sky" means the direction of height. It includes the sphere according to the one who said that the beginning of rain is from it, and it includes the clouds according to the one who said that the beginning of rain is from them, and it includes the causes that stir up the clouds, such as the winds. The indefiniteness of *māʾ* (water) here is for the sense of kind, that is, a kind of water, and it is rainwater.

﴿And brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾: that is, He brought forth by that water from various fruits a provision for the children of Adam by which they live. The *min* in ﴿min al-thamarāt﴾ is for specification, like your saying "I spent of the dirhams." It was also said that it is for partitive meaning, because among the fruits some are provision for the children of Adam and some are not provision for them, namely those they do not eat and do not benefit from.

﴿And He subjected to you the ships to run through the sea by His command﴾: they run according to your will, and you use them for your interests. Therefore He said ﴿to run through the sea as you wish﴾ and according to what you seek, by His command, that is, by the command and will of Allah. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Baqarah.

﴿And He subjected to you the rivers﴾: that is, He made them submissive to you, so that you ride upon them and direct them where you wish.

﴿And He subjected to you the sun and the moon, constant [in their courses]﴾, for you to benefit by them and to be illuminated by their light. The accusative of *dāʾibayn* is a circumstantial state (ḥal). *Al-duʾūb* is the passing of a thing in its work in a customary manner, that is, constant in setting right what they set right of plants and other things. It was also said: constant in motion in obedience to the command of Allah. The meaning is that they run until the Day of Resurrection without slackening, and their course does not cease.

﴿And He subjected to you the night and the day﴾, alternating. The day is for your striving in matters of your livelihood and what you need of the affairs of your worldly life, and the night is for you to rest, as He the Glorified said: (p-749) ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty﴾ (al-Qasas 28:73).

﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾. Al-Akhfash said: that is, He gave you of every thing you asked of Him something, so *shayʾan* (something) was omitted. It was also said: the meaning is "He gave you of all that you asked of Him and of all that you did not ask of Him," so the other clause was omitted. This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

It was also said: the *min* is extra, meaning "He gave you all that you asked of Him." It was said: it is for partitive meaning, meaning "He gave you some of all that you asked of Him."

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and Qatadah read ﴿min kullin﴾ with tanwin on *kull*. On this reading it is permissible that *ma* be negative, meaning "He gave you of all of that while you were not asking for it." It is also permissible that *ma* be relative, meaning "He gave you of every thing which you asked of Him."

﴿And if you count the blessing of Allah, you cannot number it﴾: that is, if you undertake to count the blessings of Allah which He has bestowed upon you, even in summary, let alone in detail, you will not be able to enumerate them in any way, nor will you be able to confine them in any state. The origin of *iḥṣāʾ* (enumeration) is that the reckoner, when he reaches a particular unit of numbers, places a pebble to keep count with it. It is well known that if any single one of the servants tried to enumerate what Allah has bestowed upon him in the creation of one of his limbs, or one of his senses, he would never be able to do so, nor would it be possible for him at all. How then with what is beyond that of blessings in all that Allah created in his body? How then with what is beyond that of blessings reaching him at every moment, in their variety and the diversity of their kinds?

O Allah, indeed we thank You for every blessing You have bestowed upon us, those which none knows but You, and those we know, a thanks that no measure encompasses and no counting confines, and for the number of what the thankful have thanked You with every tongue in every age. ﴿Indeed, man is ever a wrongdoer﴾ to himself, by neglecting to thank Allah for His blessings upon him. Its apparent meaning includes every human being.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-insān* is a generic noun by which the disbeliever specifically is intended, as He said: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ (al-ʿAṣr 103:2). ﴿Ungrateful﴾: that is, extremely ungrateful for the blessings of Allah upon him, denying them, not thankful to Allah, the Glorified, for them, as is fitting and obligatory for him.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Saʿid ibn Mansur, al-Bukhari, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief?﴾ He said: they are the disbelievers of the people of Makkah.

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab concerning His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief?﴾ He said: they are the two most wicked clans of Quraysh: Banu al-Mughirah and Banu Umayyah. As for Banu al-Mughirah, you were sufficient against them on the day of Badr; and as for Banu Umayyah, they were given enjoyment for a time.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, from ʿUmar, something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through several chains from ʿAli concerning the verse something similar as well.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu al-Tufayl that Ibn al-Kawwa asked ʿAli about those who exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief. He said: they are the wicked of Quraysh, whom you were sufficient against on the day of Badr.

He said: "Then who are those whose effort went astray in the life of this world?" He said: "Among them are the people of Harurah."

Something similar has been narrated from ʿAli through several chains concerning the explanation of this verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse, he said: they are Jabalah ibn al-Ayham and those among the Arabs who followed him, who joined the Romans.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿and caused their people to alight in the abode of ruin﴾, he said: "the ruin," that is, destruction.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And they set up rivals to Allah﴾, he said: they associated others with Allah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verse 28–34 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding ﴿And He subjected for you the rivers﴾ that he said: "With every benefit."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And He subjected for you the sun and the moon, both constant﴾ that he said: "Their constancy in obedience to Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ikrimah regarding ﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾ that he said: "Of everything you desired from Him."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid the like of it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan who said: "Of all that you asked of Him."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Sulayman al-Taymi who said: "Indeed Allah bestows blessings upon the servants according to their capacity, and He obligates them to give thanks according to their capacity."

Both of them (Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi) also narrated from Bakr ibn Abd Allah al-Muzani who said: "O son of Adam, if you wish to know the measure of what Allah has bestowed upon you, then close your eyes."

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu al-Darda' who said: "Whoever does not recognize the blessing of Allah upon him except in his food and drink, then his deeds have become few and his punishment has drawn near."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Ayyub al-Qurashi, client of the Banu Hashim, who said: "Dawud, peace be upon him, said: 'My Lord, inform me of the least of Your blessings upon me.' So He revealed to him: 'O Dawud, breathe.' He breathed, and then He said: 'This is the least of My blessings upon you.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "O Allah, forgive me my wrongdoing and my disbelief." Someone said: "O Commander of the Faithful, this is wrongdoing, so what about disbelief?" He said: "Indeed, man is surely a wrongdoer, a great disbeliever" (﴿Indeed, the human being is [often] wrongdoing and ungrateful﴾).

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 14, verses 28–34 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿Have you not seen?﴾ This is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone suited to it. It expresses wonder at the state of the disbelievers, who replaced the blessing of Allah upon them with disbelief. That is, instead of thanking Him for it, they disbelieved in it. This was by their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) when Allah raised him up from among them and bestowed His blessing upon them through him.

The majority of the exegetes held that they are the disbelievers of Makkah and that the verse was revealed concerning them. It was also said that it was revealed concerning those who fought the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Badr. It was said that it was revealed concerning two clans of the tribes of Quraysh, Banu Makhzum and Banu Umayyah. It was said that it was revealed concerning the Arabs who had become Christians, namely Jabalah ibn al-Ayham and his companions. But this is open to question, for Jabalah and his companions did not embrace Islam until the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). It was also said that it is general, covering all the polytheists. And it was said that the meaning of ﴿replaced the blessing of Allah with disbelief﴾ is that when they disbelieved in it, Allah took it away from them, so they became those who had exchanged it for disbelief. ﴿And caused their people to alight in the abode of ruin﴾: that is, they brought their people down into the abode of ruin, because of what they had made attractive to them of disbelief. ﴿The abode of ruin﴾ is Hell. Al-bawar means destruction. It was also said that they are the leaders of Quraysh who caused their people to alight, on the day of Badr, in the abode of ruin, that is, destruction, which is the killing by which they were struck. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"I have not seen their like, champions of war, on the morning of battle when ruin was feared."*

The first interpretation is preferable because of His saying ﴿Hell﴾, which is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to ﴿the abode of ruin﴾. The phrase ﴿they will burn in it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥal), or it is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnaf) explaining how they come to dwell in it. ﴿And wretched is the settling place﴾: that is, wretched is their settling place therein, or wretched is Hell as a dwelling place. The object of the blame is omitted.

﴿And they set up rivals to Allah﴾ is conjoined to ﴿and caused [them] to alight﴾. That is, they made partners for Allah in lordship, or in naming, and these are the idols.

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿liyaḍillū﴾ with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, meaning "that they might lead themselves astray from the way of Allah." The lām here is the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿaqibah), meaning that their setting up rivals to Allah was followed by their going astray, since a rational person does not intend the misguidance of himself. The use of the lam of consequence here is apt, because it resembles the purpose and end in that it occurs at the final stage, and resemblance is one of the features that justify a figurative usage (majaz).

The rest read it with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, ﴿liyuḍillū﴾, meaning "that they might cause their people to go astray from the way of Allah." This is the purpose of their setting up rivals to Allah.

Then He threatened them, the Glorified, and said to His Prophet (ﷺ): **Say: "Enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire."** That is, enjoy what you are in of desires, and what your own souls have made attractive to you of ingratitude for blessings and misguidance of people. ﴿For your destination is to the Fire﴾: that is, your return and your place of return is to it, and nothing else. Since this was their state, and because of their extreme avidity for it and their immersion in it, they would not desist from it nor accept the advice of those who counsel them, the command to engage in it was placed in the position of a prohibition of approaching it, to make clear what their outcome would be and that they would inevitably proceed to the Fire, so they must take up the means that bring that about. Thus the clause ﴿for your destination is to the Fire﴾ is a justification for the command to enjoy. There is in it a threat beyond measure. It is also permissible that this clause be an answer to an omitted condition indicated by the context of the speech, as if it were said: "If you persist in that, then your destination is to the Fire." The first is preferable, and the Qur'anic structure points to it. This is like what is said to one who strives to oppose the ruler: "Do whatever opposition you wish, for your destination is the sword."

﴿Say to My servants who have believed: let them establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾. Since He had commanded him to say to those who changed the blessing of Allah into disbelief and set up rivals to Allah what he had said to them, He commanded him to say this to the group opposed to them, namely the group of believers. The majority said: the secret is what is hidden, and the open is what is manifest. It was also said: the secret is voluntary charity, and the open is obligatory charity. The explanation of this has already been given at the commentary on His saying: ﴿If you disclose your charities, it is good﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:271).
