Both of them (Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi) also narrated from Bakr ibn Abd Allah al-Muzani who said: "O son of Adam, if you wish to know the measure of what Allah has bestowed upon you, then close your eyes."

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu al-Darda' who said: "Whoever does not recognize the blessing of Allah upon him except in his food and drink, then his deeds have become few and his punishment has drawn near."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Ayyub al-Qurashi, client of the Banu Hashim, who said: "Dawud, peace be upon him, said: 'My Lord, inform me of the least of Your blessings upon me.' So He revealed to him: 'O Dawud, breathe.' He breathed, and then He said: 'This is the least of My blessings upon you.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "O Allah, forgive me my wrongdoing and my disbelief." Someone said: "O Commander of the Faithful, this is wrongdoing, so what about disbelief?" He said: "Indeed, man is surely a wrongdoer, a great disbeliever" (﴿Indeed, the human being is [often] wrongdoing and ungrateful﴾).

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 14, verses 28–34 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿Have you not seen?﴾ This is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone suited to it. It expresses wonder at the state of the disbelievers, who replaced the blessing of Allah upon them with disbelief. That is, instead of thanking Him for it, they disbelieved in it. This was by their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) when Allah raised him up from among them and bestowed His blessing upon them through him.

The majority of the exegetes held that they are the disbelievers of Makkah and that the verse was revealed concerning them. It was also said that it was revealed concerning those who fought the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Badr. It was said that it was revealed concerning two clans of the tribes of Quraysh, Banu Makhzum and Banu Umayyah. It was said that it was revealed concerning the Arabs who had become Christians, namely Jabalah ibn al-Ayham and his companions. But this is open to question, for Jabalah and his companions did not embrace Islam until the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). It was also said that it is general, covering all the polytheists. And it was said that the meaning of ﴿replaced the blessing of Allah with disbelief﴾ is that when they disbelieved in it, Allah took it away from them, so they became those who had exchanged it for disbelief. ﴿And caused their people to alight in the abode of ruin﴾: that is, they brought their people down into the abode of ruin, because of what they had made attractive to them of disbelief. ﴿The abode of ruin﴾ is Hell. Al-bawar means destruction. It was also said that they are the leaders of Quraysh who caused their people to alight, on the day of Badr, in the abode of ruin, that is, destruction, which is the killing by which they were struck. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"I have not seen their like, champions of war, on the morning of battle when ruin was feared."*

The first interpretation is preferable because of His saying ﴿Hell﴾, which is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to ﴿the abode of ruin﴾. The phrase ﴿they will burn in it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥal), or it is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnaf) explaining how they come to dwell in it. ﴿And wretched is the settling place﴾: that is, wretched is their settling place therein, or wretched is Hell as a dwelling place. The object of the blame is omitted.

﴿And they set up rivals to Allah﴾ is conjoined to ﴿and caused [them] to alight﴾. That is, they made partners for Allah in lordship, or in naming, and these are the idols.

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿liyaḍillū﴾ with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, meaning "that they might lead themselves astray from the way of Allah." The lām here is the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿaqibah), meaning that their setting up rivals to Allah was followed by their going astray, since a rational person does not intend the misguidance of himself. The use of the lam of consequence here is apt, because it resembles the purpose and end in that it occurs at the final stage, and resemblance is one of the features that justify a figurative usage (majaz).

The rest read it with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, ﴿liyuḍillū﴾, meaning "that they might cause their people to go astray from the way of Allah." This is the purpose of their setting up rivals to Allah.

Then He threatened them, the Glorified, and said to His Prophet (ﷺ): **Say: "Enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire."** That is, enjoy what you are in of desires, and what your own souls have made attractive to you of ingratitude for blessings and misguidance of people. ﴿For your destination is to the Fire﴾: that is, your return and your place of return is to it, and nothing else. Since this was their state, and because of their extreme avidity for it and their immersion in it, they would not desist from it nor accept the advice of those who counsel them, the command to engage in it was placed in the position of a prohibition of approaching it, to make clear what their outcome would be and that they would inevitably proceed to the Fire, so they must take up the means that bring that about. Thus the clause ﴿for your destination is to the Fire﴾ is a justification for the command to enjoy. There is in it a threat beyond measure. It is also permissible that this clause be an answer to an omitted condition indicated by the context of the speech, as if it were said: "If you persist in that, then your destination is to the Fire." The first is preferable, and the Qur'anic structure points to it. This is like what is said to one who strives to oppose the ruler: "Do whatever opposition you wish, for your destination is the sword."

﴿Say to My servants who have believed: let them establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾. Since He had commanded him to say to those who changed the blessing of Allah into disbelief and set up rivals to Allah what he had said to them, He commanded him to say this to the group opposed to them, namely the group of believers. The thing said is omitted, indicated by what is mentioned: that is, "Say to My servants: establish [the prayer] and spend." So ﴿let them establish﴾ is in the jussive because it is the answer to the omitted imperative, and likewise ﴿let them spend﴾. Al-Farraʾ mentioned this meaning.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿let them establish﴾ is jussive in the sense of the lam (of command), meaning "so that they may establish," and the lam was dropped. Then he mentioned another reason for the jussive, similar to what al-Farraʾ mentioned. As for ﴿secretly and openly﴾, it is in the accusative either as a circumstantial state (ḥal), meaning "those who spend secretly and openly," or as an infinitive (maṣdar), meaning "spending in secret and spending openly," or as an adverb of time (ẓarf), meaning "at a time of secrecy and at a time of openness."

The majority said: the secret is what is hidden, and the open is what is manifest. It was also said: the secret is voluntary charity, and the open is obligatory charity. The explanation of this has already been given at the commentary on His saying: ﴿If you disclose your charities, it is good﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:271).

﴿Before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship﴾. Abu ʿUbaydah said: "trade" here means ransom, and "khilal" means friendship, and it is a verbal noun. Al-Wahidi said: this is the saying of all the people of the language.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: it is permissible that it be the plural of *khullah*, like *burmah* and *biram*, and *ʿulbah* and *ʿilab*. The meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection there is no trade, so that one who fell short in deeds may ransom himself from the punishment of Allah by giving some compensation for it; and there is no friendship, so that a close friend may intercede for his friend and rescue him from the punishment. So the Glorified commanded them to spend, in the ways of goodness, from what Allah has provided them while they are still in this worldly life and able to spend their wealth, before the Day of Resurrection comes, for they will not be able to do that then, indeed they will have no wealth at that time. So the clause, I mean ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship﴾, is for emphasizing the content of the command to spend from what Allah has provided.

It is possible that there is also in it an emphasis on the content of the command to establish the prayer, because neglecting it often comes from being occupied with trade and with caring for the rights of friends. The explanation of trade and friendship has already been given in al-Baqarah.

﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, He originated and invented them without a precedent, and created what is in them of celestial and terrestrial bodies. The noble name is the subject, and what follows is its predicate.

﴿And sent down from the sky water﴾: here "sky" means the direction of height. It includes the sphere according to the one who said that the beginning of rain is from it, and it includes the clouds according to the one who said that the beginning of rain is from them, and it includes the causes that stir up the clouds, such as the winds. The indefiniteness of *māʾ* (water) here is for the sense of kind, that is, a kind of water, and it is rainwater.

﴿And brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾: that is, He brought forth by that water from various fruits a provision for the children of Adam by which they live. The *min* in ﴿min al-thamarāt﴾ is for specification, like your saying "I spent of the dirhams." It was also said that it is for partitive meaning, because among the fruits some are provision for the children of Adam and some are not provision for them, namely those they do not eat and do not benefit from.

﴿And He subjected to you the ships to run through the sea by His command﴾: they run according to your will, and you use them for your interests. Therefore He said ﴿to run through the sea as you wish﴾ and according to what you seek, by His command, that is, by the command and will of Allah. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Baqarah.

﴿And He subjected to you the rivers﴾: that is, He made them submissive to you, so that you ride upon them and direct them where you wish.

﴿And He subjected to you the sun and the moon, constant [in their courses]﴾, for you to benefit by them and to be illuminated by their light. The accusative of *dāʾibayn* is a circumstantial state (ḥal). *Al-duʾūb* is the passing of a thing in its work in a customary manner, that is, constant in setting right what they set right of plants and other things. It was also said: constant in motion in obedience to the command of Allah. The meaning is that they run until the Day of Resurrection without slackening, and their course does not cease.

﴿And He subjected to you the night and the day﴾, alternating. The day is for your striving in matters of your livelihood and what you need of the affairs of your worldly life, and the night is for you to rest, as He the Glorified said: (p-749) ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty﴾ (al-Qasas 28:73).

﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾. Al-Akhfash said: that is, He gave you of every thing you asked of Him something, so *shayʾan* (something) was omitted. It was also said: the meaning is "He gave you of all that you asked of Him and of all that you did not ask of Him," so the other clause was omitted. This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

It was also said: the *min* is extra, meaning "He gave you all that you asked of Him." It was said: it is for partitive meaning, meaning "He gave you some of all that you asked of Him."

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and Qatadah read ﴿min kullin﴾ with tanwin on *kull*. On this reading it is permissible that *ma* be negative, meaning "He gave you of all of that while you were not asking for it." It is also permissible that *ma* be relative, meaning "He gave you of every thing which you asked of Him."

﴿And if you count the blessing of Allah, you cannot number it﴾: that is, if you undertake to count the blessings of Allah which He has bestowed upon you, even in summary, let alone in detail, you will not be able to enumerate them in any way, nor will you be able to confine them in any state. The origin of *iḥṣāʾ* (enumeration) is that the reckoner, when he reaches a particular unit of numbers, places a pebble to keep count with it. It is well known that if any single one of the servants tried to enumerate what Allah has bestowed upon him in the creation of one of his limbs, or one of his senses, he would never be able to do so, nor would it be possible for him at all. How then with what is beyond that of blessings in all that Allah created in his body? How then with what is beyond that of blessings reaching him at every moment, in their variety and the diversity of their kinds?

O Allah, indeed we thank You for every blessing You have bestowed upon us, those which none knows but You, and those we know, a thanks that no measure encompasses and no counting confines, and for the number of what the thankful have thanked You with every tongue in every age. ﴿Indeed, man is ever a wrongdoer﴾ to himself, by neglecting to thank Allah for His blessings upon him. Its apparent meaning includes every human being.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-insān* is a generic noun by which the disbeliever specifically is intended, as He said: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ (al-ʿAṣr 103:2). ﴿Ungrateful﴾: that is, extremely ungrateful for the blessings of Allah upon him, denying them, not thankful to Allah, the Glorified, for them, as is fitting and obligatory for him.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Saʿid ibn Mansur, al-Bukhari, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief?﴾ He said: they are the disbelievers of the people of Makkah.

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab concerning His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief?﴾ He said: they are the two most wicked clans of Quraysh: Banu al-Mughirah and Banu Umayyah. As for Banu al-Mughirah, you were sufficient against them on the day of Badr; and as for Banu Umayyah, they were given enjoyment for a time.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, from ʿUmar, something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through several chains from ʿAli concerning the verse something similar as well.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu al-Tufayl that Ibn al-Kawwa asked ʿAli about those who exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief. He said: they are the wicked of Quraysh, whom you were sufficient against on the day of Badr.

He said: "Then who are those whose effort went astray in the life of this world?" He said: "Among them are the people of Harurah."

Something similar has been narrated from ʿAli through several chains concerning the explanation of this verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse, he said: they are Jabalah ibn al-Ayham and those among the Arabs who followed him, who joined the Romans.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿and caused their people to alight in the abode of ruin﴾, he said: "the ruin," that is, destruction.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And they set up rivals to Allah﴾, he said: they associated others with Allah.

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and Qatadah read ﴿min kullin﴾ with tanwin on *kull*. On this reading it is permissible that *ma* be negative, meaning "He gave you of all of that while you were not asking for it." It is also permissible that *ma* be relative, meaning "He gave you of every thing which you asked of Him."

﴿And if you count the blessing of Allah, you cannot number it﴾: that is, if you undertake to count the blessings of Allah which He has bestowed upon you, even in summary, let alone in detail, you will not be able to enumerate them in any way, nor will you be able to confine them in any state. The origin of *iḥṣāʾ* (enumeration) is that the reckoner, when he reaches a particular unit of numbers, places a pebble to keep count with it. It is well known that if any single one of the servants tried to enumerate what Allah has bestowed upon him in the creation of one of his limbs, or one of his senses, he would never be able to do so, nor would it be possible for him at all. How then with what is beyond that of blessings in all that Allah created in his body? How then with what is beyond that of blessings reaching him at every moment, in their variety and the diversity of their kinds?

O Allah, indeed we thank You for every blessing You have bestowed upon us, those which none knows but You, and those we know, a thanks that no measure encompasses and no counting confines, and for the number of what the thankful have thanked You with every tongue in every age. ﴿Indeed, man is ever a wrongdoer﴾ to himself, by neglecting to thank Allah for His blessings upon him. Its apparent meaning includes every human being.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-insān* is a generic noun by which the disbeliever specifically is intended, as He said: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ (al-ʿAṣr 103:2). ﴿Ungrateful﴾: that is, extremely ungrateful for the blessings of Allah upon him, denying them, not thankful to Allah, the Glorified, for them, as is fitting and obligatory for him.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Saʿid ibn Mansur, al-Bukhari, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief?﴾ He said: they are the disbelievers of the people of Makkah.

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab concerning His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief?﴾ He said: they are the two most wicked clans of Quraysh: Banu al-Mughirah and Banu Umayyah. As for Banu al-Mughirah, you were sufficient against them on the day of Badr; and as for Banu Umayyah, they were given enjoyment for a time.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, from ʿUmar, something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through several chains from ʿAli concerning the verse something similar as well.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, al-Nasaʾi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu al-Tufayl that Ibn al-Kawwa asked ʿAli about those who exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief. He said: they are the wicked of Quraysh, whom you were sufficient against on the day of Badr.

He said: "Then who are those whose effort went astray in the life of this world?" He said: "Among them are the people of Harurah."

Something similar has been narrated from ʿAli through several chains concerning the explanation of this verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the verse, he said: they are Jabalah ibn al-Ayham and those among the Arabs who followed him, who joined the Romans.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿and caused their people to alight in the abode of ruin﴾, he said: "the ruin," that is, destruction.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And they set up rivals to Allah﴾, he said: they associated others with Allah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verse 28–34 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding ﴿And He subjected for you the rivers﴾ that he said: "With every benefit."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And He subjected for you the sun and the moon, both constant﴾ that he said: "Their constancy in obedience to Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ikrimah regarding ﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾ that he said: "Of everything you desired from Him."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid the like of it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan who said: "Of all that you asked of Him."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Sulayman al-Taymi who said: "Indeed Allah bestows blessings upon the servants according to their capacity, and He obligates them to give thanks according to their capacity."

Both of them (Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi) also narrated from Bakr ibn Abd Allah al-Muzani who said: "O son of Adam, if you wish to know the measure of what Allah has bestowed upon you, then close your eyes."

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu al-Darda' who said: "Whoever does not recognize the blessing of Allah upon him except in his food and drink, then his deeds have become few and his punishment has drawn near."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Ayyub al-Qurashi, client of the Banu Hashim, who said: "Dawud, peace be upon him, said: 'My Lord, inform me of the least of Your blessings upon me.' So He revealed to him: 'O Dawud, breathe.' He breathed, and then He said: 'This is the least of My blessings upon you.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "O Allah, forgive me my wrongdoing and my disbelief." Someone said: "O Commander of the Faithful, this is wrongdoing, so what about disbelief?" He said: "Indeed, man is surely a wrongdoer, a great disbeliever" (﴿Indeed, the human being is [often] wrongdoing and ungrateful﴾).

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 14, verses 28–34 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿Have you not seen?﴾ This is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone suited to it. It expresses wonder at the state of the disbelievers, who replaced the blessing of Allah upon them with disbelief. That is, instead of thanking Him for it, they disbelieved in it. This was by their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) when Allah raised him up from among them and bestowed His blessing upon them through him.

The majority of the exegetes held that they are the disbelievers of Makkah and that the verse was revealed concerning them. It was also said that it was revealed concerning those who fought the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Badr. It was said that it was revealed concerning two clans of the tribes of Quraysh, Banu Makhzum and Banu Umayyah. It was said that it was revealed concerning the Arabs who had become Christians, namely Jabalah ibn al-Ayham and his companions. But this is open to question, for Jabalah and his companions did not embrace Islam until the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). It was also said that it is general, covering all the polytheists. And it was said that the meaning of ﴿replaced the blessing of Allah with disbelief﴾ is that when they disbelieved in it, Allah took it away from them, so they became those who had exchanged it for disbelief. ﴿And caused their people to alight in the abode of ruin﴾: that is, they brought their people down into the abode of ruin, because of what they had made attractive to them of disbelief. ﴿The abode of ruin﴾ is Hell. Al-bawar means destruction. It was also said that they are the leaders of Quraysh who caused their people to alight, on the day of Badr, in the abode of ruin, that is, destruction, which is the killing by which they were struck. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"I have not seen their like, champions of war, on the morning of battle when ruin was feared."*

The first interpretation is preferable because of His saying ﴿Hell﴾, which is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to ﴿the abode of ruin﴾. The phrase ﴿they will burn in it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥal), or it is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnaf) explaining how they come to dwell in it. ﴿And wretched is the settling place﴾: that is, wretched is their settling place therein, or wretched is Hell as a dwelling place. The object of the blame is omitted.

﴿And they set up rivals to Allah﴾ is conjoined to ﴿and caused [them] to alight﴾. That is, they made partners for Allah in lordship, or in naming, and these are the idols.

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿liyaḍillū﴾ with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, meaning "that they might lead themselves astray from the way of Allah." The lām here is the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿaqibah), meaning that their setting up rivals to Allah was followed by their going astray, since a rational person does not intend the misguidance of himself. The use of the lam of consequence here is apt, because it resembles the purpose and end in that it occurs at the final stage, and resemblance is one of the features that justify a figurative usage (majaz).

The rest read it with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, ﴿liyuḍillū﴾, meaning "that they might cause their people to go astray from the way of Allah." This is the purpose of their setting up rivals to Allah.

Then He threatened them, the Glorified, and said to His Prophet (ﷺ): **Say: "Enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire."** That is, enjoy what you are in of desires, and what your own souls have made attractive to you of ingratitude for blessings and misguidance of people. ﴿For your destination is to the Fire﴾: that is, your return and your place of return is to it, and nothing else. Since this was their state, and because of their extreme avidity for it and their immersion in it, they would not desist from it nor accept the advice of those who counsel them, the command to engage in it was placed in the position of a prohibition of approaching it, to make clear what their outcome would be and that they would inevitably proceed to the Fire, so they must take up the means that bring that about. Thus the clause ﴿for your destination is to the Fire﴾ is a justification for the command to enjoy. There is in it a threat beyond measure. It is also permissible that this clause be an answer to an omitted condition indicated by the context of the speech, as if it were said: "If you persist in that, then your destination is to the Fire." The first is preferable, and the Qur'anic structure points to it. This is like what is said to one who strives to oppose the ruler: "Do whatever opposition you wish, for your destination is the sword."

﴿Say to My servants who have believed: let them establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾. Since He had commanded him to say to those who changed the blessing of Allah into disbelief and set up rivals to Allah what he had said to them, He commanded him to say this to the group opposed to them, namely the group of believers. The thing said is omitted, indicated by what is mentioned: that is, "Say to My servants: establish [the prayer] and spend." So ﴿let them establish﴾ is in the jussive because it is the answer to the omitted imperative, and likewise ﴿let them spend﴾. Al-Farraʾ mentioned this meaning.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿let them establish﴾ is jussive in the sense of the lam (of command), meaning "so that they may establish," and the lam was dropped. Then he mentioned another reason for the jussive, similar to what al-Farraʾ mentioned. As for ﴿secretly and openly﴾, it is in the accusative either as a circumstantial state (ḥal), meaning "those who spend secretly and openly," or as an infinitive (maṣdar), meaning "spending in secret and spending openly," or as an adverb of time (ẓarf), meaning "at a time of secrecy and at a time of openness."

The majority said: the secret is what is hidden, and the open is what is manifest. It was also said: the secret is voluntary charity, and the open is obligatory charity. The explanation of this has already been given at the commentary on His saying: ﴿If you disclose your charities, it is good﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:271).

﴿Before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship﴾. Abu ʿUbaydah said: "trade" here means ransom, and "khilal" means friendship, and it is a verbal noun. Al-Wahidi said: this is the saying of all the people of the language.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: it is permissible that it be the plural of *khullah*, like *burmah* and *biram*, and *ʿulbah* and *ʿilab*. The meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection there is no trade, so that one who fell short in deeds may ransom himself from the punishment of Allah by giving some compensation for it; and there is no friendship, so that a close friend may intercede for his friend and rescue him from the punishment. So the Glorified commanded them to spend, in the ways of goodness, from what Allah has provided them while they are still in this worldly life and able to spend their wealth, before the Day of Resurrection comes, for they will not be able to do that then, indeed they will have no wealth at that time. So the clause, I mean ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trade and no friendship﴾, is for emphasizing the content of the command to spend from what Allah has provided.

It is possible that there is also in it an emphasis on the content of the command to establish the prayer, because neglecting it often comes from being occupied with trade and with caring for the rights of friends. The explanation of trade and friendship has already been given in al-Baqarah.

﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, He originated and invented them without a precedent, and created what is in them of celestial and terrestrial bodies. The noble name is the subject, and what follows is its predicate.

﴿And sent down from the sky water﴾: here "sky" means the direction of height. It includes the sphere according to the one who said that the beginning of rain is from it, and it includes the clouds according to the one who said that the beginning of rain is from them, and it includes the causes that stir up the clouds, such as the winds. The indefiniteness of *māʾ* (water) here is for the sense of kind, that is, a kind of water, and it is rainwater.

﴿And brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾: that is, He brought forth by that water from various fruits a provision for the children of Adam by which they live. The *min* in ﴿min al-thamarāt﴾ is for specification, like your saying "I spent of the dirhams." It was also said that it is for partitive meaning, because among the fruits some are provision for the children of Adam and some are not provision for them, namely those they do not eat and do not benefit from.

﴿And He subjected to you the ships to run through the sea by His command﴾: they run according to your will, and you use them for your interests. Therefore He said ﴿to run through the sea as you wish﴾ and according to what you seek, by His command, that is, by the command and will of Allah. The explanation of this has already been given in al-Baqarah.

﴿And He subjected to you the rivers﴾: that is, He made them submissive to you, so that you ride upon them and direct them where you wish.

﴿And He subjected to you the sun and the moon, constant [in their courses]﴾, for you to benefit by them and to be illuminated by their light. The accusative of *dāʾibayn* is a circumstantial state (ḥal). *Al-duʾūb* is the passing of a thing in its work in a customary manner, that is, constant in setting right what they set right of plants and other things. It was also said: constant in motion in obedience to the command of Allah. The meaning is that they run until the Day of Resurrection without slackening, and their course does not cease.

﴿And He subjected to you the night and the day﴾, alternating. The day is for your striving in matters of your livelihood and what you need of the affairs of your worldly life, and the night is for you to rest, as He the Glorified said: (p-749) ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty﴾ (al-Qasas 28:73).

﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾. Al-Akhfash said: that is, He gave you of every thing you asked of Him something, so *shayʾan* (something) was omitted. It was also said: the meaning is "He gave you of all that you asked of Him and of all that you did not ask of Him," so the other clause was omitted. This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

It was also said: the *min* is extra, meaning "He gave you all that you asked of Him." It was said: it is for partitive meaning, meaning "He gave you some of all that you asked of Him."

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and Qatadah read ﴿min kullin﴾ with tanwin on *kull*. On this reading it is permissible that *ma* be negative, meaning "He gave you of all of that while you were not asking for it." It is also permissible that *ma* be relative, meaning "He gave you of every thing which you asked of Him."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14 (Ibrahim), verses 35–41 (part 1 of 2):

.
His saying: "And when Ibrahim said" is related to an omitted verb: meaning, "Remember the time when he said." Perhaps the purpose, in the context of what Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said in this place, is to show the disbelief of the Quraysh in the particular blessings that belong to them, namely their settlement in Makkah, after he had shown their disbelief in the general blessings. It was also said that the mention of the story of Ibrahim here is an example of the good word (al-kalimah al-tayyibah). It was also said that it is for the purpose of calling to monotheism (tawhid) and rejecting the worship of idols. "My Lord, make this city secure." The city here means Makkah. Ibrahim asked his Lord to make it secure, meaning: (p-750) possessing security. He placed the request for security before the other requests mentioned after it, because when security is absent, a person cannot devote himself to anything else of the affairs of the religion and of the world. The interpretation of a verse like this has already been given in al-Baqarah at His saying, Exalted is He: "My Lord, make this a secure city" [Al-Baqarah: 126]. The difference between what is here and what is there is that what is wanted here is merely the security of the city, while what is wanted there is the city's being a city (balad-iyyah) together with its security. "And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols." It is said: jannabtuhu kadhā, ajnabtuhu, and jannabtuhu, meaning: I kept him far from it. The meaning is: keep me far away, and keep my sons far from the worship of idols. It was said: he meant his sons from his loins, and they were eight. It was said: he meant those who were existing at the time of his supplication from among his sons and his sons' sons. It was said: he meant all of his offspring as they multiplied. This is supported by what has been said, that none of Ibrahim's descendants worshipped an idol. The idol (sanam) is the image which the people of the pre-Islamic age (Jahiliyyah) used to make from stones and the like, and then worship.
Al-Jahdari and Isa ibn Umar read "wa-ajnibni" with a hamzah (ajnibni), on the basis that its original form is ajnaba.
"My Lord, indeed they have led many of the people astray." He attributed the leading astray to the idols, although they are inanimate objects that do not understand, because they are a cause of their going astray, so it is as if they had led them astray. This sentence is a justification for his supplication to his Lord. Then he said: "So whoever follows me," meaning whoever follows my religion among the people and becomes a Muslim, a monotheist, "then he is of me," meaning of the people of my religion. He made the people of his religion like himself, as an emphasis. "And whoever disobeys me," so does not follow me and does not enter my religion, "then You are Forgiving and Merciful," capable of forgiving him. It was said: he said this before he knew that Allah does not forgive that He be associated with (shirk), as happened when he sought forgiveness for his father while he was a polytheist. Thus said Ibn al-Anbari. It was also said: the disobedience meant here is in matters less than shirk. It was also said: this forgiveness is conditional upon repentance from shirk.
Then he said: "Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring" [...]. Al-Farra' said: "min" (some of) is for partitive meaning, i.e., some of my offspring.
Ibn al-Anbari said: it is superfluous (zā'idah), meaning: I have settled my offspring. The first is more correct, because he only settled Isma'il, who is a part of his children, "in a valley without cultivation," meaning without any crops in it, and this is the valley of Makkah, "by Your Sacred House," meaning the house in which what is permitted elsewhere is forbidden. It was said: it is forbidden to the tyrants. It was said: it is forbidden in that its sanctity may not be violated or made light of.
What is sufficient instead of repetition has already been mentioned in Surat al-Ma'idah (the chapter of the Table). Then he said: "Our Lord, that they may establish prayer." The lam (in li-yuqimu) is related to "I have settled," meaning: I have settled them so that they may establish prayer there, turning toward it and seeking blessing from it. He singled it out over all the other acts of worship because of its great excellence. Perhaps the repetition of the address (rabbana) is to show complete care for this act of worship. "So make hearts (af'idah) among the people incline toward them." Af'idah is the plural of fu'ad, which is the heart; it is used to refer to the whole body, because the heart is the most noble organ in it.
It was also said: it is the plural of wafd (delegation), and the original form is awfidah, then the fa' was moved forward and the waw was changed into a ya', so it is as if he said: "and make delegations of the people incline toward them." The "min" in "min al-nas" (from among the people) is partitive. It was also said: it is superfluous, and it does not necessarily follow from it that Jews and Christians would perform the pilgrimage, by being included under the word "people," because what is wanted is directing the hearts of the people toward them for the purpose of dwelling with them and bringing things to them, not directing them toward the pilgrimage. If this were intended, he would have said "incline toward it." It was also said: "min" is for the beginning (ibtida'), like your saying: "the heart from me is sick," meaning my heart. The meaning of "tahwi ilayhim" (incline toward them) is: yearn toward them. It is said: hawa nahwahu, when he inclined toward him. Al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir, on Surah 14, verses 35–41 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Zuhri that he said: "Indeed Allah transported a village from the villages of al-Sham and placed it at al-Ta'if, in response to the supplication of Ibrahim."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related, al-Suyuti said with a good (hasan) chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "If Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had said, 'So make the hearts of people incline towards them,' the Jews, the Christians and all people would have performed Hajj. But he said, ﴿hearts from among the people﴾, and so he specified it for the believers."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him (Ibn 'Abbas) regarding His words: ﴿What we conceal and what we reveal﴾ that he said: "From grief."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i regarding His words: ﴿Our Lord, indeed You know what we conceal﴾ that he said: "From love for Isma'il and his mother." And ﴿and what we reveal﴾: "What we show to Sarah of harshness towards them both."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾ that he said: "This was after a while."

Ibn Jarir related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "Ibrahim was given the glad tidings after one hundred and seventeen years."

But he said, ﴿hearts from among the people﴾, and so he specified it for the believers."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him (Ibn 'Abbas) regarding His words: ﴿What we conceal and what we reveal﴾ that he said: "From grief."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i regarding His words: ﴿Our Lord, indeed You know what we conceal﴾ that he said: "From love for Isma'il and his mother." And ﴿and what we reveal﴾: "What we show to Sarah of harshness towards them both."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾ that he said: "This was after a while."

Ibn Jarir related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "Ibrahim was given the glad tidings after one hundred and seventeen years."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14 (Ibrahim), verses 35–41 (part 1 of 2):

.
His saying: "And when Ibrahim said" is related to an omitted verb: meaning, "Remember the time when he said." Perhaps the purpose, in the context of what Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said in this place, is to show the disbelief of the Quraysh in the particular blessings that belong to them, namely their settlement in Makkah, after he had shown their disbelief in the general blessings. It was also said that the mention of the story of Ibrahim here is an example of the good word (al-kalimah al-tayyibah). It was also said that it is for the purpose of calling to monotheism (tawhid) and rejecting the worship of idols. "My Lord, make this city secure." The city here means Makkah. Ibrahim asked his Lord to make it secure, meaning: (p-750) possessing security. He placed the request for security before the other requests mentioned after it, because when security is absent, a person cannot devote himself to anything else of the affairs of the religion and of the world. The interpretation of a verse like this has already been given in al-Baqarah at His saying, Exalted is He: "My Lord, make this a secure city" [Al-Baqarah: 126]. The difference between what is here and what is there is that what is wanted here is merely the security of the city, while what is wanted there is the city's being a city (balad-iyyah) together with its security. "And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols." It is said: jannabtuhu kadhā, ajnabtuhu, and jannabtuhu, meaning: I kept him far from it. The meaning is: keep me far away, and keep my sons far from the worship of idols. It was said: he meant his sons from his loins, and they were eight. It was said: he meant those who were existing at the time of his supplication from among his sons and his sons' sons. It was said: he meant all of his offspring as they multiplied. This is supported by what has been said, that none of Ibrahim's descendants worshipped an idol. The idol (sanam) is the image which the people of the pre-Islamic age (Jahiliyyah) used to make from stones and the like, and then worship.
Al-Jahdari and Isa ibn Umar read "wa-ajnibni" with a hamzah (ajnibni), on the basis that its original form is ajnaba.
"My Lord, indeed they have led many of the people astray." He attributed the leading astray to the idols, although they are inanimate objects that do not understand, because they are a cause of their going astray, so it is as if they had led them astray. This sentence is a justification for his supplication to his Lord. Then he said: "So whoever follows me," meaning whoever follows my religion among the people and becomes a Muslim, a monotheist, "then he is of me," meaning of the people of my religion. He made the people of his religion like himself, as an emphasis. "And whoever disobeys me," so does not follow me and does not enter my religion, "then You are Forgiving and Merciful," capable of forgiving him. It was said: he said this before he knew that Allah does not forgive that He be associated with (shirk), as happened when he sought forgiveness for his father while he was a polytheist. Thus said Ibn al-Anbari. It was also said: the disobedience meant here is in matters less than shirk. It was also said: this forgiveness is conditional upon repentance from shirk.
Then he said: "Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring" [...]. Al-Farra' said: "min" (some of) is for partitive meaning, i.e., some of my offspring.
Ibn al-Anbari said: it is superfluous (zā'idah), meaning: I have settled my offspring. The first is more correct, because he only settled Isma'il, who is a part of his children, "in a valley without cultivation," meaning without any crops in it, and this is the valley of Makkah, "by Your Sacred House," meaning the house in which what is permitted elsewhere is forbidden. It was said: it is forbidden to the tyrants. It was said: it is forbidden in that its sanctity may not be violated or made light of.
What is sufficient instead of repetition has already been mentioned in Surat al-Ma'idah (the chapter of the Table). Then he said: "Our Lord, that they may establish prayer." The lam (in li-yuqimu) is related to "I have settled," meaning: I have settled them so that they may establish prayer there, turning toward it and seeking blessing from it. He singled it out over all the other acts of worship because of its great excellence. Perhaps the repetition of the address (rabbana) is to show complete care for this act of worship. "So make hearts (af'idah) among the people incline toward them." Af'idah is the plural of fu'ad, which is the heart; it is used to refer to the whole body, because the heart is the most noble organ in it.
It was also said: it is the plural of wafd (delegation), and the original form is awfidah, then the fa' was moved forward and the waw was changed into a ya', so it is as if he said: "and make delegations of the people incline toward them." The "min" in "min al-nas" (from among the people) is partitive. It was also said: it is superfluous, and it does not necessarily follow from it that Jews and Christians would perform the pilgrimage, by being included under the word "people," because what is wanted is directing the hearts of the people toward them for the purpose of dwelling with them and bringing things to them, not directing them toward the pilgrimage. If this were intended, he would have said "incline toward it." It was also said: "min" is for the beginning (ibtida'), like your saying: "the heart from me is sick," meaning my heart. The meaning of "tahwi ilayhim" (incline toward them) is: yearn toward them. It is said: hawa nahwahu, when he inclined toward him. Hawat al-naqatu tahwi hawyan, so she is hawiyah, when she ran with a strong run, as if she were falling into a well. It is possible that the meaning is: come to them or hasten to them, and the meanings are close.
"And provide for them from the fruits," meaning: provide for my offspring whom You have settled there, or for them and those who live with them among the people, with kinds of fruits that grow in it or are brought to it, "so that perhaps they may give thanks for Your blessings with which You have blessed them."
"Our Lord, indeed You know what we conceal and what we disclose." That is, what we hide and what we make apparent, because the apparent and the hidden are equal with respect to Him, Glorified is He.
It was said: what is meant here by "what we conceal" is what is opposite to "what we disclose," so the meaning is what we make apparent and what we do not make apparent. He placed "what we conceal" before "what we disclose" to show that the two are equal in the knowledge of Allah, Glorified is He.
The apparent wording of the Qur'an is the generality of everything that is not apparent and everything that is apparent, without restriction to any specific thing of that. It was said: what is meant is what Ibrahim conceals of his grief over Isma'il and his mother when he settled them in a valley without cultivation, and what he discloses of that. It was said: what Ibrahim conceals of the grief and what he discloses of weeping and supplication. The use of the plural pronoun indicates that Ibrahim did not mean himself only, but meant all of the servants, so the meaning is as if: Allah, Glorified is He, knows everything that the servants make apparent and everything that they do not make apparent.
As for His saying: "Nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven" [Ali 'Imran: 5] (actually this verse is: "And nothing is hidden from Allah of anything on the earth or in the heaven"), the majority of the commentators said: it is from the speech of Allah, Glorified is He, confirming what Ibrahim said, that He, Glorified is He, knows what the servants conceal and what they disclose. So He, Glorified is He, said: nothing of the existing things is hidden from Allah, whatever it may be. He mentioned the heavens and the earth only because they are what is witnessed by the servants; otherwise His knowledge, Glorified is He, encompasses everything that is within the world and everything that is outside it, and nothing of it is hidden from Him.
It was said: it is possible that this is from the speech of Ibrahim, confirming his first statement, and generalizing after specifying.
Then He praised Allah, Glorified is He, for some of His blessings that reached him, saying: "Praise be to Allah, who has given me in old age Isma'il and Ishaq." That is, He gave me in my old age and the old age of my wife. It was said: Isma'il was born to him when he was ninety-nine years old, and Ishaq was born to him when he was a hundred and twelve years old. It was also said: "'ala" (in "'ala al-kibar") here means "ma'a" (with), meaning: He gave me along with my old age and my despair of having a child. "Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication," meaning the Responder to supplication, from the saying of them: "He heard his speech" when he answered it, took it into account, and acted in accordance with its requirement. This is from the attribution of an attribute that implies exaggeration to the object, and the meaning is: indeed You are abundant in responding to the supplication of those who call upon You.
Then he asked Allah, Glorified is He, to make him one who establishes the prayer and maintains it, neglecting nothing of it. Then he said: "And from my offspring," meaning some of my offspring: that is, make me and make some of my offspring establish the prayer. He singled out only some of his offspring because he knew that among them there were some who would not establish it as it should be established.
Al-Zajjaj said: meaning, make from my offspring those who establish the prayer. Then he asked Allah, Glorified is He, to accept his supplication generally, and his supplication in this station enters into that first.
It was said: the meaning of the "supplication" here is worship, so the meaning is: "and accept my worship" (p-751) with which I worship You.
Then he asked Allah, Glorified is He, to forgive him what had occurred from him of that which Allah deserves to forgive, even if it was not a major sin, due to what is known of the infallibility of the prophets from major sins.
Then he asked Allah, Glorified is He, to forgive his parents.
It has been said that he supplicated for their forgiveness before he knew that they were enemies of Allah, Glorified is He, as in His saying, Glorified is He: "And the request for forgiveness by Ibrahim for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to Allah, he disassociated himself from him" [Al-Tawbah: 114].
It was said: his mother was a Muslim. It was said: by his parents he meant Adam and Hawwa'.
Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "wa-li-walidi" (and for my father) in the singular, intending the father alone.
Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read "wa-li-waladi" (and for my child), meaning Isma'il and Ishaq, and Yahya ibn Ya'mur also read it thus. Then he sought forgiveness for the believers.
Its apparent meaning includes every believer, whether he was from his offspring or not. It was said: he meant only the believers from among his offspring. "On the day when the reckoning will take place," meaning the day on which the account of the accountable is established at the gathering place. The word "yaqum" (stands), which is its literal meaning in the standing of a man, was borrowed for it to indicate that it is in the utmost uprightness. It was said: the meaning is "the day when people stand for the reckoning," and the first is more correct.
Ibn Jarir has transmitted from Mujahid, regarding His saying: "And when Ibrahim said" (the verse), that he said: Allah answered Ibrahim's supplication concerning his offspring, so none of his offspring worshipped an idol after his supplication. Allah answered him, made this city secure, provided for its people with fruits, made him a leader (imam), made from his offspring those who establish the prayer, accepted his supplication, and showed him his rites, and He turned in forgiveness toward him.
Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il (The Proofs of Prophethood) has transmitted from Aqil ibn Abi Talib that when the Prophet (ﷺ) came to the six men from the Ansar, he sat with them at the Jamrat al-'Aqabah. He called them to Allah and to His worship and to supporting His religion. They asked him to present to them what had been revealed to him, so he recited from Surat Ibrahim: "And when Ibrahim said: My Lord, make this city secure, and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols" to the end of the surah. The people were moved and became humble when they heard what they heard from him, and they responded to him.
Al-Waqidi and Ibn 'Asakir have transmitted through the chain of 'Amir ibn Sa'd from his father, who said: Sarah was under Ibrahim, and she remained with him for a long time without being granted a child by him. When she saw that, she gave him Hajar, her Coptic slave-girl, and she bore Isma'il to him. Sarah was jealous because of that, found something in herself, and blamed Hajar. She swore that she would cut off three limbs from her. Ibrahim said to her: "Would you like to fulfil your oath?" She said: "How shall I do it?" He said: "Pierce her ears and lower them," and the lowering (khafd) is circumcision. So she did that to her, and Hajar put two earrings in her ears, and she increased in beauty by them.
Sarah said: "I see that I have only increased her in beauty." She did not let her remain with him, and Ibrahim found a great longing for her. So he moved her to Makkah, and he used to visit her every day from al-Sham upon the Buraq, out of his passion for her and his lack of patience with separation from her.
Ibn Jarir has transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: "I have settled some of my offspring": he settled Isma'il and his mother in Makkah.
Ibn al-Mundhir has transmitted from him that he said: when Ibrahim said: "So make hearts from among the people incline toward them," if he had said "the hearts of the people incline toward them," Persia and Byzantium would have crowded upon it.
Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim have transmitted from al-Hakam, who said: I asked 'Ikrimah, Tawus and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah about this verse: "So make hearts from among the people incline toward them." They said: the House, toward which their hearts incline; they come to it. In another wording they said: their longing is toward Makkah, that they may perform the pilgrimage.
'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir have transmitted from Qatadah regarding His saying "incline toward them": he said: they yearn toward them.
Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim have transmitted from Muhammad ibn Muslim al-Ta'ifi that when Ibrahim supplicated for the Sacred Precinct: "And provide for its people with fruits," Allah moved al-Ta'if from Palestine.

Al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir, on Surah 14, verses 35–41 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Zuhri that he said: "Indeed Allah transported a village from the villages of al-Sham and placed it at al-Ta'if, in response to the supplication of Ibrahim."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related, al-Suyuti said with a good (hasan) chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "If Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had said, 'So make the hearts of people incline towards them,' the Jews, the Christians and all people would have performed Hajj. But he said, ﴿hearts from among the people﴾, and so he specified it for the believers."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him (Ibn 'Abbas) regarding His words: ﴿What we conceal and what we reveal﴾ that he said: "From grief."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i regarding His words: ﴿Our Lord, indeed You know what we conceal﴾ that he said: "From love for Isma'il and his mother." And ﴿and what we reveal﴾: "What we show to Sarah of harshness towards them both."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has granted me, in old age, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾ that he said: "This was after a while."

Ibn Jarir related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "Ibrahim was given the glad tidings after one hundred and seventeen years."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verses 42–46 (part 1 of 2):

.
His saying: ﴿And do not think﴾ is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is an indirect address to his community. It is as if He said: "And do not think, O Muhammad, that your community..." It is also permissible that it be an address to everyone among the responsible (mukallafun) who is fit for it. Even if the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) without an indirect address to his community, its meaning is affirmation (tathbit) upon what he was already upon, namely not thinking so, like His saying: ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ and similar. It has been said: the meaning is, "Do not think that He treats them as one who is heedless of what they do, but rather as one who watches over them." Or the meaning of the prohibition of thinking is an announcement (idhan) that He knows that, and nothing of it is hidden from Him.

In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and information for the polytheists that the delay of the punishment from them is not because He is pleased with their deeds. Rather, it is the sunnah of Allah, glorified is He, in granting respite to the disobedient (p-752) ﴿He only delays them until a Day when eyes will stare fixedly﴾, meaning He delays their recompense and does not seize them for their wrongdoing.

This sentence is a justification (ta'lil) for the preceding prohibition.

Al-Hasan and al-Sulami, and it is a narration from Abu 'Amr, read ﻧُﺆَﺧِّﺮُﻫﻢ with the nun (نُؤَخِّرُهم). The rest read it with the yā' (بِالتَّحْتِيَّةِ).

Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, because of His saying ﴿And do not think Allah...﴾. The meaning of ﴿a Day when eyes will stare fixedly﴾ is that the eyes of the people of the place of standing (al-mawqif) are raised and do not close, because of the horror of what they see on that Day. Thus said al-Farra'.

It is said: shakhasa al-rajul basarahu (شَخَصَ الرَّجُلُ بَصَرَهُ), and shakhasa al-basar itself, meaning the eye was raised toward the sky from the horror of what it sees. The meaning is that the eyes remain open, not moving, from intense bewilderment and astonishment.

﴿Hastening﴾ (muhti'in), meaning hurrying, from ahta'a yahta'u ihta'an (أَهْطَعَ يَهْطَعُ إهْطاعًا): when he hurried. It has been said: the muhti' is one who looks in humiliation and submission.

From this is the line:
"Their dwelling is in Dijla, and indeed I see them in Dijla, gazing up at the sky."

It has been said: the muhti' is one who keeps his gaze fixed. Abu 'Ubayda said: both meanings may be intended together, meaning hurrying together with keeping the gaze fixed. It has been said: the muhti' is one who does not raise his head.

Tha'lab said: the muhti' is one who looks in humiliation and submission. It has been said: he is the silent one.

Al-Nahhas said: the known usage in the language is ahta'a, meaning he hurried.

﴿Raising their heads﴾ (muqni'i ru'usihim), meaning lifting their heads. Iqna' al-ra's (إقْناعُ الرَّأْسِ) is raising it, and aqna'a sawtahu (أقْنَعَ صَوْتَهُ) means when he raised his voice. The meaning is that on that Day they will be raising their heads toward the sky, looking at it with a look of terror and humiliation, and none of them will look at another.

It has been said: iqna' al-ra's is lowering it (nakthuhu, نَكْسُهُ). It has been said: aqna'a means he raised his head, and aqna'a also means he lowered it in humiliation and submission. The verse admits both meanings.

Al-Mubarrad said: the first view is better known in the language.

The poet said:
"He bent his head toward me and raised it high, as if he had seen something that made him hopeful."

﴿Their gaze will not return to them﴾, meaning their eyes will not come back to them. The root of tarf is the movement of the eyelids, and the eye was called tarf because it is by it. From the use of tarf for the eye is the saying of Antara:
"I lower my gaze when my neighbor appears to me, until my neighbor's shelter covers her."

﴿And their hearts are empty﴾ (hawa'): in the language, hawa' is the hollow, empty thing that is not occupied by bodies. The meaning is that their hearts are empty of intellect and understanding, because of what they witnessed of terror, bewilderment and astonishment. Making them the very essence of emptiness is hyperbole. From this it is said of the foolish and the coward: "his heart is hawa'," meaning he has no opinion in it and no strength. It has been said: the meaning of the verse is that their hearts have left their places and become in their throats.

It has been said: the meaning is that the hearts of the disbelievers in this world are empty of good. It has been said: the meaning is "their hearts are possessors of emptiness."

Among what is close in meaning to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the heart of Umm Musa became empty﴾ [al-Qasas: 10], meaning empty of everything except the concern for Musa.

﴿And warn the people﴾. This is a return to the address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to warn the people, and the intended meaning is people in general. It has been said: the intended meaning is the disbelievers of Makkah. It has been said: the disbelievers in general.

The first view is preferable, because warning applies to the disbeliever and also to the believer. From this is His saying: ﴿You only warn the one who follows the Reminder﴾ [Ya-Sin: 11]. The meaning of ﴿the Day when the punishment will come to them﴾ is the Day of Resurrection, meaning: frighten them with this Day, which is the day of the arrival of punishment. It was only mentioned in terms of the arrival of punishment, though it is also the day of the arrival of reward, because the context is one of threat. It has been said: the intended meaning is the day of their death, for it is the first of the times of the arrival of punishment. It has been said: the intended meaning is the day of their destruction by an immediate punishment.

The accusative of yawm (يَوْمَ) is that it is the second object (maf'ul thani, مَفْعُولٌ ثانٍ) of andhir (أَنْذِرْ).

﴿Then those who wronged will say: "Our Lord, delay us to a near term"﴾. Those who wronged here are the people, meaning: they will say. The shift to the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to indicate that wrongdoing is the cause of what befell them. This is when the intended people are the disbelievers.

If the intended meaning includes the Muslims, then the meaning is: "Then those among them who wronged, namely the disbelievers, will say: ﴿Our Lord, delay us﴾, grant us respite ﴿to a near term﴾, to a limited, not distant, period of time, ﴿and we will answer Your call﴾, meaning Your call to Your servants through the tongues of Your prophets to Your Oneness, ﴿and follow the Messengers﴾, the messengers sent from You to us, ﴿so we will act upon what they conveyed to us of Your laws, and make up for what we neglected of heedlessness.

The Messengers are described in the plural because their call to Oneness is one and the same, so following one of them is following all of them. This is a request from them to return to the world, after the truth became manifest to them in the Hereafter, ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

Then He, glorified is He, related what they will be answered with when they say this statement. He said: ﴿Did you not swear before that you would have no decline?﴾ meaning it will be said to them this statement as rebuke and reproach, meaning: Did you not swear before this Day that you would have no departure from the abode of this world? It has been said: they had no actual oath, but their state of being was like that, due to their absorption in desires and their inclination toward the life of this world. It has been said: their oath is what Allah related of them in His saying: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most solemn oaths that Allah would not resurrect whoever dies﴾ [al-Nahl: 38], and the answer to the oath is ﴿you have no decline﴾. The address form appeared in "ما لَكَمَ مِن زَوالٍ" (mā lakum min zawāl) to match "أقْسَمْتُمْ" (aqsamtum), and were it not for that, it would have said: "mā lanā min zawāl."

﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾, meaning you settled, as one says sakana al-dar and sakana fiha. These are the lands of Thamud and others like them among the disbelievers who wronged themselves by disbelieving in Allah and disobeying Him. ﴿And it became clear to you how We dealt with them﴾. Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read نُبَيِّنُ (nubayyinu) with the nun and the present tense verb. Others read it with the taʾ (التَّاءِ الفَوْقِيَّةِ) and the past tense verb, meaning: it became clear to you through witnessing the traces how We dealt with them with punishment and severe chastisement for what they committed of sins. The subject of tabayyana (تَبَيَّنَ) is what the sentence after it indicates, meaning: Our wondrous action toward them became clear to you. ﴿And We set forth for you the parables﴾ in the books of Allah and on the tongues of His messengers, as clarification for you and establishment and completion of the proof against you.

﴿And they had already devised their plot﴾. The sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal, حَالٌ), meaning: We dealt with them as We dealt, while they had already plotted in rejecting the truth and establishing falsehood their great plot, into which they exhausted their capacity. ﴿And their plot is with Allah﴾, meaning the recompense of their plot is with Allah, or their plot is recorded with Allah, so He will repay them for it. Or: with Allah is their plot that He will plot against them, with the plot being attributed to its object. It has been said: the intended people are the people of Muhammad (ﷺ), who plotted against the Prophet (ﷺ) when they resolved to kill him or to expel him. It has been said: the intended meaning is what (p-753) occurred from Namrud when he tried to ascend to the sky, so he made for himself a chest (tabut) and tied its legs to four eagles.

﴿Though their plot was such that the mountains would be removed by it﴾. Umar, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy read: "وإنْ كادَ مَكْرُهم" (wa-in kāda makruhum) with the unpointed dal (بِالدّالِ المُهْمَلَةِ) in place of the nun. The other reciters read "وإنْ كانَ" (wa-in kāna) with the nun.

Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Jurayj and al-Kisa'i read "لَتَزُولُ" (latazūlu) with a fatha on the lam, taking it as the lam of beginning (lam al-ibtida', لامُ الِابْتِداءِ). The majority read it with a kasra, taking it as the lam of denial (lam al-juhud, لامُ الجُحُودِ).

Ibn Jarir said: the preferred reading is this, meaning the reading of the majority, because if the mountains had actually been removed, they would not have remained firm. On the reading of al-Kisa'i and those with him, in is the lightened form of the heavy (in hiya al-mukhaffafa min al-thaqila), and the lam is the distinguishing lam (al-lam al-fariqa). The removal of the mountains is a metaphor for the greatness and severity of their plot. That is: the matter was that their plot was prepared for that.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Though their plot reached in its scheming to removing the mountains, Allah will still support His religion." On the reading of the majority, it allows two possibilities. The first is that in is the lightened form of the heavy, and the meaning is as already mentioned. The second is that it is negative, and the lam with a kasra is for emphasizing the negation, like His saying: ﴿And Allah would never have caused your faith to be lost﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. The meaning is: "It is impossible that the mountains could be removed by their plot," with the mountains being a metaphor for the signs of Allah and His laws, which remain fixed in their state for all time. Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatada: ﴿hastening﴾, he said: "hurrying."

The meaning of ﴿a Day when eyes will stare fixedly﴾ is that the eyes of the people of the place of standing (al-mawqif) are raised and do not close, because of the horror of what they see on that Day. Thus said al-Farra'.

It is said: shakhasa al-rajul basarahu (شَخَصَ الرَّجُلُ بَصَرَهُ), and shakhasa al-basar itself, meaning the eye was raised toward the sky from the horror of what it sees. The meaning is that the eyes remain open, not moving, from intense bewilderment and astonishment.

﴿Hastening﴾ (muhti'in), meaning hurrying, from ahta'a yahta'u ihta'an (أَهْطَعَ يَهْطَعُ إهْطاعًا): when he hurried. It has been said: the muhti' is one who looks in humiliation and submission.

From this is the line:
"Their dwelling is in Dijla, and indeed I see them in Dijla, gazing up at the sky."

It has been said: the muhti' is one who keeps his gaze fixed. Abu 'Ubayda said: both meanings may be intended together, meaning hurrying together with keeping the gaze fixed. It has been said: the muhti' is one who does not raise his head.

Tha'lab said: the muhti' is one who looks in humiliation and submission. It has been said: he is the silent one.

Al-Nahhas said: the known usage in the language is ahta'a, meaning he hurried.

﴿Raising their heads﴾ (muqni'i ru'usihim), meaning lifting their heads. Iqna' al-ra's (إقْناعُ الرَّأْسِ) is raising it, and aqna'a sawtahu (أقْنَعَ صَوْتَهُ) means when he raised his voice. The meaning is that on that Day they will be raising their heads toward the sky, looking at it with a look of terror and humiliation, and none of them will look at another.

It has been said: iqna' al-ra's is lowering it (nakthuhu, نَكْسُهُ). It has been said: aqna'a means he raised his head, and aqna'a also means he lowered it in humiliation and submission. The verse admits both meanings.

Al-Mubarrad said: the first view is better known in the language.

The poet said:
"He bent his head toward me and raised it high, as if he had seen something that made him hopeful."

﴿Their gaze will not return to them﴾, meaning their eyes will not come back to them. The root of tarf is the movement of the eyelids, and the eye was called tarf because it is by it. From the use of tarf for the eye is the saying of Antara:
"I lower my gaze when my neighbor appears to me, until my neighbor's shelter covers her."

﴿And their hearts are empty﴾ (hawa'): in the language, hawa' is the hollow, empty thing that is not occupied by bodies. The meaning is that their hearts are empty of intellect and understanding, because of what they witnessed of terror, bewilderment and astonishment. It has been said: the meaning of the verse is that their hearts have left their places and become in their throats.

It has been said: the meaning is that the hearts of the disbelievers in this world are empty of good. It has been said: the meaning is "their hearts are possessors of emptiness."

The meaning of ﴿the Day when the punishment will come to them﴾ is the Day of Resurrection, meaning: frighten them with this Day, which is the day of the arrival of punishment. It was only mentioned in terms of the arrival of punishment, though it is also the day of the arrival of reward, because the context is one of threat. It has been said: the intended meaning is the day of their death, for it is the first of the times of the arrival of punishment. It has been said: the intended meaning is the day of their destruction by an immediate punishment.

The accusative of yawm (يَوْمَ) is that it is the second object (maf'ul thani, مَفْعُولٌ ثانٍ) of andhir (أَنْذِرْ).

﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾, meaning you settled, as one says sakana al-dar and sakana fiha. These are the lands of Thamud and others like them among the disbelievers who wronged themselves by disbelieving in Allah and disobeying Him. ﴿And it became clear to you how We dealt with them﴾. Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read نُبَيِّنُ (nubayyinu) with the nun and the present tense verb. Others read it with the taʾ (التَّاءِ الفَوْقِيَّةِ) and the past tense verb, meaning: it became clear to you through witnessing the traces how We dealt with them with punishment and severe chastisement for what they committed of sins. The subject of tabayyana (تَبَيَّنَ) is what the sentence after it indicates, meaning: Our wondrous action toward them became clear to you. ﴿And We set forth for you the parables﴾ in the books of Allah and on the tongues of His messengers, as clarification for you and establishment and completion of the proof against you.

﴿And they had already devised their plot﴾. The sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal, حَالٌ), meaning: We dealt with them as We dealt, while they had already plotted in rejecting the truth and establishing falsehood their great plot, into which they exhausted their capacity. ﴿And their plot is with Allah﴾, meaning the recompense of their plot is with Allah, or their plot is recorded with Allah, so He will repay them for it. Or: with Allah is their plot that He will plot against them, with the plot being attributed to its object. It has been said: the intended people are the people of Muhammad (ﷺ), who plotted against the Prophet (ﷺ) when they resolved to kill him or to expel him. It has been said: the intended meaning is what (p-753) occurred from Namrud when he tried to ascend to the sky, so he made for himself a chest (tabut) and tied its legs to four eagles.

﴿Though their plot was such that the mountains would be removed by it﴾. Umar, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy read: "وإنْ كادَ مَكْرُهم" (wa-in kāda makruhum) with the unpointed dal (بِالدّالِ المُهْمَلَةِ) in place of the nun. The other reciters read "وإنْ كانَ" (wa-in kāna) with the nun.

Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Jurayj and al-Kisa'i read "لَتَزُولُ" (latazūlu) with a fatha on the lam, taking it as the lam of beginning (lam al-ibtida', لامُ الِابْتِداءِ). The majority read it with a kasra, taking it as the lam of denial (lam al-juhud, لامُ الجُحُودِ).

The removal of the mountains is a metaphor for the greatness and severity of their plot. That is: the matter was that their plot was prepared for that.
