It has been said: the intended meaning is the day of their destruction by an immediate punishment.

The accusative of yawm (يَوْمَ) is that it is the second object (maf'ul thani, مَفْعُولٌ ثانٍ) of andhir (أَنْذِرْ).

﴿Then those who wronged will say: "Our Lord, delay us to a near term"﴾. Those who wronged here are the people, meaning: they will say. The shift to the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to indicate that wrongdoing is the cause of what befell them. This is when the intended people are the disbelievers.

If the intended meaning includes the Muslims, then the meaning is: "Then those among them who wronged, namely the disbelievers, will say: ﴿Our Lord, delay us﴾, grant us respite ﴿to a near term﴾, to a limited, not distant, period of time, ﴿and we will answer Your call﴾, meaning Your call to Your servants through the tongues of Your prophets to Your Oneness, ﴿and follow the Messengers﴾, the messengers sent from You to us, ﴿so we will act upon what they conveyed to us of Your laws, and make up for what we neglected of heedlessness.

The Messengers are described in the plural because their call to Oneness is one and the same, so following one of them is following all of them. This is a request from them to return to the world, after the truth became manifest to them in the Hereafter, ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

Then He, glorified is He, related what they will be answered with when they say this statement. He said: ﴿Did you not swear before that you would have no decline?﴾ meaning it will be said to them this statement as rebuke and reproach, meaning: Did you not swear before this Day that you would have no departure from the abode of this world? It has been said: they had no actual oath, but their state of being was like that, due to their absorption in desires and their inclination toward the life of this world. It has been said: their oath is what Allah related of them in His saying: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most solemn oaths that Allah would not resurrect whoever dies﴾ [al-Nahl: 38], and the answer to the oath is ﴿you have no decline﴾. The address form appeared in "ما لَكَمَ مِن زَوالٍ" (mā lakum min zawāl) to match "أقْسَمْتُمْ" (aqsamtum), and were it not for that, it would have said: "mā lanā min zawāl."

﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾, meaning you settled, as one says sakana al-dar and sakana fiha. These are the lands of Thamud and others like them among the disbelievers who wronged themselves by disbelieving in Allah and disobeying Him. ﴿And it became clear to you how We dealt with them﴾. Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read نُبَيِّنُ (nubayyinu) with the nun and the present tense verb. Others read it with the taʾ (التَّاءِ الفَوْقِيَّةِ) and the past tense verb, meaning: it became clear to you through witnessing the traces how We dealt with them with punishment and severe chastisement for what they committed of sins. The subject of tabayyana (تَبَيَّنَ) is what the sentence after it indicates, meaning: Our wondrous action toward them became clear to you. ﴿And We set forth for you the parables﴾ in the books of Allah and on the tongues of His messengers, as clarification for you and establishment and completion of the proof against you.

﴿And they had already devised their plot﴾. The sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal, حَالٌ), meaning: We dealt with them as We dealt, while they had already plotted in rejecting the truth and establishing falsehood their great plot, into which they exhausted their capacity. ﴿And their plot is with Allah﴾, meaning the recompense of their plot is with Allah, or their plot is recorded with Allah, so He will repay them for it. Or: with Allah is their plot that He will plot against them, with the plot being attributed to its object. It has been said: the intended people are the people of Muhammad (ﷺ), who plotted against the Prophet (ﷺ) when they resolved to kill him or to expel him. It has been said: the intended meaning is what (p-753) occurred from Namrud when he tried to ascend to the sky, so he made for himself a chest (tabut) and tied its legs to four eagles.

﴿Though their plot was such that the mountains would be removed by it﴾. Umar, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy read: "وإنْ كادَ مَكْرُهم" (wa-in kāda makruhum) with the unpointed dal (بِالدّالِ المُهْمَلَةِ) in place of the nun. The other reciters read "وإنْ كانَ" (wa-in kāna) with the nun.

Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Jurayj and al-Kisa'i read "لَتَزُولُ" (latazūlu) with a fatha on the lam, taking it as the lam of beginning (lam al-ibtida', لامُ الِابْتِداءِ). The majority read it with a kasra, taking it as the lam of denial (lam al-juhud, لامُ الجُحُودِ).

Ibn Jarir said: the preferred reading is this, meaning the reading of the majority, because if the mountains had actually been removed, they would not have remained firm. On the reading of al-Kisa'i and those with him, in is the lightened form of the heavy (in hiya al-mukhaffafa min al-thaqila), and the lam is the distinguishing lam (al-lam al-fariqa). The removal of the mountains is a metaphor for the greatness and severity of their plot. That is: the matter was that their plot was prepared for that.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Though their plot reached in its scheming to removing the mountains, Allah will still support His religion." On the reading of the majority, it allows two possibilities. The first is that in is the lightened form of the heavy, and the meaning is as already mentioned. The second is that it is negative, and the lam with a kasra is for emphasizing the negation, like His saying: ﴿And Allah would never have caused your faith to be lost﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. The meaning is: "It is impossible that the mountains could be removed by their plot," with the mountains being a metaphor for the signs of Allah and His laws, which remain fixed in their state for all time. So on this view the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "makaru" (they plotted), not from His saying ﴿and their plot is with Allah﴾, meaning: while their plot was not such that the mountains would be removed by it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Kharaʾiti in Masawi al-Akhlaq related from Maymun ibn Mihran concerning His saying: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾, that he said: "It is consolation for the oppressed and a warning for the oppressor."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada concerning His saying: ﴿a Day when eyes will stare fixedly﴾, that he said: "By Allah, their eyes became fixed upon it, and they do not return to them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿hastening﴾, that he said: "He means by ihta' the gaze without blinking." ﴿Raising their heads﴾, he said: "al-iqna' is raising their heads." ﴿Their gaze will not return to them﴾, he said: "Their eyes are fixed." ﴿And their hearts are hawa'﴾, he said: "There is nothing of good in them, so they are like a ruin."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid: ﴿hastening﴾, he said: "keeping the gaze fixed."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatada: ﴿hastening﴾, he said: "hurrying."

These same related from Qatada concerning His saying: ﴿And their hearts are hawa'﴾, he said: "There is nothing in them; they came out of their chests and lodged in their throats."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Murra: ﴿And their hearts are hawa'﴾, he said: "They are torn open and understand nothing."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada concerning His saying: ﴿And warn the people of the Day when the punishment will come to them﴾, he says: "Warn them in this world before the punishment comes to them."

Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid, he said: "﴿the Day when the punishment will come to them﴾ is the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas: ﴿You have no decline﴾, he said: "From what you are in, to what you say."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi concerning His saying: ﴿You have no decline﴾, he said: "Resurrection after death."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Hasan concerning His saying: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾, he said: "You acted like their deeds."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And though their plot⁠ ⁠⁠ ⁠⁠⁠— ⁠⁠ ⁠⁠ ⁠—﴾, he says: "Their plot was not such that..." ﴿that the mountains would be removed by it﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas: ﴿And though their plot⁠—﴾, he says: "Their shirk," like His saying: ﴿The heavens are nearly torn apart from it, and the earth splits open, and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾ [Maryam: 90].

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Anbari reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he recited this verse, ﴿And indeed their plotting was such that the mountains would be moved by it﴾, and then explained it, saying: A tyrant among the tyrants said, "I will not desist until I look at what is in the heaven." So he ordered that young eagles be fed meat until they grew strong and large. He then ordered a chest (tabut) to be carpentered, large enough for two men, and he placed a pole (khashaba) in its middle. Then he tied their feet to pegs, and he starved them. Then he placed meat on the top of the pole. He and his companion then entered the chest, and he tied the eagles to the legs of the chest. Then he released them, wanting the meat, and they flew off with it for as long as God willed. Then he said to his companion, "Open up and look, what do you see?" So he opened and said, "Look at the mountains, they look like flies." He said, "Close up," and he closed. They flew with him for as long as God willed. Then he said, "Open up," and he opened, and said, "Look, what do you see?" He said, "I see nothing but the sky, and I see it only growing further away." He said, "Tilt the pole," and he tilted it, and they swooped down, seeking the meat. Then he heard the mountains crashing, and they nearly moved from their places.

A story similar to this has been related about Bukht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar) and about Nimrod through several chains, which are mentioned in al-Durr al-Manthur.

.

It is also permissible that it be an address to everyone among the responsible (mukallafun) who is fit for it. Even if the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) without an indirect address to his community, its meaning is affirmation (tathbit) upon what he was already upon, namely not thinking so, like His saying: ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ and similar. It has been said: the meaning is, "Do not think that He treats them as one who is heedless of what they do, but rather as one who watches over them." Or the meaning of the prohibition of thinking is an announcement (idhan) that He knows that, and nothing of it is hidden from Him.

In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and information for the polytheists that the delay of the punishment from them is not because He is pleased with their deeds. Rather, it is the sunnah of Allah, glorified is He, in granting respite to the disobedient (p-752) ﴿He only delays them until a Day when eyes will stare fixedly﴾, meaning He delays their recompense and does not seize them for their wrongdoing.

This sentence is a justification (ta'lil) for the preceding prohibition.

Al-Hasan and al-Sulami, and it is a narration from Abu 'Amr, read ﻧُﺆَﺧِّﺮُﻫﻢ with the nun (نُؤَخِّرُهم). The rest read it with the yā' (بِالتَّحْتِيَّةِ).

It has been said: the muhti' is one who keeps his gaze fixed. Abu 'Ubayda said: both meanings may be intended together, meaning hurrying together with keeping the gaze fixed. It has been said: the muhti' is one who does not raise his head.

Tha'lab said: the muhti' is one who looks in humiliation and submission. It has been said: he is the silent one.

Al-Nahhas said: the known usage in the language is ahta'a, meaning he hurried.

﴿Raising their heads﴾ (muqni'i ru'usihim), meaning lifting their heads. Iqna' al-ra's (إقْناعُ الرَّأْسِ) is raising it, and aqna'a sawtahu (أقْنَعَ صَوْتَهُ) means when he raised his voice. The meaning is that on that Day they will be raising their heads toward the sky, looking at it with a look of terror and humiliation, and none of them will look at another.

It has been said: iqna' al-ra's is lowering it (nakthuhu, نَكْسُهُ). It has been said: aqna'a means he raised his head, and aqna'a also means he lowered it in humiliation and submission. The verse admits both meanings.

Al-Mubarrad said: the first view is better known in the language.

The poet said:
"He bent his head toward me and raised it high, as if he had seen something that made him hopeful."

﴿Their gaze will not return to them﴾, meaning their eyes will not come back to them. The root of tarf is the movement of the eyelids, and the eye was called tarf because it is by it. From the use of tarf for the eye is the saying of Antara:
"I lower my gaze when my neighbor appears to me, until my neighbor's shelter covers her."

﴿And their hearts are empty﴾ (hawa'): in the language, hawa' is the hollow, empty thing that is not occupied by bodies. The meaning is that their hearts are empty of intellect and understanding, because of what they witnessed of terror, bewilderment and astonishment. Making them the very essence of emptiness is hyperbole. From this it is said of the foolish and the coward: "his heart is hawa'," meaning he has no opinion in it and no strength. It has been said: the meaning of the verse is that their hearts have left their places and become in their throats.

It has been said: the meaning is that the hearts of the disbelievers in this world are empty of good. It has been said: the meaning is "their hearts are possessors of emptiness."

﴿And warn the people﴾. This is a return to the address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to warn the people, and the intended meaning is people in general. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verses 42–46 (part 1 of 2):

.
His saying: ﴿And do not think﴾ is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is an indirect address to his community. It is as if He said: "And do not think, O Muhammad, that your community..." It is also permissible that it be an address to everyone among the responsible (mukallafun) who is fit for it. Even if the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) without an indirect address to his community, its meaning is affirmation (tathbit) upon what he was already upon, namely not thinking so, like His saying: ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ and similar. It has been said: the meaning is, "Do not think that He treats them as one who is heedless of what they do, but rather as one who watches over them." Or the meaning of the prohibition of thinking is an announcement (idhan) that He knows that, and nothing of it is hidden from Him.

In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and information for the polytheists that the delay of the punishment from them is not because He is pleased with their deeds. Rather, it is the sunnah of Allah, glorified is He, in granting respite to the disobedient (p-752) ﴿He only delays them until a Day when eyes will stare fixedly﴾, meaning He delays their recompense and does not seize them for their wrongdoing.

This sentence is a justification (ta'lil) for the preceding prohibition.

Al-Hasan and al-Sulami, and it is a narration from Abu 'Amr, read ﻧُﺆَﺧِّﺮُﻫﻢ with the nun (نُؤَخِّرُهم). The rest read it with the yā' (بِالتَّحْتِيَّةِ).

Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, because of His saying ﴿And do not think Allah...﴾. The meaning of ﴿a Day when eyes will stare fixedly﴾ is that the eyes of the people of the place of standing (al-mawqif) are raised and do not close, because of the horror of what they see on that Day. Thus said al-Farra'.

It is said: shakhasa al-rajul basarahu (شَخَصَ الرَّجُلُ بَصَرَهُ), and shakhasa al-basar itself, meaning the eye was raised toward the sky from the horror of what it sees. The meaning is that the eyes remain open, not moving, from intense bewilderment and astonishment.

﴿Hastening﴾ (muhti'in), meaning hurrying, from ahta'a yahta'u ihta'an (أَهْطَعَ يَهْطَعُ إهْطاعًا): when he hurried. It has been said: the muhti' is one who looks in humiliation and submission.

From this is the line:
"Their dwelling is in Dijla, and indeed I see them in Dijla, gazing up at the sky."

It has been said: the muhti' is one who keeps his gaze fixed. Abu 'Ubayda said: both meanings may be intended together, meaning hurrying together with keeping the gaze fixed. It has been said: the muhti' is one who does not raise his head.

Tha'lab said: the muhti' is one who looks in humiliation and submission. It has been said: he is the silent one.

Al-Nahhas said: the known usage in the language is ahta'a, meaning he hurried.

﴿Raising their heads﴾ (muqni'i ru'usihim), meaning lifting their heads. Iqna' al-ra's (إقْناعُ الرَّأْسِ) is raising it, and aqna'a sawtahu (أقْنَعَ صَوْتَهُ) means when he raised his voice. The meaning is that on that Day they will be raising their heads toward the sky, looking at it with a look of terror and humiliation, and none of them will look at another.

It has been said: iqna' al-ra's is lowering it (nakthuhu, نَكْسُهُ). It has been said: aqna'a means he raised his head, and aqna'a also means he lowered it in humiliation and submission. The verse admits both meanings.

Al-Mubarrad said: the first view is better known in the language.

The poet said:
"He bent his head toward me and raised it high, as if he had seen something that made him hopeful."

﴿Their gaze will not return to them﴾, meaning their eyes will not come back to them. The root of tarf is the movement of the eyelids, and the eye was called tarf because it is by it. From the use of tarf for the eye is the saying of Antara:
"I lower my gaze when my neighbor appears to me, until my neighbor's shelter covers her."

﴿And their hearts are empty﴾ (hawa'): in the language, hawa' is the hollow, empty thing that is not occupied by bodies. The meaning is that their hearts are empty of intellect and understanding, because of what they witnessed of terror, bewilderment and astonishment. Making them the very essence of emptiness is hyperbole. From this it is said of the foolish and the coward: "his heart is hawa'," meaning he has no opinion in it and no strength. It has been said: the meaning of the verse is that their hearts have left their places and become in their throats.

It has been said: the meaning is that the hearts of the disbelievers in this world are empty of good. It has been said: the meaning is "their hearts are possessors of emptiness."

Among what is close in meaning to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the heart of Umm Musa became empty﴾ [al-Qasas: 10], meaning empty of everything except the concern for Musa.

﴿And warn the people﴾. This is a return to the address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to warn the people, and the intended meaning is people in general. It has been said: the intended meaning is the disbelievers of Makkah. It has been said: the disbelievers in general.

The first view is preferable, because warning applies to the disbeliever and also to the believer. From this is His saying: ﴿You only warn the one who follows the Reminder﴾ [Ya-Sin: 11]. The meaning of ﴿the Day when the punishment will come to them﴾ is the Day of Resurrection, meaning: frighten them with this Day, which is the day of the arrival of punishment. It was only mentioned in terms of the arrival of punishment, though it is also the day of the arrival of reward, because the context is one of threat. It has been said: the intended meaning is the day of their death, for it is the first of the times of the arrival of punishment. It has been said: the intended meaning is the day of their destruction by an immediate punishment.

The accusative of yawm (يَوْمَ) is that it is the second object (maf'ul thani, مَفْعُولٌ ثانٍ) of andhir (أَنْذِرْ).

﴿Then those who wronged will say: "Our Lord, delay us to a near term"﴾. Those who wronged here are the people, meaning: they will say. The shift to the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to indicate that wrongdoing is the cause of what befell them. This is when the intended people are the disbelievers.

If the intended meaning includes the Muslims, then the meaning is: "Then those among them who wronged, namely the disbelievers, will say: ﴿Our Lord, delay us﴾, grant us respite ﴿to a near term﴾, to a limited, not distant, period of time, ﴿and we will answer Your call﴾, meaning Your call to Your servants through the tongues of Your prophets to Your Oneness, ﴿and follow the Messengers﴾, the messengers sent from You to us, ﴿so we will act upon what they conveyed to us of Your laws, and make up for what we neglected of heedlessness.

The Messengers are described in the plural because their call to Oneness is one and the same, so following one of them is following all of them. This is a request from them to return to the world, after the truth became manifest to them in the Hereafter, ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

Then He, glorified is He, related what they will be answered with when they say this statement. He said: ﴿Did you not swear before that you would have no decline?﴾ meaning it will be said to them this statement as rebuke and reproach, meaning: Did you not swear before this Day that you would have no departure from the abode of this world? It has been said: they had no actual oath, but their state of being was like that, due to their absorption in desires and their inclination toward the life of this world. It has been said: their oath is what Allah related of them in His saying: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most solemn oaths that Allah would not resurrect whoever dies﴾ [al-Nahl: 38], and the answer to the oath is ﴿you have no decline﴾. The address form appeared in "ما لَكَمَ مِن زَوالٍ" (mā lakum min zawāl) to match "أقْسَمْتُمْ" (aqsamtum), and were it not for that, it would have said: "mā lanā min zawāl."

﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾, meaning you settled, as one says sakana al-dar and sakana fiha. These are the lands of Thamud and others like them among the disbelievers who wronged themselves by disbelieving in Allah and disobeying Him. ﴿And it became clear to you how We dealt with them﴾. Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read نُبَيِّنُ (nubayyinu) with the nun and the present tense verb. Others read it with the taʾ (التَّاءِ الفَوْقِيَّةِ) and the past tense verb, meaning: it became clear to you through witnessing the traces how We dealt with them with punishment and severe chastisement for what they committed of sins. The subject of tabayyana (تَبَيَّنَ) is what the sentence after it indicates, meaning: Our wondrous action toward them became clear to you. ﴿And We set forth for you the parables﴾ in the books of Allah and on the tongues of His messengers, as clarification for you and establishment and completion of the proof against you.

﴿And they had already devised their plot﴾. The sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal, حَالٌ), meaning: We dealt with them as We dealt, while they had already plotted in rejecting the truth and establishing falsehood their great plot, into which they exhausted their capacity. ﴿And their plot is with Allah﴾, meaning the recompense of their plot is with Allah, or their plot is recorded with Allah, so He will repay them for it. Or: with Allah is their plot that He will plot against them, with the plot being attributed to its object. It has been said: the intended people are the people of Muhammad (ﷺ), who plotted against the Prophet (ﷺ) when they resolved to kill him or to expel him. It has been said: the intended meaning is what (p-753) occurred from Namrud when he tried to ascend to the sky, so he made for himself a chest (tabut) and tied its legs to four eagles.

﴿Though their plot was such that the mountains would be removed by it﴾. Umar, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy read: "وإنْ كادَ مَكْرُهم" (wa-in kāda makruhum) with the unpointed dal (بِالدّالِ المُهْمَلَةِ) in place of the nun. The other reciters read "وإنْ كانَ" (wa-in kāna) with the nun.

Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Jurayj and al-Kisa'i read "لَتَزُولُ" (latazūlu) with a fatha on the lam, taking it as the lam of beginning (lam al-ibtida', لامُ الِابْتِداءِ). The majority read it with a kasra, taking it as the lam of denial (lam al-juhud, لامُ الجُحُودِ).

Ibn Jarir said: the preferred reading is this, meaning the reading of the majority, because if the mountains had actually been removed, they would not have remained firm. On the reading of al-Kisa'i and those with him, in is the lightened form of the heavy (in hiya al-mukhaffafa min al-thaqila), and the lam is the distinguishing lam (al-lam al-fariqa). The removal of the mountains is a metaphor for the greatness and severity of their plot. That is: the matter was that their plot was prepared for that.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Though their plot reached in its scheming to removing the mountains, Allah will still support His religion." On the reading of the majority, it allows two possibilities. The first is that in is the lightened form of the heavy, and the meaning is as already mentioned. The second is that it is negative, and the lam with a kasra is for emphasizing the negation, like His saying: ﴿And Allah would never have caused your faith to be lost﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. The meaning is: "It is impossible that the mountains could be removed by their plot," with the mountains being a metaphor for the signs of Allah and His laws, which remain fixed in their state for all time. So on this view the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "makaru" (they plotted), not from His saying ﴿and their plot is with Allah﴾, meaning: while their plot was not such that the mountains would be removed by it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Kharaʾiti in Masawi al-Akhlaq related from Maymun ibn Mihran concerning His saying: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾, that he said: "It is consolation for the oppressed and a warning for the oppressor."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada concerning His saying: ﴿a Day when eyes will stare fixedly﴾, that he said: "By Allah, their eyes became fixed upon it, and they do not return to them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿hastening﴾, that he said: "He means by ihta' the gaze without blinking." ﴿Raising their heads﴾, he said: "al-iqna' is raising their heads." ﴿Their gaze will not return to them﴾, he said: "Their eyes are fixed." ﴿And their hearts are hawa'﴾, he said: "There is nothing of good in them, so they are like a ruin."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid: ﴿hastening﴾, he said: "keeping the gaze fixed."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatada: ﴿hastening﴾, he said: "hurrying."

These same related from Qatada concerning His saying: ﴿And their hearts are hawa'﴾, he said: "There is nothing in them; they came out of their chests and lodged in their throats."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Murra: ﴿And their hearts are hawa'﴾, he said: "They are torn open and understand nothing."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada concerning His saying: ﴿And warn the people of the Day when the punishment will come to them﴾, he says: "Warn them in this world before the punishment comes to them."

Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid, he said: "﴿the Day when the punishment will come to them﴾ is the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas: ﴿You have no decline﴾, he said: "From what you are in, to what you say."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi concerning His saying: ﴿You have no decline﴾, he said: "Resurrection after death."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Hasan concerning His saying: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾, he said: "You acted like their deeds."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And though their plot⁠ ⁠⁠ ⁠⁠⁠— ⁠⁠ ⁠⁠ ⁠—﴾, he says: "Their plot was not such that..." ﴿that the mountains would be removed by it﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas: ﴿And though their plot⁠—﴾, he says: "Their shirk," like His saying: ﴿The heavens are nearly torn apart from it, and the earth splits open, and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾ [Maryam: 90].

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Anbari reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he recited this verse, ﴿And indeed their plotting was such that the mountains would be moved by it﴾, and then explained it, saying: A tyrant among the tyrants said, "I will not desist until I look at what is in the heaven." So he ordered that young eagles be fed meat until they grew strong and large. He then ordered a chest (tabut) to be carpentered, large enough for two men, and he placed a pole (khashaba) in its middle. Then he tied their feet to pegs, and he starved them. Then he placed meat on the top of the pole. He and his companion then entered the chest, and he tied the eagles to the legs of the chest. Then he released them, wanting the meat, and they flew off with it for as long as God willed. Then he said to his companion, "Open up and look, what do you see?" So he opened and said, "Look at the mountains, they look like flies." He said, "Close up," and he closed. They flew with him for as long as God willed. Then he said, "Open up," and he opened, and said, "Look, what do you see?" He said, "I see nothing but the sky, and I see it only growing further away." He said, "Tilt the pole," and he tilted it, and they swooped down, seeking the meat. Then he heard the mountains crashing, and they nearly moved from their places.

A story similar to this has been related about Bukht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar) and about Nimrod through several chains, which are mentioned in al-Durr al-Manthur.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verses 47–52:**

*Mukhlifa* (broken, as the one who breaks) is in the accusative because it is the object (*maf'ul*) of *tahsabanna*, and *rusulahu* (His messengers) is in the accusative because it is the object of *wa'dihi* (His promise). It is said that this is by *ittisa'* (extension, a grammatical licence of word order). The meaning is: "one who breaks His promise to His messengers," i.e., *mukhlifa rusulihi wa'dahu*.

Al-Qutaybi said: "This is from the advanced (*muqaddam*) element which is clarified by the delayed (*mu'akhkhar*), and the delayed element which is clarified by the advanced. In this respect, *mukhlifa wa'dihi rusulahu* and *mukhlifa rusulihi wa'dahu* are equivalent. Similar to what is in the verse is the poet's saying:

*You see the bull in it, its head entering the shade, while the rest of it is exposed to the sun, entirely.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He placed the promise first to make known that He does not break a promise at all, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in the appointment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 9]. Then He said *rusulahu* to indicate that if He does not break His promise to anyone, and breaking promises is not part of His nature, how then would He break it to His messengers, who are His chosen and His elite?" The "promise" here means what He, glorified is He, promised them by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers﴾ [Ghafir: 51] (p-754) and ﴿Allah has decreed, "I will surely prevail, I and My messengers"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21].

It was also read (as a *qira'ah*, a canonical recitation) *mukhlifa wa'dahu rusulihi*, with *rusulihi* in the genitive and *wa'dahu* in the accusative.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "This reading is weak, like the one who reads: *qatlu awladihim shuraka'ihim* [al-An'am: 137]." ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty (*'aziz*)﴾, Overpowering, whom no one can overpower, ﴿Owner of retribution﴾, Who takes vengeance on His enemies for His allies. This sentence is a justification (*ta'lil*) for the prohibition, and its explanation has already passed at the beginning of Al 'Imran.

﴿On the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "*Yawma* is in the accusative either as a substitute (*badal*) for *yawma ya'tihim*, or as an adverb of time (*zarf*) for the retribution." End of quote. It is also permissible that it be in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by the context, meaning: "remember," or "await." *Tabdil* (change) may be in the essence, as in: "I exchanged the dirhams for dinars," or in the attributes, as in: "I exchanged the ring for a signet." The verse may bear both meanings. It has been said: the intended meaning is the change of its attributes, and most scholars held this view. It has also been said: the change of its essence. The meaning of *wa's-samawat* ("and the heavens") is: and the heavens will be changed to other than the heavens, according to the difference that has passed.

﴿And they will come forth before Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾, meaning the servants came forth before Allah, or the wrongdoers, as the context implies, i.e., they appeared from their graves, or what they had concealed of their deeds appeared. The expression of the future in the past tense is to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, as in His saying: ﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾ [al-Kahf: 99], [Ya Sin: 51]. *Al-Wahid al-Qahhar* ("the One, the Subduer") means the One who is singular in divinity, the One of great subjugation over whoever opposes Him.

﴿And you will see the criminals that day bound together in shackles﴾. It is coordinated with *barazu* ("they came forth") or with *tubaddalu* ("is changed"). The use of the present tense is to bring the scene to mind. *Al-mujrimun* ("the criminals") are the polytheists. *Yawma'idhin* means the Day of Resurrection. *Muqarranin* means bound: either by making some of them bound with others, or they are bound with the devils, as in His saying: ﴿We shall appoint for him a devil, and he will be his companion﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36], or their hands are bound to their feet. *Al-asfad* means the fetters and chains. The prepositional phrase is related to *muqarranin* or is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from its pronoun. It is said *safadtuhu safdan*, meaning: I bound him; the noun is *al-safd*. If you want to intensify, you say *saffadtuhu*.

'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

*They returned with plunder and captives, and we returned with kings in chains.*

Hassan ibn Thabit said:

*From among the captured one who ties his shackle, a falcon, who protects when he meets the battle.*

It is said *safadtuhu* and *asfadtuhu* when you give to him. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

*And I did not turn away, may you be spared the curse, with a gift (safad).*

﴿Their garments of pitch﴾. *Al-sarabil* are shirts, its singular being *sirbal*. From this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Malik:

*Bands will meet you around the Prophet, for them, of the weaving of Dawud in battle, are coats of mail.*

*Al-qatiran* is the pitch of camels with which they are smeared (*tahna'* ), i.e., their shirts are of pitch with which their skins are coated until that coating becomes like garments. Pitch was singled out because of the quick ignition of fire in it, along with the foulness of its smell.

A group said: it is copper, i.e., their shirts are of copper.

'Isa ibn 'Umar read *min qatran* with a fatha on the *qaf* and sukun on the *ta'*.

It was also read with a kasra on the *qaf* and sukun on the *ta'*, and it was read with a fatha on both the *qaf* and the *ta'*. This reading is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ya'qub. This sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

﴿And the fire will cover their faces﴾, meaning it will rise over their faces and strike them. He specified the faces because they are the most noble part of the body, and in them are the perceiving senses. This sentence is also in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

*Li-yajzia Allahu* ("so that Allah may recompense") is related to an implied verb, meaning: He will do that to them so that He may recompense every soul for what it earned of sins, i.e., a recompense corresponding to what it earned of good or evil. ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾, nothing diverts Him from it.

Its explanation has already passed.

(*Hadha balagh*) "This is a message," i.e., this which was sent down to you is a message, meaning a conveying and a sufficiency in admonition and reminder.

It has been said: the reference is to what He, glorified is He, mentioned here from His saying ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware﴾ up to ﴿swift in reckoning﴾ [Ibrahim: 42–51]; meaning this contains sufficiency apart from what the surah contains. It has been said: the reference is to the whole surah. It has been said: to the Qur'an. The meaning of *lil-nas* ("for mankind") is for the disbelievers, or for all people, according to what was said regarding His saying ﴿And warn the people﴾ [Ibrahim: 44]. (*Wa-liyunzaru bihi*) is coordinated with an implied word, meaning: so that they may be advised and so that they may be warned by it. The meaning is: so that they may be frightened by it. It was read *wa-liyanzaru* with a yaa' at the beginning and a dhal with a dot, from *nadhartu bi'l-shay'* (I knew of the thing), meaning: when you know of something and prepare for it. ﴿And so that they may know that He is only one God﴾, i.e., so that they may know by the cosmic proofs mentioned earlier the oneness of Allah, glorified is He, and that He has no partner. ﴿And so that people of understanding may take heed﴾, i.e., so that the possessors of minds may be admonished. These *lam*s (of purpose) are related to an implied word, the estimate being: "And thus We sent it down," or they are related to the mentioned *balagh* (message), meaning: a sufficiency for them so that they may be advised, warned, and know, through the proofs and demonstrations that Allah has established, His oneness, glorified is He, and that He has no partner; and so that the possessors of minds that understand and perceive may be admonished by that.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Owner of retribution﴾, that he said: "Almighty, by Allah, in His command; His scheme is firm and He gives respite. Then, when He takes vengeance, He takes it with power."

Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Thawban who said: "A man from the Jews came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Where will people be on the day the earth is changed to other than the earth?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'In darkness, beyond the Bridge.'"

Muslim also narrated, and others, from the hadith of 'Aishah who said: "I was the first to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this verse, ﴿the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾. I said: 'Where will people be that day?' He said: 'On the Sirat (bridge).'"

Al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th, and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, concerning Allah's saying ﴿the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾: 'It is a white earth, as if it were silver, in which no unlawful blood has been shed and no sin has been committed.'"

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated the like of it from him as a *mawquf* (a statement of a Companion), and al-Bayhaqi said: "The *mawquf* is more authentic."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit who said: "The Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he said: 'They have come to ask me, and I will inform them before they ask me.' ﴿The day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾. He said: (p-755) 'It is a white earth like silver.' He asked them and they said: 'A white earth like pure bread.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali, as a *marfu'* (attributed to the Prophet), something similar to what preceded from Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, as a *mawquf*, something similar to it. Something similar to this has been narrated from a group of Companions. It is established in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection upon a white land, pure, like a loaf of pure bread.'"

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verses 47–52:**

*Mukhlifa* (broken, as the one who breaks) is in the accusative because it is the object (*maf'ul*) of *tahsabanna*, and *rusulahu* (His messengers) is in the accusative because it is the object of *wa'dihi* (His promise). It is said that this is by *ittisa'* (extension, a grammatical licence of word order). The meaning is: "one who breaks His promise to His messengers," i.e., *mukhlifa rusulihi wa'dahu*.

Al-Qutaybi said: "This is from the advanced (*muqaddam*) element which is clarified by the delayed (*mu'akhkhar*), and the delayed element which is clarified by the advanced. In this respect, *mukhlifa wa'dihi rusulahu* and *mukhlifa rusulihi wa'dahu* are equivalent. Similar to what is in the verse is the poet's saying:

*You see the bull in it, its head entering the shade, while the rest of it is exposed to the sun, entirely.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He placed the promise first to make known that He does not break a promise at all, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in the appointment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 9]. Then He said *rusulahu* to indicate that if He does not break His promise to anyone, and breaking promises is not part of His nature, how then would He break it to His messengers, who are His chosen and His elite?" The "promise" here means what He, glorified is He, promised them by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers﴾ [Ghafir: 51] (p-754) and ﴿Allah has decreed, "I will surely prevail, I and My messengers"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21].

It was also read (as a *qira'ah*, a canonical recitation) *mukhlifa wa'dahu rusulihi*, with *rusulihi* in the genitive and *wa'dahu* in the accusative.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "This reading is weak, like the one who reads: *qatlu awladihim shuraka'ihim* [al-An'am: 137]." ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty (*'aziz*)﴾, Overpowering, whom no one can overpower, ﴿Owner of retribution﴾, Who takes vengeance on His enemies for His allies. This sentence is a justification (*ta'lil*) for the prohibition, and its explanation has already passed at the beginning of Al 'Imran.

﴿On the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "*Yawma* is in the accusative either as a substitute (*badal*) for *yawma ya'tihim*, or as an adverb of time (*zarf*) for the retribution." End of quote. It is also permissible that it be in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by the context, meaning: "remember," or "await." *Tabdil* (change) may be in the essence, as in: "I exchanged the dirhams for dinars," or in the attributes, as in: "I exchanged the ring for a signet." The verse may bear both meanings. It has been said: the intended meaning is the change of its attributes, and most scholars held this view. It has also been said: the change of its essence. The meaning of *wa's-samawat* ("and the heavens") is: and the heavens will be changed to other than the heavens, according to the difference that has passed.

﴿And they will come forth before Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾, meaning the servants came forth before Allah, or the wrongdoers, as the context implies, i.e., they appeared from their graves, or what they had concealed of their deeds appeared. The expression of the future in the past tense is to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, as in His saying: ﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾ [al-Kahf: 99], [Ya Sin: 51]. *Al-Wahid al-Qahhar* ("the One, the Subduer") means the One who is singular in divinity, the One of great subjugation over whoever opposes Him.

﴿And you will see the criminals that day bound together in shackles﴾. It is coordinated with *barazu* ("they came forth") or with *tubaddalu* ("is changed"). The use of the present tense is to bring the scene to mind. *Al-mujrimun* ("the criminals") are the polytheists. *Yawma'idhin* means the Day of Resurrection. *Muqarranin* means bound: either by making some of them bound with others, or they are bound with the devils, as in His saying: ﴿We shall appoint for him a devil, and he will be his companion﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36], or their hands are bound to their feet. *Al-asfad* means the fetters and chains. The prepositional phrase is related to *muqarranin* or is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from its pronoun. It is said *safadtuhu safdan*, meaning: I bound him; the noun is *al-safd*. If you want to intensify, you say *saffadtuhu*.

'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

*They returned with plunder and captives, and we returned with kings in chains.*

Hassan ibn Thabit said:

*From among the captured one who ties his shackle, a falcon, who protects when he meets the battle.*

It is said *safadtuhu* and *asfadtuhu* when you give to him. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

*And I did not turn away, may you be spared the curse, with a gift (safad).*

﴿Their garments of pitch﴾. *Al-sarabil* are shirts, its singular being *sirbal*. From this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Malik:

*Bands will meet you around the Prophet, for them, of the weaving of Dawud in battle, are coats of mail.*

*Al-qatiran* is the pitch of camels with which they are smeared (*tahna'* ), i.e., their shirts are of pitch with which their skins are coated until that coating becomes like garments. Pitch was singled out because of the quick ignition of fire in it, along with the foulness of its smell.

A group said: it is copper, i.e., their shirts are of copper.

'Isa ibn 'Umar read *min qatran* with a fatha on the *qaf* and sukun on the *ta'*.

It was also read with a kasra on the *qaf* and sukun on the *ta'*, and it was read with a fatha on both the *qaf* and the *ta'*. This reading is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ya'qub. This sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

﴿And the fire will cover their faces﴾, meaning it will rise over their faces and strike them. He specified the faces because they are the most noble part of the body, and in them are the perceiving senses. This sentence is also in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

*Li-yajzia Allahu* ("so that Allah may recompense") is related to an implied verb, meaning: He will do that to them so that He may recompense every soul for what it earned of sins, i.e., a recompense corresponding to what it earned of good or evil. ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾, nothing diverts Him from it.

Its explanation has already passed.

(*Hadha balagh*) "This is a message," i.e., this which was sent down to you is a message, meaning a conveying and a sufficiency in admonition and reminder.

It has been said: the reference is to what He, glorified is He, mentioned here from His saying ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware﴾ up to ﴿swift in reckoning﴾ [Ibrahim: 42–51]; meaning this contains sufficiency apart from what the surah contains. It has been said: the reference is to the whole surah. It has been said: to the Qur'an. The meaning of *lil-nas* ("for mankind") is for the disbelievers, or for all people, according to what was said regarding His saying ﴿And warn the people﴾ [Ibrahim: 44]. (*Wa-liyunzaru bihi*) is coordinated with an implied word, meaning: so that they may be advised and so that they may be warned by it. The meaning is: so that they may be frightened by it. It was read *wa-liyanzaru* with a yaa' at the beginning and a dhal with a dot, from *nadhartu bi'l-shay'* (I knew of the thing), meaning: when you know of something and prepare for it. ﴿And so that they may know that He is only one God﴾, i.e., so that they may know by the cosmic proofs mentioned earlier the oneness of Allah, glorified is He, and that He has no partner. ﴿And so that people of understanding may take heed﴾, i.e., so that the possessors of minds may be admonished. These *lam*s (of purpose) are related to an implied word, the estimate being: "And thus We sent it down," or they are related to the mentioned *balagh* (message), meaning: a sufficiency for them so that they may be advised, warned, and know, through the proofs and demonstrations that Allah has established, His oneness, glorified is He, and that He has no partner; and so that the possessors of minds that understand and perceive may be admonished by that.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Owner of retribution﴾, that he said: "Almighty, by Allah, in His command; His scheme is firm and He gives respite. Then, when He takes vengeance, He takes it with power."

Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Thawban who said: "A man from the Jews came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Where will people be on the day the earth is changed to other than the earth?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'In darkness, beyond the Bridge.'"

Muslim also narrated, and others, from the hadith of 'Aishah who said: "I was the first to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this verse, ﴿the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾. I said: 'Where will people be that day?' He said: 'On the Sirat (bridge).'"

*Mukhlifa* (broken, as the one who breaks) is in the accusative because it is the object (*maf'ul*) of *tahsabanna*, and *rusulahu* (His messengers) is in the accusative because it is the object of *wa'dihi* (His promise). It is said that this is by *ittisa'* (extension, a grammatical licence of word order). The meaning is: "one who breaks His promise to His messengers," i.e., *mukhlifa rusulihi wa'dahu*.

Al-Qutaybi said: "This is from the advanced (*muqaddam*) element which is clarified by the delayed (*mu'akhkhar*), and the delayed element which is clarified by the advanced. In this respect, *mukhlifa wa'dihi rusulahu* and *mukhlifa rusulihi wa'dahu* are equivalent. Similar to what is in the verse is the poet's saying:

*You see the bull in it, its head entering the shade, while the rest of it is exposed to the sun, entirely.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He placed the promise first to make known that He does not break a promise at all, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in the appointment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 9]. Then He said *rusulahu* to indicate that if He does not break His promise to anyone, and breaking promises is not part of His nature, how then would He break it to His messengers, who are His chosen and His elite?" The "promise" here means what He, glorified is He, promised them by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers﴾ [Ghafir: 51] (p-754) and ﴿Allah has decreed, "I will surely prevail, I and My messengers"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21].

It was also read (as a *qira'ah*, a canonical recitation) *mukhlifa wa'dahu rusulihi*, with *rusulihi* in the genitive and *wa'dahu* in the accusative.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "This reading is weak, like the one who reads: *qatlu awladihim shuraka'ihim* [al-An'am: 137]." ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty (*'aziz*)﴾, Overpowering, whom no one can overpower, ﴿Owner of retribution﴾, Who takes vengeance on His enemies for His allies. This sentence is a justification (*ta'lil*) for the prohibition, and its explanation has already passed at the beginning of Al 'Imran.

﴿On the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "*Yawma* is in the accusative either as a substitute (*badal*) for *yawma ya'tihim*, or as an adverb of time (*zarf*) for the retribution." End of quote. It is also permissible that it be in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by the context, meaning: "remember," or "await." *Tabdil* (change) may be in the essence, as in: "I exchanged the dirhams for dinars," or in the attributes, as in: "I exchanged the ring for a signet." The verse may bear both meanings. It has been said: the intended meaning is the change of its attributes, and most scholars held this view. It has also been said: the change of its essence. The meaning of *wa's-samawat* ("and the heavens") is: and the heavens will be changed to other than the heavens, according to the difference that has passed.

﴿And they will come forth before Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾, meaning the servants came forth before Allah, or the wrongdoers, as the context implies, i.e., they appeared from their graves, or what they had concealed of their deeds appeared. The expression of the future in the past tense is to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, as in His saying: ﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾ [al-Kahf: 99], [Ya Sin: 51]. *Al-Wahid al-Qahhar* ("the One, the Subduer") means the One who is singular in divinity, the One of great subjugation over whoever opposes Him.

﴿And you will see the criminals that day bound together in shackles﴾. It is coordinated with *barazu* ("they came forth") or with *tubaddalu* ("is changed"). The use of the present tense is to bring the scene to mind. *Al-mujrimun* ("the criminals") are the polytheists. *Yawma'idhin* means the Day of Resurrection. *Muqarranin* means bound: either by making some of them bound with others, or they are bound with the devils, as in His saying: ﴿We shall appoint for him a devil, and he will be his companion﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36], or their hands are bound to their feet. *Al-asfad* means the fetters and chains. The prepositional phrase is related to *muqarranin* or is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from its pronoun. It is said *safadtuhu safdan*, meaning: I bound him; the noun is *al-safd*. If you want to intensify, you say *saffadtuhu*.

'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

Hassan ibn Thabit said:

*From among the captured one who ties his shackle, a falcon, who protects when he meets the battle.*

It is said *safadtuhu* and *asfadtuhu* when you give to him. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

*And I did not turn away, may you be spared the curse, with a gift (safad).*

﴿Their garments of pitch﴾. *Al-sarabil* are shirts, its singular being *sirbal*. From this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Malik:

*Bands will meet you around the Prophet, for them, of the weaving of Dawud in battle, are coats of mail.*

*Al-qatiran* is the pitch of camels with which they are smeared (*tahna'* ), i.e., their shirts are of pitch with which their skins are coated until that coating becomes like garments. Pitch was singled out because of the quick ignition of fire in it, along with the foulness of its smell.

A group said: it is copper, i.e., their shirts are of copper.

'Isa ibn 'Umar read *min qatran* with a fatha on the *qaf* and sukun on the *ta'*.

It was also read with a kasra on the *qaf* and sukun on the *ta'*, and it was read with a fatha on both the *qaf* and the *ta'*. This reading is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ya'qub. This sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

﴿And the fire will cover their faces﴾, meaning it will rise over their faces and strike them. He specified the faces because they are the most noble part of the body, and in them are the perceiving senses. This sentence is also in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

*Li-yajzia Allahu* ("so that Allah may recompense") is related to an implied verb, meaning: He will do that to them so that He may recompense every soul for what it earned of sins, i.e., a recompense corresponding to what it earned of good or evil. ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾, nothing diverts Him from it.

Its explanation has already passed.

(*Hadha balagh*) "This is a message," i.e., this which was sent down to you is a message, meaning a conveying and a sufficiency in admonition and reminder.

It has been said: the reference is to what He, glorified is He, mentioned here from His saying ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware﴾ up to ﴿swift in reckoning﴾ [Ibrahim: 42–51]; meaning this contains sufficiency apart from what the surah contains. It has been said: the reference is to the whole surah. It has been said: to the Qur'an. The meaning of *lil-nas* ("for mankind") is for the disbelievers, or for all people, according to what was said regarding His saying ﴿And warn the people﴾ [Ibrahim: 44]. (*Wa-liyunzaru bihi*) is coordinated with an implied word, meaning: so that they may be advised and so that they may be warned by it. The meaning is: so that they may be frightened by it. It was read *wa-liyanzaru* with a yaa' at the beginning and a dhal with a dot, from *nadhartu bi'l-shay'* (I knew of the thing), meaning: when you know of something and prepare for it. ﴿And so that they may know that He is only one God﴾, i.e., so that they may know by the cosmic proofs mentioned earlier the oneness of Allah, glorified is He, and that He has no partner. ﴿And so that people of understanding may take heed﴾, i.e., so that the possessors of minds may be admonished. These *lam*s (of purpose) are related to an implied word, the estimate being: "And thus We sent it down," or they are related to the mentioned *balagh* (message), meaning: a sufficiency for them so that they may be advised, warned, and know, through the proofs and demonstrations that Allah has established, His oneness, glorified is He, and that He has no partner; and so that the possessors of minds that understand and perceive may be admonished by that.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Owner of retribution﴾, that he said: "Almighty, by Allah, in His command; His scheme is firm and He gives respite. Then, when He takes vengeance, He takes it with power."

Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Thawban who said: "A man from the Jews came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Where will people be on the day the earth is changed to other than the earth?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'In darkness, beyond the Bridge.'"

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 14, verses 47–52:**

*Mukhlifa* (broken, as the one who breaks) is in the accusative because it is the object (*maf'ul*) of *tahsabanna*, and *rusulahu* (His messengers) is in the accusative because it is the object of *wa'dihi* (His promise). It is said that this is by *ittisa'* (extension, a grammatical licence of word order). The meaning is: "one who breaks His promise to His messengers," i.e., *mukhlifa rusulihi wa'dahu*.

Al-Qutaybi said: "This is from the advanced (*muqaddam*) element which is clarified by the delayed (*mu'akhkhar*), and the delayed element which is clarified by the advanced. In this respect, *mukhlifa wa'dihi rusulahu* and *mukhlifa rusulihi wa'dahu* are equivalent. Similar to what is in the verse is the poet's saying:

*You see the bull in it, its head entering the shade, while the rest of it is exposed to the sun, entirely.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He placed the promise first to make known that He does not break a promise at all, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in the appointment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 9]. Then He said *rusulahu* to indicate that if He does not break His promise to anyone, and breaking promises is not part of His nature, how then would He break it to His messengers, who are His chosen and His elite?" The "promise" here means what He, glorified is He, promised them by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers﴾ [Ghafir: 51] (p-754) and ﴿Allah has decreed, "I will surely prevail, I and My messengers"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21].

It was also read (as a *qira'ah*, a canonical recitation) *mukhlifa wa'dahu rusulihi*, with *rusulihi* in the genitive and *wa'dahu* in the accusative.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "This reading is weak, like the one who reads: *qatlu awladihim shuraka'ihim* [al-An'am: 137]." ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty (*'aziz*)﴾, Overpowering, whom no one can overpower, ﴿Owner of retribution﴾, Who takes vengeance on His enemies for His allies. This sentence is a justification (*ta'lil*) for the prohibition, and its explanation has already passed at the beginning of Al 'Imran.

﴿On the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "*Yawma* is in the accusative either as a substitute (*badal*) for *yawma ya'tihim*, or as an adverb of time (*zarf*) for the retribution." End of quote. It is also permissible that it be in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by the context, meaning: "remember," or "await." *Tabdil* (change) may be in the essence, as in: "I exchanged the dirhams for dinars," or in the attributes, as in: "I exchanged the ring for a signet." The verse may bear both meanings. It has been said: the intended meaning is the change of its attributes, and most scholars held this view. It has also been said: the change of its essence. The meaning of *wa's-samawat* ("and the heavens") is: and the heavens will be changed to other than the heavens, according to the difference that has passed.

﴿And they will come forth before Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾, meaning the servants came forth before Allah, or the wrongdoers, as the context implies, i.e., they appeared from their graves, or what they had concealed of their deeds appeared. The expression of the future in the past tense is to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, as in His saying: ﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾ [al-Kahf: 99], [Ya Sin: 51]. *Al-Wahid al-Qahhar* ("the One, the Subduer") means the One who is singular in divinity, the One of great subjugation over whoever opposes Him.

﴿And you will see the criminals that day bound together in shackles﴾. It is coordinated with *barazu* ("they came forth") or with *tubaddalu* ("is changed"). The use of the present tense is to bring the scene to mind. *Al-mujrimun* ("the criminals") are the polytheists. *Yawma'idhin* means the Day of Resurrection. *Muqarranin* means bound: either by making some of them bound with others, or they are bound with the devils, as in His saying: ﴿We shall appoint for him a devil, and he will be his companion﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36], or their hands are bound to their feet. *Al-asfad* means the fetters and chains. The prepositional phrase is related to *muqarranin* or is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from its pronoun. It is said *safadtuhu safdan*, meaning: I bound him; the noun is *al-safd*. If you want to intensify, you say *saffadtuhu*.

'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

*They returned with plunder and captives, and we returned with kings in chains.*

Hassan ibn Thabit said:

*From among the captured one who ties his shackle, a falcon, who protects when he meets the battle.*

It is said *safadtuhu* and *asfadtuhu* when you give to him. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

*And I did not turn away, may you be spared the curse, with a gift (safad).*

﴿Their garments of pitch﴾. *Al-sarabil* are shirts, its singular being *sirbal*. From this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Malik:

*Bands will meet you around the Prophet, for them, of the weaving of Dawud in battle, are coats of mail.*

*Al-qatiran* is the pitch of camels with which they are smeared (*tahna'* ), i.e., their shirts are of pitch with which their skins are coated until that coating becomes like garments. Pitch was singled out because of the quick ignition of fire in it, along with the foulness of its smell.

A group said: it is copper, i.e., their shirts are of copper.

'Isa ibn 'Umar read *min qatran* with a fatha on the *qaf* and sukun on the *ta'*.

It was also read with a kasra on the *qaf* and sukun on the *ta'*, and it was read with a fatha on both the *qaf* and the *ta'*. This reading is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ya'qub. This sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

﴿And the fire will cover their faces﴾, meaning it will rise over their faces and strike them. He specified the faces because they are the most noble part of the body, and in them are the perceiving senses. This sentence is also in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

*Li-yajzia Allahu* ("so that Allah may recompense") is related to an implied verb, meaning: He will do that to them so that He may recompense every soul for what it earned of sins, i.e., a recompense corresponding to what it earned of good or evil. ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾, nothing diverts Him from it.

Its explanation has already passed.

(*Hadha balagh*) "This is a message," i.e., this which was sent down to you is a message, meaning a conveying and a sufficiency in admonition and reminder.

It has been said: the reference is to what He, glorified is He, mentioned here from His saying ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware﴾ up to ﴿swift in reckoning﴾ [Ibrahim: 42–51]; meaning this contains sufficiency apart from what the surah contains. It has been said: the reference is to the whole surah. It has been said: to the Qur'an. The meaning of *lil-nas* ("for mankind") is for the disbelievers, or for all people, according to what was said regarding His saying ﴿And warn the people﴾ [Ibrahim: 44]. (*Wa-liyunzaru bihi*) is coordinated with an implied word, meaning: so that they may be advised and so that they may be warned by it. The meaning is: so that they may be frightened by it. It was read *wa-liyanzaru* with a yaa' at the beginning and a dhal with a dot, from *nadhartu bi'l-shay'* (I knew of the thing), meaning: when you know of something and prepare for it. ﴿And so that they may know that He is only one God﴾, i.e., so that they may know by the cosmic proofs mentioned earlier the oneness of Allah, glorified is He, and that He has no partner. ﴿And so that people of understanding may take heed﴾, i.e., so that the possessors of minds may be admonished. These *lam*s (of purpose) are related to an implied word, the estimate being: "And thus We sent it down," or they are related to the mentioned *balagh* (message), meaning: a sufficiency for them so that they may be advised, warned, and know, through the proofs and demonstrations that Allah has established, His oneness, glorified is He, and that He has no partner; and so that the possessors of minds that understand and perceive may be admonished by that.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Owner of retribution﴾, that he said: "Almighty, by Allah, in His command; His scheme is firm and He gives respite. Then, when He takes vengeance, He takes it with power."

Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Thawban who said: "A man from the Jews came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Where will people be on the day the earth is changed to other than the earth?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'In darkness, beyond the Bridge.'"

Muslim also narrated, and others, from the hadith of 'Aishah who said: "I was the first to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this verse, ﴿the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾. I said: 'Where will people be that day?' He said: 'On the Sirat (bridge).'"

Al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th, and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, concerning Allah's saying ﴿the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾: 'It is a white earth, as if it were silver, in which no unlawful blood has been shed and no sin has been committed.'"

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated the like of it from him as a *mawquf* (a statement of a Companion), and al-Bayhaqi said: "The *mawquf* is more authentic."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit who said: "The Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he said: 'They have come to ask me, and I will inform them before they ask me.' ﴿The day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾. He said: (p-755) 'It is a white earth like silver.' He asked them and they said: 'A white earth like pure bread.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali, as a *marfu'* (attributed to the Prophet), something similar to what preceded from Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, as a *mawquf*, something similar to it. Something similar to this has been narrated from a group of Companions. It is established in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection upon a white land, pure, like a loaf of pure bread.'"

Also in the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The earth on the Day of Resurrection will be one loaf, which the Mighty One will turn over in His hand," the hadith.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿bound together in shackles﴾, that he said: "The fetters (*kubul*)."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah, regarding ﴿in shackles﴾, that he said: "The bonds and chains."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: "In chains."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿in shackles﴾, that he said: "In bondage."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿their garments﴾, that he said: "Their shirts."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Zayd the like of it.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan, regarding His saying ﴿of pitch﴾, that he said: "The pitch of camels."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Ikrimah regarding the verse, that he said: "This is pitch which is smeared on them until it catches fire."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "It is molten copper."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he read ﴿of pitch﴾ and said: "*Al-qatr* is brass, and *al-an* is the hot."

Abu 'Ubayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Ikrimah something similar.

Muslim and others narrated from Abu Malik al-Ash'ari who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The wailing woman, if she does not repent before her death, will be raised on the Day of Resurrection wearing a garment of pitch and a coat of scab." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd, regarding His saying ﴿This is a message for mankind﴾, that he said: "The Qur'an." And ﴿and so that they may be warned by it﴾, he said: "The Qur'an."
